c12_acc_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_acc_ch01.scenario: On a summer internship, a Class 12 student lends ₹50,000 to a friend's cloud-kitchen and takes 10% of monthly profits instead of fixed interest. When the kitchen defaults on a supplier's bill, the supplier claims she is a partner and must pay up.
c12_acc_ch01.prompt: Is she liable as a partner?

options.text: No — Section 6 of the Partnership Act says a lender whose return varies with profits is not a partner; she has no mutual agency, so profit-sharing alone doesn't make her one.
options.outcome: Profit share is only one feature; without the authority to act for and bind the firm, there's no partnership — the supplier can't touch her.

options.text: Yes — anyone who takes a share of business profits is a partner, so she's jointly and severally liable for the debt.
options.outcome: That over-generalises profit-sharing: the Act explicitly excludes lenders paid from profits, and she cannot bind the firm.

options.text: No — the firm was never registered, so no partnership can legally exist and nobody is liable.
options.outcome: Registration isn't what creates a partnership — but she still isn't a partner because mutual agency is missing, not because paperwork is missing.

c12_acc_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_acc_ch02.scenario: Three friends run a college fest food-stall venture sharing profits 3:2:1. They admit a new baker for a 1/6 share, and their deal says she takes 1/12 from the first friend and 1/12 from the second. The treasurer assumes the 'sacrificing ratio' is simply the old 3:2:1.
c12_acc_ch02.prompt: How should the sacrifice actually be shared?

options.text: Follow the agreement: she acquires equally from two partners, so the sacrificing ratio is 1:1 — the sacrificing ratio is whatever proportion the new share is actually taken in, not the old ratio.
options.outcome: Sacrificing ratio = the ratio in which old partners give up share. When the acquisition split is specified, that split IS the sacrificing ratio; old ratio is only the default.

options.text: Sacrificing ratio is always the old profit-sharing ratio, so goodwill gets credited 3:2:1.
options.outcome: That default applies only when the deed is silent on how the new partner's share is acquired — here an explicit 1:1 split overrides it.

options.text: Divide the new partner's 1/6 share by three — every old partner must sacrifice equally.
options.outcome: Nothing forces equal sacrifice; the new partner's share comes only from those who actually give it up, per their agreement.

c12_acc_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_acc_ch03.scenario: A student-run print shop has three partners sharing 5:3:2. The third partner retires and the other two agree to share future profits 3:2. The junior accountant adjusts the retiring partner's ₹12,000 goodwill share by debiting the continuing partners in 3:2.

options.text: No — goodwill is compensated in the gaining ratio (new share minus old share): A gains 6/10−5/10=1/10 and B gains 4/10−3/10=1/10, so it's 1:1, i.e. ₹6,000 each.
options.outcome: The gaining ratio is derived from how much each continuing partner's share rose, not from the new profit-sharing ratio itself.

options.text: Yes — the new profit-sharing ratio 3:2 is the gaining ratio, so debit ₹7,200 and ₹4,800.
options.outcome: That confuses the new ratio with the gaining ratio — the classic board-exam trap; gains must be computed as New minus Old for each partner.

options.text: Split it equally anyway — retirement always means equal gains for continuing partners.
options.outcome: Equal gains happen here by coincidence of the numbers; the rule is gain = new share − old share, which is often unequal.

c12_acc_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_acc_ch04.scenario: A two-partner baking-supplies firm loses one partner to retirement; the survivor brings in a new partner and keeps trading. Their accounts intern opens a Realisation Account 'to record the retirement'.

options.text: No — the business continues, so this is only dissolution of partnership (reconstitution); assets and liabilities are revalued through a Revaluation Account, not sold off.
options.outcome: Realisation Account is for firm closure — assets realised, liabilities paid, business ended. Retirement with continuation just re-slices the agreement.

options.text: Yes — any change in the partners means the firm is dissolved, so assets must be realised and liabilities paid.
options.outcome: That collapses the legal distinction: admission, retirement or death end the agreement, not the business — only closure dissolves the firm.

options.text: Open no account at all — a retirement is a personal matter between partners and the books stay untouched.
options.outcome: Reconstitution still needs accounting: assets/liabilities get revalued so the continuing firm carries fair values.

c12_acc_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_acc_ch05.scenario: A college entrepreneur needs ₹50 lakh for her D2C brand. A risk-averse uncle will invest only for a fixed return and wants no say in decisions; a friend wants voting rights and accepts that dividends will vary with profits.
c12_acc_ch05.prompt: How should she match instruments to investors?

options.text: Issue preference shares to the uncle — fixed dividend paid before equity and priority on repayment, normally no voting — and equity shares to the friend, who gets votes on every resolution and a residual, variable dividend.
options.outcome: Each share class fits the investor: preference is a hybrid for conservative fixed-return money; equity is ownership with control and residual risk-return.

options.text: Give the uncle debentures instead — they're identical to preference shares since both carry a fixed return.
options.outcome: They're not identical: preference dividend is an appropriation of profit, not a charge like interest, and preference shareholders are members, not creditors — skipping their dividend doesn't trigger bankruptcy.

options.text: Issue equity to the uncle too — all shareholders get the same dividend anyway.
options.outcome: Equity dividend isn't fixed and comes only after preference dividend; in a lean year he'd get nothing despite wanting a fixed return.

c12_acc_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_acc_ch06.scenario: An EV startup raises money through debentures carrying a second charge on factory land already mortgaged to an earlier debenture issue. A trainee accountant files these 'Second Debentures' under Unsecured Loans in the draft balance sheet.

options.text: No — 'secured' asks whether a charge on assets exists, 'first/second' is the ranking among charges; these debentures have a charge, so they're Secured Second Debentures.
options.outcome: Security and priority are separate classification bases — a debenture can be secured yet rank second in repayment order.

options.text: Yes — second in line for repayment means unsecured, since the first charge holders get paid ahead of them.
options.outcome: Ranking lower in priority doesn't remove the charge; they're still secured creditors, just behind the first charge.

options.text: Reclassify them as shareholders' funds — debenture holders are part-owners of the company.
options.outcome: Debenture holders are creditors with a contractual fixed interest and repayment claim — never owners, regardless of security.

c12_acc_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_acc_ch07.scenario: At a fintech internship, a student drafts the startup's first annual balance sheet in the old sole-proprietor style — horizontal layout, one merged 'Capital' line. The founder waves it through: 'the totals match, that's what matters.'
c12_acc_ch07.prompt: Will this pass as the company's financial statements?

options.text: No — Section 129 read with Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes a vertical format with current/non-current splits and separate disclosure of share capital and each reserve; matching totals don't cure a wrong format.
options.outcome: Company statements are statutory documents for absentee shareholders, lenders and regulators — the mandated structure is what makes them comparable across firms.

options.text: Yes — a balance sheet is correct whenever assets equal liabilities plus capital, whatever the layout.
options.outcome: For a company, presentation is a legal requirement, not a style choice; aggregating 'Capital' hides equity composition and liquidity.

options.text: Only add a Cash Flow Statement on top — the two Class 11-style statements plus cash flow make a complete set.
options.outcome: A complete set also needs the Statement of Changes in Equity and Notes to Accounts, all in Schedule III form — not just three proprietorship-era statements.

c12_acc_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_acc_ch08.scenario: Interning at a bank's loan desk, a student appraises a textile firm: Current Ratio 2:1 (comfortable), but inventory is ₹50 lakh of the ₹80 lakh current assets and the Quick Ratio is 0.75:1 against an industry norm of 1:1. Her manager asks whether to sanction a ₹20 lakh working-capital loan.
c12_acc_ch08.prompt: What does the analysis actually say?

options.text: Flag the divergence: the current ratio is inventory-driven while the quick ratio sits below industry — sanction only with conditions like inventory hypothecation and turnover monitoring.
options.outcome: Ratios are whistle-blowers, not verdicts: interpretation against benchmarks and composition turns numbers into a decision.

options.text: Approve unconditionally — a 2:1 current ratio meets the textbook norm, so liquidity is fine.
options.outcome: That's calculation, not analysis: 62% of the current assets are inventory, which the quick ratio exposes as weak immediate liquidity.

options.text: Reject outright — a quick ratio below 1:1 means the firm is insolvent.
options.outcome: A single sub-norm ratio signals risk, not death; analysis weighs the whole picture — strong gross current cover plus slow-moving stock argues for a conditional sanction, not a blanket no.

c12_acc_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_acc_ch09.scenario: Helping in his uncle's bakery over the break, a student sees the P&L show ₹50,000 profit — but the bank balance has fallen. The uncle suspects the accountant fudged the books.

options.text: Profit is accrual-based, cash is not: credit sales, a cash purchase of a new oven (investing outflow) and a loan repayment (financing outflow) can shrink cash while profit stays positive — a cash flow statement would show it.
options.outcome: AS-3 splits flows into operating, investing and financing so exactly this mystery — profit up, cash down — gets explained.

options.text: The accountant must be wrong — profit and bank balance are the same thing measured two ways.
options.outcome: Profit counts revenue when earned, not when cash arrives; non-cash charges like depreciation and credit sales decouple the two legitimately.

options.text: The oven bought by issuing shares to the supplier should appear as an investing outflow in the cash flow statement.
options.outcome: No cash moved — AS-3 excludes non-cash investing/financing transactions from the statement (they're disclosed elsewhere), so it can't explain the cash drop.

c12_biotech_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch01.scenario: For a biotech-lab summer project, a student team wants E. coli to propagate a human gene. Their mentor hands them a plasmid carrying an ampicillin-resistance gene but no origin of replication that E. coli can read, and says 'just transform it in.'
c12_biotech_ch01.prompt: Will the plasmid be maintained in the bacteria?

options.text: No — a cloning vector needs an origin of replication recognised by the host plus a selectable marker, cloning sites and small size; without a compatible ori it can't replicate and is lost at cell division, marker or not.
options.outcome: Host-vector compatibility is the core rule: the host's replication machinery must recognise the vector's ori, and the marker only selects cells that actually took up a replicating vector.

options.text: Yes — the antibiotic marker lets you select transformed cells, and selection alone keeps the plasmid going.
options.outcome: Selection finds cells carrying the plasmid but can't maintain it; without a functional ori the plasmid never replicates and gets diluted out.

options.text: Yes, if they add a strong promoter — that's what makes any plasmid a cloning vector.
options.outcome: Promoters belong to expression vectors; a cloning vector's essentials are ori, selectable marker, cloning sites and small size.

c12_biotech_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch02.scenario: In a school lab practical, a team must insert a DNA fragment into a vector. They can cut both with EcoRI, which leaves 5′-AATT sticky overhangs, or SmaI, which cuts dead centre and leaves blunt ends. A teammate votes SmaI 'because blunt ends are simpler'.
c12_biotech_ch02.prompt: Which enzyme gives the better cloning strategy?

options.text: EcoRI — sticky ends base-pair across the insert–vector junction, stabilising it and making ligation 10–100× more efficient; they can also enforce insert orientation.
options.outcome: Cohesive ends turn a random collision into a matched join; blunt-end ligation works but is far less efficient and orientation-free.

options.text: SmaI — blunt ends join any fragment to any vector, so ligation is simpler and just as efficient.
options.outcome: Blunt ends have no complementary overhangs to anneal, so ligase works far slower and the insert can go in backwards.

options.text: It doesn't matter — any restriction enzyme cutting DNA at a defined site is equally good for cloning.
options.outcome: Cleavage geometry differs: Type II enzymes cutting within their palindrome give sticky ends, central cutters give blunt — and end type drives ligation success.

c12_biotech_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch03.scenario: A student team's science-exhibition project aims to get E. coli to produce a human hormone whose gene has four introns. They plan to cut the whole gene straight out of human genomic DNA and ligate it into a bacterial plasmid.
c12_biotech_ch03.prompt: Will bacteria translate it into functional protein?

options.text: No — clone cDNA made from the tissue's mRNA instead: E. coli has no spliceosome, so introns retained from genomic DNA wreck the message; cDNA is already spliced and directly translatable.
options.outcome: A 'complete' gene isn't an expressible one in bacteria — the intron-free cDNA is what the host can actually turn into protein.

options.text: Yes — the genomic copy is the complete gene, and a complete gene must give the complete protein.
options.outcome: Eukaryotic introns need spliceosome removal, which bacteria can't do; the transcript would carry non-coding inserts and fold into junk.

options.text: Skip the vector — just PCR the gene; PCR and gene cloning both amplify DNA so they're interchangeable.
options.outcome: PCR is a cell-free reaction giving a tube of amplicons; cloning needs a vector, a host and transformation to yield a propagatable recombinant organism.

c12_biotech_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch04.scenario: A biotech startup interns a student on their insulin project. The plan on the whiteboard: express the full human preproinsulin sequence as one polypeptide in E. coli and 'let the bacteria secrete mature insulin into the medium'.

options.text: E. coli has no ER or Golgi — it can't cleave the signal peptide or C-peptide or form disulfide bonds; express the A and B chains separately as fusions, cleave them off, and refold oxidatively.
options.outcome: That's the Humulin strategy: bacteria transcribe and translate fine but can't do eukaryotic post-translational processing.

options.text: The plan is sound — E. coli secretes recombinant human proteins into the medium the way human cells do.
options.outcome: Bacteria lack a secretory pathway for complex eukaryotic proteins; the precursor would sit unprocessed, likely as inclusion bodies.

options.text: It only needs a stronger promoter — low yield, not processing, is the bottleneck.
options.outcome: More expression makes more unprocessed precursor, not more insulin; the defect is the missing processing machinery.

c12_biotech_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch05.scenario: For a bioinformatics club poster, a student finds that onion's genome (~16,000 Mb) is five times the human genome (~3,200 Mb) — and declares onions must be five times 'more complex' than people.
c12_biotech_ch05.prompt: Does the data support her claim?

options.text: No — genome size (C-value) tracks non-coding and repetitive DNA, not gene count: onion packs ~30,000 genes into 16,000 Mb while humans fit ~20,000 into 3,200 Mb; rice even beats humans on gene number with a far smaller genome.
options.outcome: The C-value paradox: complexity lives in regulation and splicing, not raw DNA tonnage — gene density, not genome size, is the meaningful comparison.

options.text: Yes — a genome is just the sum of an organism's genes, so five times the DNA means roughly five times the genes.
options.outcome: Genome ≠ gene set: it also holds introns, regulatory regions, repeats and organellar DNA, which dominate eukaryotic size differences.

options.text: No — but only because the human nuclear chromosomes were counted without mitochondrial DNA, which would close the gap.
options.outcome: Organellar DNA is part of the genome but tiny; even including it, the paradox stands — size still fails to predict gene number.

c12_biotech_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch06.scenario: Interning at a tissue-culture nursery, a student is told to clone a rare orchid. 'Every plant cell is totipotent,' he reasons, and harvests mature xylem vessel strands from the stem as his explant.
c12_biotech_ch06.prompt: Will this explant regenerate a plant?

options.text: No — totipotency needs a living, nucleated cell that can dedifferentiate and re-enter the cell cycle; mature xylem vessels are dead, enucleate and lignified. Use living parenchyma or mesophyll tissue.
options.outcome: Haberlandt's 'theoretically all cells' has limits: cell viability, genotype and epigenetic state decide whether the potential can actually be expressed.

options.text: Yes — totipotency means any plant cell can always regenerate a whole plant, so xylem works.
options.outcome: Steward's carrot proof used living phloem cells; dead, nucleus-free cells have nothing left to reprogram.

options.text: No — but only because xylem lacks chloroplasts; a cell with chlorophyll can always regenerate.
options.outcome: Chloroplasts aren't the criterion — a living nucleus and competent cytoplasm are; plenty of non-photosynthetic tissues regenerate fine.

c12_biotech_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch07.scenario: A nursery intern is asked to run the shoot-multiplication stage for banana plantlets. The medium she prepares is rich in auxin but low in cytokinin — and the cultures keep sprouting roots instead of multiplying shoots.
c12_biotech_ch07.prompt: What went wrong, and what's the fix?

options.text: The hormone ratio is inverted: shoot multiplication (Stage II) needs high cytokinin:auxin; a high auxin:cytokinin mix triggers rooting — that's Stage III's job.
options.outcome: Skoog–Miller logic runs the whole protocol: cytokinin-heavy drives shoots, auxin-heavy drives roots, and hardening uses none — matching stage to ratio fixes it.

options.text: Nothing — auxin is the shoot hormone, so the shoots will multiply once the dose kicks in.
options.outcome: That's the classic swap: auxin promotes rooting and callus; cytokinin is what pushes shoot buds to proliferate.

options.text: The cultures failed because micropropagation genetically modifies the plant and the cells are rejecting the foreign genes.
options.outcome: No foreign DNA is inserted — micropropagation is clonal vegetative propagation; hormones only redirect expression of existing genes.

c12_biotech_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch08.scenario: During a pharma-lab internship, a student watches a liver-cell line clear a new drug in a toxicity screen. She proposes the company skip animal studies entirely: 'it's the same cells — the dish tells us everything.'
c12_biotech_ch08.prompt: Can cell-culture data alone clear the drug?

options.text: No — culture gives controlled, reproducible screening on a homogeneous population, but it can't reproduce whole-body pharmacokinetics, immune responses or inter-organ metabolism, so regulators still need in vivo data.
options.outcome: Cell culture is a reductionist model, not a replica: great for ranking compounds early, blind to effects that need a whole organism.

options.text: Yes — the same cells behave identically in a flask as in the organism, so a clean screen means a safe drug.
options.outcome: In vitro cells lose systemic regulation — hormones, circulation, immune cells — and can miss a drug that's only toxic after the body metabolises it.

options.text: No — cultured cells are too artificial to be useful at all; go straight to animal testing.
options.outcome: That throws away real advantages: no ethical clearance, reproducible dose-response curves and scalable screening make culture the right first filter.

c12_biotech_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch09.scenario: A private clinic advertises to a heart-attack patient: 'Bone-marrow stem cell injections will regrow your damaged heart muscle.' The family asks the student, who just studied stem cells, whether the claim holds up.
c12_biotech_ch09.prompt: Can bone-marrow HSCs rebuild heart muscle?

options.text: No — hematopoietic stem cells are multipotent: they self-renew but differentiate only into blood lineages; making cardiomyocytes is outside their potency, so the ad overpromises.
options.outcome: Potency is lineage-restricted for adult stem cells — 'stem cell' on a brochure doesn't mean 'can become anything'; heart repair needs other cell types.

options.text: Yes — stem cells self-renew indefinitely, so injected cells will just keep dividing until the heart is rebuilt.
options.outcome: Self-renewal without potency is mere proliferation — and uncontrolled self-renewal is closer to cancer than repair.

options.text: Yes — the injected cells are pluripotent, so they can form every tissue including a placenta.
options.outcome: Even pluripotent cells can't form extra-embryonic tissues — and adult marrow cells aren't pluripotent anyway; the claim stacks two errors.

c12_biotech_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch10.scenario: A vaccine manufacturer wants to scale up Hepatitis B surface antigen for a recombinant vaccine. A junior engineer suggests switching the production host from yeast to E. coli 'for faster growth and higher yield'.
c12_biotech_ch10.prompt: Is E. coli the right host here?

options.text: No — HBsAg must form disulfide bonds and self-assemble into virus-like particles, which needs eukaryotic folding machinery; in E. coli it lands in inclusion bodies and never becomes immunogenic VLPs.
options.outcome: Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) performs the post-translational processing that makes the antigen fold and assemble correctly — yield is useless without conformation.

options.text: Yes — E. coli is the standard cloning host and its higher yield means more vaccine per batch.
options.outcome: High yield of misfolded antigen is worthless; the immunogenic epitopes depend on correct folding and particle assembly bacteria can't do.

options.text: Yes — the vaccine works by delivering the HBsAg gene into the patient's cells anyway, so the production host barely matters.
options.outcome: That confuses a recombinant vaccine with a DNA vaccine: the shot contains yeast-made protein VLPs, not plasmid DNA.

c12_biotech_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch11.scenario: At an agri-biotech internship, the team must put a drought-tolerance gene into wheat. A colleague insists on Agrobacterium-mediated transformation because 'it always gives clean, single-copy inserts' — but weeks of co-cultivation keep failing.
c12_biotech_ch11.prompt: How should they deliver the gene?

options.text: Switch to biolistics — wheat is a monocot that poorly induces Agrobacterium's vir genes, so the gene gun's physical DNA delivery bypasses the host-range barrier, accepting messier, multi-copy inserts as the trade-off.
options.outcome: Agrobacterium's clean T-DNA transfer is preferred for dicots; monocots' weak wound response makes particle bombardment the practical route.

options.text: Persist with Agrobacterium — it always produces single-copy inserts and single copy is what regulators demand.
options.outcome: The biological block isn't about insert quality — monocots barely trigger vir induction, so T-DNA transfer barely happens; biolistics exists precisely for this.

options.text: Agrobacterium injects its whole Ti plasmid into the plant, so moving the gene to a different spot on the plasmid will fix it.
options.outcome: Only the T-DNA segment between the border repeats is transferred; the vir genes and backbone stay in the bacterium — repositioning outside the borders won't help.

c12_biotech_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch12.scenario: For a student startup pitch, a team plans to turn the canteen's waste cooking oil into biodiesel. Their pitch deck says the oil will be 'fermented by yeast, then distilled — same as making bioethanol'.
c12_biotech_ch12.prompt: Does the process description hold up?

options.text: No — biodiesel comes from trans-esterification of triglycerides with methanol/ethanol and a catalyst, giving fatty-acid methyl esters plus glycerol; yeast fermentation of sugars makes bioethanol, a different pathway.
options.outcome: Both are biofuels but the biochemistry differs — grouping by product category instead of process is the pitch-killing error.

options.text: Yes — biodiesel and bioalcohol are both biofuels, so they're made by the same fermentation process.
options.outcome: One is an esterification of fats, the other a fermentation of sugars; the shared label 'biofuel' hides different feedstocks and chemistry.

options.text: Yes — and anyway environmental biotechnology is just bioremediation, so the pitch barely counts as biotech.
options.outcome: The sector covers prevention too — biofuels, biogas and biodegradable products are core environmental biotech, not only pollution cleanup.

c12_biotech_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c12_biotech_ch13.scenario: A family WhatsApp group gets a forward claiming 'GMO foods cause infertility' over a photo of a tumour-covered rat. An aunt wants to blast it to every group she knows; the Class 12 biotech student is asked to weigh in.

options.text: Check the source and the consensus before sharing — that image traces to a retracted rat study, while major science academies affirm approved GM foods; and remember opposition is driven by trust and values, not just facts.
options.outcome: Perception ≠ ignorance: media framing, corporate distrust and cultural values shape GMO attitudes, so engagement means dialogue plus verifiable evidence — not a forwarded scare.

options.text: Forward it — until scientists prove zero risk, treating every claim as probably true is the safe move.
options.outcome: That mistakes an outlier for consensus; 'no evidence of harm' from decades of data beats a retracted, sensational study.

options.text: Reply with a fact-sheet only — people oppose GMOs purely because they don't understand the science.
options.outcome: That's the deficit model: evidence shows facts alone can even polarise — distrust of regulators and 'unnaturalness' concerns need addressing too.

c12_bio_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch01.scenario: A banana grower's entire plantation — all raised from suckers of one parent plant — gets wiped out by a new fungus, while a nearby patch grown from seeds shows mixed survival. He asks the agri-student intern why his field had zero resistant plants.

options.text: Suckers are asexual clones — genetically identical, so no variation in resistance existed; the seed-grown patch came through meiosis and fertilisation, so some plants carried resistance combinations.
options.outcome: Clonal propagation is fast and uniform, but uniformity means one pathogen can fell the whole field; variation is the insurance sexual reproduction buys.

options.text: The fungus was simply too strong — the mode of reproduction makes no difference to whether plants resist disease.
options.outcome: Resistance is genetic; with identical genomes every plant shares the same susceptibility, so reproduction mode is exactly what decided the outcome.

options.text: Asexual reproduction is a primitive, failed strategy — the farmer should never have used suckers at all.
options.outcome: In stable conditions cloning is cheap and rapid — it's the standard for uniform crops; the real cost is losing variation for new threats, not that the mode is 'primitive'.

c12_bio_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch02.scenario: On a herbarium field project, a student presses a small greenish flower that has no petals at all but does carry both stamens and carpels. She labels the sheet 'incomplete flower, therefore unisexual'.

options.text: Half right — missing a whorl makes it incomplete, but both androecium and gynoecium are present, so it's still bisexual; completeness counts whorls, sexuality counts reproductive organs.
options.outcome: The two terms operate at different levels — a flower can be incomplete yet bisexual, and that distinction decides pollination questions.

options.text: Correct — a flower missing a whorl is unisexual because 'incomplete' and 'unisexual' describe the same thing.
options.outcome: That conflates whorl count with sex condition; the flower has functional male and female organs, so it is bisexual.

options.text: It can't be bisexual — without petals there's no corolla, and bisexual flowers need all four whorls.
options.outcome: Bisexuality needs only both reproductive whorls; petals are for attracting pollinators, not for determining sex.

c12_bio_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch03.scenario: A relative is anxious before a vasectomy, having heard 'you'll produce no semen at all and your manhood hormones will crash'. His niece, a biology student, is asked what's actually true.
c12_bio_ch03.prompt: What does cutting the vas deferens really do?

options.text: It blocks sperm transport only: semen volume barely drops since most fluid comes from the seminal vesicles and prostate, and testosterone keeps flowing because Leydig cells release it straight into blood.
options.outcome: Sperm are only a small part of ejaculate and testicular hormones don't travel down the vas — so contraception happens without ending semen or androgens.

options.text: He's right to worry — all of semen travels through the vas deferens, so cutting it means no ejaculate.
options.outcome: The vas carries only sperm; accessory gland secretions join downstream via their own ducts, so semen volume stays nearly normal.

options.text: Testosterone will drop because the testes are disconnected from the body.
options.outcome: Testosterone enters the bloodstream at the testis, not the duct system — spermatogenesis even continues, with sperm phagocytosed in the epididymis.

c12_bio_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch04.scenario: A student volunteers at a community reproductive-health camp that offers only condom distribution and STI screening. The organiser declares: 'Disease-free plus contraception — that's reproductive health covered.'
c12_bio_ch04.prompt: Does the camp meet the WHO definition?

options.text: No — reproductive health also means mental and social well-being and the freedom to decide if, when and how often to reproduce; add counselling on consent, menstrual hygiene and infertility support.
options.outcome: The WHO definition is rights-based and holistic: absence of disease is necessary but a person can be disease-free yet coerced, stigmatised or uninformed.

options.text: Yes — eliminate infections and supply contraceptives and reproductive health is achieved.
options.outcome: That covers only physical well-being; a population could be STI-free yet face child marriage or zero contraceptive choice — still unhealthy by WHO standards.

options.text: Yes — reproductive health is basically family planning, and contraceptive supply is family planning.
options.outcome: Family planning is one slice; the definition spans physical, mental and social well-being plus reproductive autonomy.

c12_bio_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch05.scenario: In a kitchen-garden genetics project, a student crosses pure tall and dwarf pea plants and gets all tall F1. He writes in his log: 'the tall allele has destroyed the dwarf allele — dwarfness is gone for good from this line.'
c12_bio_ch05.prompt: What will the F2 from selfed F1 show?

options.text: About a quarter dwarfs — dominance only masks the recessive allele in the heterozygote; the allele stays intact and segregates into gametes, reappearing when homozygous.
options.outcome: Segregation is the giveaway: alleles separate unchanged in meiosis, so F2 shows roughly 3 tall : 1 dwarf — masking is not destruction.

options.text: All tall forever — the dominant allele permanently suppresses or eliminates the recessive one.
options.outcome: That's blending thinking; the recessive allele is transmitted unchanged and resurfaces in F2 — the classic 3:1 ratio.

options.text: A 1:1 mix of tall and dwarf, since the two alleles each 'win' half the offspring.
options.outcome: Gametes are 1:1 but zygotes aren't phenotypes: three of four zygote classes carry at least one dominant allele and look tall.

c12_bio_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch06.scenario: For a science-fair poster on 'How we know DNA is the genetic material', a student credits the 1928 Griffith mouse experiment: 'Griffith proved DNA carries heredity.' The teacher asks her to defend or correct the caption.

options.text: Fix it — Griffith showed only that a 'transforming principle' passes from dead S-strain to live R-strain bacteria; Hershey and Chase identified it as DNA in 1952 using ³²P and ³⁵S isotopes.
options.outcome: The two experiments answer different questions: transformation exists vs which molecule does it — the poster needs both names, correctly credited.

options.text: It's right — Griffith's heat-killed extract transformed bacteria, so he proved DNA is genetic material.
options.outcome: Griffith never identified the chemical nature of the principle; both DNA and denatured protein sat in that extract — chemical proof came later.

options.text: Fix it differently — Hershey and Chase's blender is what pushed phage DNA into the bacteria.
options.outcome: The blender only sheared off empty protein coats after infection; DNA had already entered — misreading the apparatus repeats the error in reverse.

c12_bio_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch07.scenario: A student's origin-of-life project ends with the claim: 'Miller and Urey proved life began exactly as Oparin and Haldane described — lightning in a pond made the first cell.'
c12_bio_ch07.prompt: What did the 1953 spark experiment actually establish?

options.text: Only stage two — that inorganic gases (CH₄, NH₃, H₂, H₂O) under sparking can abiotically yield amino acids; polymerisation into macromolecules and bounded protocells remained undemonstrated.
options.outcome: Chemical evolution is multi-stage: showing monomers can form isn't showing a living cell arose — the claim overgeneralises partial evidence.

options.text: The claim stands — amino acids appeared, so the whole pathway to the first cell is proven.
options.outcome: Finding bricks isn't building the house: stages 3 and 4 (polymers, protocells with metabolism and heredity) were never part of that apparatus.

options.text: It failed anyway — without free oxygen in the gas mix, no organic molecules could form.
options.outcome: Backwards: the reducing, oxygen-free atmosphere was essential — free O₂ would have oxidised and destroyed nascent organics.

c12_bio_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch08.scenario: A neighbour's child has a runny nose, sneezing and a mild sore throat — a classic common cold. The parent wants to start leftover antibiotic tablets 'to kill the infection fast' and asks the biology student for a second opinion.

options.text: No — the cold is caused by rhinovirus, and viruses have no cell wall or ribosomes for antibiotics to hit; rest and hygiene help, while the pills only feed antimicrobial resistance.
options.outcome: Antibiotics like ceftriaxone work on bacterial machinery; against a virus they do nothing to the patient and everything to the resistance problem.

options.text: Yes — fever plus cold symptoms means infection, and antibiotics kill infections.
options.outcome: That conflates pathogen types: bacteria (typhoid, pneumococcal pneumonia) respond; rhinovirus is viral and has no antibiotic target.

options.text: Yes — but only a double dose, since colds are 'weaker' infections that need catching early.
options.outcome: Dose size can't fix a missing drug target; doubling a useless drug just raises harm without benefit.

c12_bio_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch09.scenario: A dairy farmer brags that his shed is so clean he has stopped vaccinating the herd and skipped deworming 'to save money'. The vet-college student interning with him is asked whether that's sound management.
c12_bio_ch09.prompt: Can spotless housing replace preventive health care?

options.text: No — hygiene cuts pathogen load but can't break every cycle: worm eggs persist in soil for years and airborne or vector-borne diseases arrive regardless; vaccination primes immunity and deworming interrupts parasite cycles.
options.outcome: Husbandry is four interdependent pillars — feeding, breeding, health and housing; excellent housing can't substitute for the health pillar.

options.text: Yes — a clean shed removes the source of disease, so vaccines and dewormers become redundant.
options.outcome: Cleanliness lowers exposure but can't stop wind-borne FMD or nematode eggs lying dormant in pasture soil for years.

options.text: Yes — and the money saved can go to extra calories, since feed quantity alone decides milk yield.
options.outcome: Milk synthesis needs a balanced ration — protein, minerals, fibre, not just calories — and a sick or wormy cow won't convert feed to milk anyway.

c12_bio_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch10.scenario: Two students run a kitchen experiment: identical milk and starter curd, one bowl kept at 15°C and one at 35°C. After 8 hours the warm bowl is firm and tangy while the cold bowl is still liquid — the cold-batch student concludes 'the Lactobacillus died'.

options.text: Lactobacillus is mesophilic with an optimum around 30–40°C — at 15°C it grows but far more slowly, so too little lactic acid accumulates to coagulate casein in 8 hours; it isn't dead, just slow.
options.outcome: Growth rate, not survival, is the limit — give the cold batch more time or warmer conditions and the same starter still sets curd.

options.text: He's right — 15°C kills the starter bacteria, which is why no curd formed.
options.outcome: Suboptimal temperature only stretches generation time; the population creeps up instead of crashing.

options.text: The cold bowl just needed no starter at all — milk left at room temperature curdles on its own anyway.
options.outcome: Without a starter, random contaminants dominate and spoil the milk; the inoculum is what drives clean lactic fermentation.

c12_bio_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch11.scenario: A startup's engineered bacteria produce human enzyme beautifully in shake flasks, but in the 10,000-litre fermenter the yield collapses — oxygen starves the dense culture and product clumps into inclusion bodies. A young scientist proposes 'the gene is faulty, let's re-clone it'.

options.text: It's a bioprocess problem, not a genetic one — scale-up needs optimised oxygen transfer, feed rate, pH and shear; a perfect strain still fails in a poorly run fermenter.
options.outcome: Biotechnology rests on two equal pillars: genetic engineering builds the strain, bioprocess engineering makes it produce at scale — re-cloning solves nothing here.

options.text: Re-clone it — biotechnology is genetic engineering, so any product failure must trace back to the gene construct.
options.outcome: The strain already proved it makes the enzyme in flasks; the breakdown is in fermentation parameters — treating bioprocess as a black box is the mistake.

options.text: Just run the same flask recipe in the big tank — scale doesn't change biology.
options.outcome: At high cell density, oxygen transfer, heat removal and mixing all change; a shaken flask recipe doesn't transfer directly to a stirred tank.

c12_bio_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch12.scenario: A farmer switching to Bt cotton hears two rumours at the mandi: 'the plant's own poison kills every insect including the bees' and 'once you plant Bt you never spray again'. He asks the agri-science student what's actually true.
c12_bio_ch12.prompt: How does Bt toxin really behave?

options.text: It's narrowly specific: the Cry protoxin activates only in the alkaline gut of lepidopteran larvae and binds receptors bees and humans lack — but sucking pests like aphids and whitefly escape, so spraying for them continues.
options.outcome: Bt cotton cuts bollworm sprays drastically without harming pollinators — yet it's not broad-spectrum, so integrated pest management still applies.

options.text: First rumour is right — a plant that makes insecticide poisons every insect that touches it, including bees and ladybirds.
options.outcome: Bees lack the alkaline midgut and cadherin receptors the protoxin needs; field studies show pollinator and predator populations unharmed.

options.text: Second rumour is right — the plant produces its own insecticide, so all pesticide use ends.
options.outcome: Cry proteins hit only caterpillars; aphids, jassids and whiteflies still attack the crop and must be managed separately.

c12_bio_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bio_ch13.scenario: For a school biodiversity assignment on the tiger, a student submits: 'Niche — the forest; it eats deer.' His teacher returns it marked incomplete.

options.text: The forest is only the habitat — the address; the niche is the profession: solitary territorial ambush predator, largely nocturnal, needing a large home range and specific prey interactions.
options.outcome: Niche spans diet, activity timing, social structure, reproduction and interactions — not just where the animal lives and one thing it eats.

options.text: Nothing — niche means habitat plus diet, and 'forest plus deer' covers both.
options.outcome: That strips out behaviour, temporal activity and trophic interactions; 'address plus one meal' is exactly the truncated definition exams penalise.

options.text: Nothing — and since a niche is genetically fixed, the tiger's role can't differ between the Sundarbans and central India.
options.outcome: The fundamental niche is constrained, but the realised niche shifts with context — Sundarbans tigers swim, drink saline water and hunt fish.

c12_bs_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bs_ch01.scenario: A bakery owner reviews the month: the team baked all 2,000 loaves ordered, but burned through 10% extra flour and 20% extra labour hours versus standard. Her assistant calls it 'a perfectly managed month'.

options.text: Only half — the bakery was effective (goal achieved) but not efficient (inputs exceeded standard); good management means hitting the target at minimum cost.
options.outcome: Effectiveness is doing the right task; efficiency is doing it with least resources — meeting output while overspending inputs is exactly the 'effective but inefficient' case.

options.text: Yes — the target was met, so management was both effective and efficient.
options.outcome: Target-hit proves effectiveness only; efficiency is judged on the input side, where flour and labour both overshot.

options.text: No — because efficiency was poor, the month counts as ineffective too.
options.outcome: The goal was achieved, so effectiveness held; the two dimensions are independent and both must be judged.

c12_bs_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bs_ch02.scenario: A marketing executive keeps getting campaign orders from the Marketing Head and conflicting budget orders from the Finance Head. Deadlines slip, and nobody is sure whose instruction wins.
c12_bs_ch02.prompt: Which principle is broken and what follows?

options.text: Unity of Command — one subordinate should receive orders from only one superior; dual subordination creates confusion, delay and divided loyalty for the individual.
options.outcome: Distinct from Unity of Direction (one head, one plan for the whole organisation) — here the fix is a single reporting line, not a merged plan.

options.text: Unity of Direction — two heads means two plans, and that principle targets the individual employee.
options.outcome: That swaps the pair: Unity of Direction guards against overlapping plans at organisational level; the individual's double-boss problem is Unity of Command.

options.text: Equity — the real violation is that the executive isn't being treated fairly.
options.outcome: Fairness isn't the structural issue; even two equally kind bosses producing contradictory orders still violate Unity of Command.

c12_bs_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bs_ch03.scenario: An intern briefing a kirana-store owner says: 'A new competitor next door is a general force that affects all firms equally, while the new digital-billing mandate is a specific force aimed only at your shop.'
c12_bs_ch03.prompt: Did she classify the forces correctly?

options.text: She has it backwards — a new competitor is a specific force hitting this firm directly, while a billing mandate is a general (legal) force applying to all enterprises indirectly.
options.outcome: Specific forces (customers, competitors, suppliers, investors) act on one firm directly; general forces (social, political, legal, technological) press on every firm at once.

options.text: Yes — whatever affects many firms is 'specific' to the industry, and a government rule naming a threshold targets only some firms.
options.outcome: Scope, not personal naming, decides the class: the mandate applies economy-wide even though it bites each firm differently.

options.text: Yes — and since both are external forces, the distinction doesn't matter for planning.
options.outcome: It matters a lot: specific forces get firm-level responses (differentiate from the rival); general forces get compliance and positioning responses.

c12_bs_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bs_ch04.scenario: A startup CEO sets the objective 'market leader in AI education in 3 years' and asks the marketing head to plan it. The head immediately signs an ad agency. The CEO rejects it: 'That is not a plan.'
c12_bs_ch04.prompt: Why doesn't the agency hire count as planning?

options.text: Planning means deciding in advance among alternatives — he skipped identifying options (content, partnerships, referrals), evaluating them against premises, and choosing a course; he jumped to executing one option.
options.outcome: An instruction to execute isn't a plan: objectives, alternatives, evaluation and future premises all have to precede the action.

options.text: It does count — planning is just forecasting demand, and hiring the agency acts on the forecast.
options.outcome: Forecasting only develops premises about the future; planning goes further — it weighs alternatives and decides a course of action.

options.text: It does count — small firms plan mentally, so nothing written was needed anyway.
options.outcome: Planning is pervasive and mental plans still involve objectives-plus-alternatives; his was neither written nor mentally deliberated.

c12_bs_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bs_ch05.scenario: A one-man dhaba grows to 50 customers a day, so the owner hires three helpers and tells them 'just help wherever needed'. Result: two helpers peel onions while nobody serves, the cash box sits unattended, and vegetables spoil unchecked.

options.text: The whole organising process — divide work into distinct jobs, group them into departments, assign duties by aptitude, and set clear authority and reporting lines so everyone knows who does what and answers to whom.
options.outcome: Hiring hands isn't organising; without role clarity and relationships you get duplication in one place and abandonment in another.

options.text: Nothing structural — he just needs to draw an organisation chart and stick it on the wall.
options.outcome: A chart is the output, not the process: without defined duties and reporting relationships, the drawing changes nothing on the floor.

options.text: He simply needs a fourth helper — more hands absorb more work.
options.outcome: The labour was idle in the wrong places, not scarce; unstructured extra hands repeat the same chaos.

c12_bs_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bs_ch06.scenario: A machine-parts firm loses a fifth of its skilled CNC operators in a year and production keeps slipping. The CEO's fix: 'just hire more operators — that's staffing.'
c12_bs_ch06.prompt: Will fresh hiring alone stop the bleeding?

options.text: No — staffing is a continuous cycle: the attrition signals gaps in appraisal, career growth and compensation, so diagnose why people leave and build development and promotion paths alongside recruitment.
options.outcome: Filling positions without keeping them filled creates a revolving door; recruitment is only one of eight steps.

options.text: Yes — staffing literally means hiring, so more recruitment solves it.
options.outcome: That shrinks staffing to its second step; the NCERT process runs estimation through compensation — retention lives in the later steps.

options.text: Yes — and anyway staffing is the HR department's job, so line managers are off the hook.
options.outcome: Staffing is a line function too: the production manager must appraise and develop his own operators; HR only supports with systems.

c12_bs_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bs_ch07.scenario: A marketing head emails 20 field executives: 'Raise fertiliser sales 15% this quarter — new price list attached.' Two weeks later sales are flat, and he concludes the team is simply lazy.

options.text: He informed but never directed — no field briefing to turn the target into daily plans, no coaching or motivation on farmer objections, no mid-quarter review and course-correction.
options.outcome: Directing initiates action continuously at every level; a one-way email is communication, and communication is only one element of directing.

options.text: Nowhere — he gave a clear written order, and directing is basically giving orders.
options.outcome: That shrinks directing to instruction; without guiding, motivating and following through, orders sit unexecuted.

options.text: Nowhere — directing flows from the top anyway, so field supervisors had nothing to add.
options.outcome: Top-down flow doesn't mean only the top directs; every level directs its own subordinates, and the skipped field level is exactly where it broke.

c12_bs_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bs_ch08.scenario: A new floor supervisor decides controlling means 'catching lazy workers', so he runs surprise checks and hands out punishments. Output doesn't improve and morale craters; a colleague suggests doing controlling 'properly'.
c12_bs_ch08.prompt: What does proper controlling look like here?

options.text: Set clear performance standards, measure actual output, compare it with the standard, analyse the cause of deviations, then fix the cause — done openly so workers know expectations and can self-correct.
options.outcome: Controlling is regulation against a standard, not policing; employees perform better when standards are known in advance — that's how it motivates.

options.text: He's already doing it — controlling exists precisely to catch slackers and instil discipline through fear.
options.outcome: Fear isn't the function: control aims to make activities conform to plans; punishment without standards, measurement and corrective action achieves none of that.

options.text: Drop the checks — small teams don't need a control system at all.
options.outcome: Controlling is pervasive at every size; a low-cost standard plus simple measurement still beats no feedback loop.

c12_bs_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bs_ch09.scenario: A newly appointed finance executive tells the board: 'Financial management simply means maximising this year's profit — so take the highest-profit project and the cheapest loan available.'

options.text: No — the objective is wealth maximisation: judge decisions by their effect on share value, which accounts for the timing of cash flows and risk, not just the accounting profit figure.
options.outcome: Two projects with equal profit differ if one's cash arrives later or is riskier; profit is a manipulable accounting number, wealth is the market's discounted verdict.

options.text: Yes — more profit automatically means more shareholder wealth, so the terms are interchangeable.
options.outcome: Profit ignores when cash arrives and how risky it is; a high-profit, high-risk bet can lower the share price while a steadier project raises it.

options.text: Yes — and procuring funds at the lowest possible cost is the whole job.
options.outcome: Cheap money badly deployed still destroys value: an 8% loan funding a 6% project loses wealth whatever the rate.

c12_bs_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bs_ch10.scenario: A manufacturer needs ₹2 crore for just six months to stock seasonal inventory. A junior analyst proposes issuing fresh equity shares to raise it.
c12_bs_ch10.prompt: Is equity the right instrument for this need?

options.text: No — match maturity to need: a six-month requirement belongs to the money market (e.g., commercial paper); equity is permanent capital with no maturity, wrong tool for a short-term gap.
options.outcome: Maturity matching avoids refinancing risk and excess cost — the market offers short-term instruments precisely for short-term needs.

options.text: Yes — any security issued by a company belongs to the capital market, and equity is the most flexible.
options.outcome: Market class is set by instrument maturity, not by the issuer: short-maturity paper like CP is money market even when a company issues it.

options.text: Yes — the financial market is the stock market, so shares are the natural route for any corporate fund-raise.
options.outcome: Financial markets span money, bond, forex and derivative markets too; 'shares for everything' mistakes the famous slice for the whole.

c12_bs_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_bs_ch11.scenario: A founder finishes building a classical-music learning app and announces: 'Product done — now for marketing. Let's run Instagram ads.' The ad spend burns through budget with almost no conversions.

options.text: Need research on what learners struggle with, features and pricing built around those needs, and distribution sorted out — ads only communicate an offering that's already been created and placed.
options.outcome: Marketing starts before the product exists and continues after the sale; promotion is just one element, so skipping to it wastes spend on an unvalidated offer.

options.text: He was right — marketing means advertising; conversions failing just means the ads were bad.
options.outcome: That collapses marketing into its promotion element; no ad quality fixes an offering nobody needed at a price nobody accepts.

options.text: He was right — marketing and selling are the same job: push whatever the team built.
options.outcome: Selling starts from the factory's output and the seller's needs; marketing starts from the customer's needs — opposite directions.

c12_ca_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ca_ch01.scenario: A trader installs accounting software and proudly declares: 'We have a computerised accounting system now — the computer posts everything, so the staff don't even need to know debit and credit.'
c12_ca_ch01.prompt: Is the system complete, and is the debit/credit knowledge really redundant?

options.text: Neither — CAS is five components (procedure, data, people, hardware, software), and the software only automates posting: staff still choose voucher types and pass journal adjustments like depreciation, which need debit/credit logic.
options.outcome: Automation replaces the ledger-posting step, not accounting judgement — a wrong voucher choice propagates the error everywhere instantly.

options.text: Yes — the software is the system, and auto-posting means no human accounting knowledge is needed.
options.outcome: Software is one pillar of five; and every voucher type has hard-coded debit/credit logic the user must trigger correctly.

options.text: Yes — since ledgers and trial balance update automatically, debit and credit have become obsolete concepts.
options.outcome: Rectification and year-end entries go through journal vouchers with no preset logic — debit/credit fluency is still required there.

c12_ca_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ca_ch02.scenario: An accountant builds a GST column: revenue in E, the 18% rate sitting in cell G1, and writes =E2*G1 in F2. Row 2 is correct, but after copying down, every row below shows GST as zero.
c12_ca_ch02.prompt: What went wrong and what's the fix?

options.text: The rate reference was relative — copying shifted it to G2, G3… which are empty; rewrite it as =E2*$G$1 so the rate cell stays locked while E2 slides down each row.
options.outcome: Absolute referencing ($G$1) pins the constant while the relative part tracks the row — one input cell then drives what-if changes everywhere.

options.text: Excel broke — the only reliable fix is to retype =E3*G1, =E4*G1 and so on by hand for every row.
options.outcome: Retyping each row defeats the point and invites typos; locking the reference once is exactly what the fill operation is built for.

options.text: Cell references never move when copied, so the zeroes must come from bad data in column E.
options.outcome: Relative references shift by design — that's why the row-2 result looked right while everything below silently multiplied by empty cells.

c12_ca_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ca_ch03.scenario: Processing March payroll, a junior accountant computes DA, HRA and PF directly on contractual Basic Pay for an employee who had 4 leave-without-pay days. The numbers look neat and she submits the sheet.
c12_ca_ch03.prompt: Where did the computation go wrong?

options.text: The allowances and PF must ride on Basic Pay Earned — BP × effective days present ÷ days in month — not on full contractual BP; using BP overstates every earning and deduction for absent days.
options.outcome: BP is the contract, BPE is what was actually earned that month — the whole payroll chain keys off BPE.

options.text: Nothing — Basic Pay is Basic Pay; days absent are handled separately, not inside salary formulas.
options.outcome: BPE exists precisely to fold attendance into pay; skipping it overpays DA, HRA and deducts excess PF for days never worked.

options.text: Nothing — and if a supervisor's HRA shows zero, the IF formula itself must be broken.
options.outcome: A zero HRA more often means the type cell reads 'Sup ' or 'sup' — text matching is exact, so data entry, not the formula, is the culprit.

c12_ca_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ca_ch04.scenario: For a board practical, a student is asked to show the trend of quarterly revenue across five years, including one loss quarter. He inserts a pie chart 'because it shows percentages clearly'.
c12_ca_ch04.prompt: Is the pie chart the right choice?

options.text: No — a pie shows one series' share of a whole at a single point; a 20-quarter trend with a negative value needs a line or column chart, where the loss quarter dips below the axis.
options.outcome: Chart type follows the question: proportions → pie, trends over time → line, category comparison → column; Excel won't rescue a mismatched choice.

options.text: Yes — Excel will arrange any data into any chart type correctly.
options.outcome: Pie charts take exactly one positive series of up to seven categories; the other quarters are silently dropped and a loss can't even be a slice.

options.text: Yes — and he can add a second ring to the pie to show both this year and last year.
options.outcome: That's a doughnut chart, and stacking rings of shares still can't render a time trend or negative quarters.

c12_chem_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_chem_ch01.scenario: Labelling samples for the chemistry practical file, a student tags a cold-drink bottle 'gaseous solution' — her reasoning: the dissolved CO₂ is a gas, so the solution must be a gas too.

options.text: No — the solvent, not the solute, sets the phase: water is the major component and is liquid, so this is a liquid solution of gas in liquid.
options.outcome: Same rule explains why mercury-in-silver amalgam is a solid solution despite mercury being liquid — the component in excess fixes the state.

options.text: Yes — the solute's physical state decides the solution's class, and CO₂ is a gas.
options.outcome: That rule would also make brass a liquid and air unclassifiable; the solvent's state is what defines the solution's.

options.text: Yes — and by the same logic brass is a liquid solution since copper and zinc can be melted.
options.outcome: Classification uses states at the given temperature, not melting points; brass at room temperature is a solid solution.

c12_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_chem_ch02.scenario: Building a Daniell cell to light an LED, a student saves effort by dipping both the zinc and copper strips into a single beaker holding a CuSO₄–ZnSO₄ mixture. The LED stays dark.

options.text: With both electrodes in one solution, Cu²⁺ is reduced directly on the metal surfaces — no electron is pushed through the wire; the half-cells must be separated and joined by a salt bridge that carries ions to keep neutrality.
options.outcome: Separating the half-reactions is what forces electrons through the external circuit; the bridge completes the loop with ions, not electrons.

options.text: The salt bridge is missing, and that's the problem because the bridge is what carries electrons between the two electrodes.
options.outcome: Close on the diagnosis, wrong on the mechanism — electrons travel the wire; the bridge migrates ions to prevent charge build-up.

options.text: The LED is fine — it just won't glow because in a galvanic cell the anode is positive, so he wired the polarity backwards.
options.outcome: In a galvanic cell the anode is the negative terminal (electrons leave there); reversed polarity labels are the electrolytic convention.

c12_chem_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_chem_ch03.scenario: For 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂, a lab group reports the rate three ways — –Δ[N₂O₅]/Δt, Δ[NO₂]/Δt and Δ[O₂]/Δt — and gets three different numbers, so they argue about which one 'is' the rate.
c12_chem_ch03.prompt: How should the rate actually be reported?

options.text: Divide each change by its stoichiometric coefficient — –(1/2)Δ[N₂O₅]/Δt = (1/4)Δ[NO₂]/Δt = Δ[O₂]/Δt — so all three collapse to one unique reaction rate.
options.outcome: The coefficient factor is what makes 'the rate' well-defined; without it every species gives a different answer for the same reaction.

options.text: Pick –Δ[N₂O₅]/Δt — the reactant's disappearance is the true rate; products can differ.
options.outcome: That privileges one species arbitrarily; the convention exists precisely so the rate is independent of which species you track.

options.text: Report the raw number with its sign — if [N₂O₅] falls, a negative rate is acceptable.
options.outcome: Rates are positive by convention: the minus sign in –Δ[R]/Δt cancels the negative change.

c12_chem_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_chem_ch04.scenario: Filling a periodic-table worksheet, a student writes: 'Zn is in the d-block and forms compounds, so it's a transition element like the rest.'
c12_chem_ch04.prompt: Does Zn actually qualify as a transition element?

options.text: No — the IUPAC test is an incomplete d subshell in the neutral atom or any common ion; Zn is 3d¹⁰ both ways and Zn²⁺ is colourless, so it's d-block but not transition.
options.outcome: Block membership follows the subshell being filled; transition status needs an incomplete d — the categories aren't identical, and Cu scrapes in only via Cu²⁺ (3d⁹).

options.text: Yes — anything sitting inside the d-block is by definition a transition element.
options.outcome: That erases the Group 12 exception: Zn, Cd and Hg fill d¹⁰ in atom and ion alike and fail the IUPAC criterion.

options.text: Yes — and its compounds are coloured, which proves transition behaviour.
options.outcome: Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰) has no d–d transitions available, so its compounds are typically colourless — the cited evidence is also wrong.

c12_chem_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_chem_ch05.scenario: A lab report says a cobalt compound of formula CoCl₃·5NH₃ precipitates only 2 mol of AgCl per mol with excess AgNO₃. The student writes its structure as [Co(NH₃)₅]Cl₃, keeping all three chlorides outside the brackets.
c12_chem_ch05.prompt: Does that formulation fit the data?

options.text: No — 2 mol AgCl means only 2 Cl⁻ are ionisable counter-ions; the third Cl⁻ is bound inside the sphere, giving [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂ with coordination number 6.
options.outcome: Precipitation counts only the primary-valence (ionisable) chlorides; coordinated Cl⁻ stays locked to the metal and never reaches Ag⁺.

options.text: Yes — 'Cl₃' in the formula means all three chlorides sit outside the brackets.
options.outcome: That would precipitate 3 mol AgCl and leave coordination number 5 — contradicting both the data and the fixed secondary valence of Co³⁺.

options.text: The AgNO₃ test itself is suspect — complexes like K₄[Fe(CN)₆] release Fe²⁺ freely anyway.
options.outcome: K₄[Fe(CN)₆] fails the Fe²⁺ test precisely because the metal stays inside the sphere — the test is exactly how sphere vs counter-ion is told apart.

c12_chem_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_chem_ch06.scenario: A student must sort three unlabelled bottles of isomeric bromobutanes. She runs warm ethanolic AgNO₃ on each: one precipitates AgBr in 2 minutes, one in 30 minutes, one not at all — and guesses they're 'all equally reactive since all are C₄H₉Br'.
c12_chem_ch06.prompt: How should she read the timings?

options.text: Fastest = 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (3°), middle = 2-bromobutane (2°), no reaction = 1-bromobutane (1°): the test runs through carbocations, and stability order 3° > 2° > 1° sets the speed.
options.outcome: Same formula, different class — counting carbons attached to the C–Br carbon predicts SN1 reactivity before any lab work.

options.text: Same molecular formula means same class, so the timing differences are just experimental noise.
options.outcome: C₄H₉Br spans primary, secondary and tertiary isomers — the timings are the classification working as intended.

options.text: Fastest must be 1-bromobutane — primary halides react fastest in every mechanism.
options.outcome: That's the SN2 order; AgNO₃/ethanol forces SN1 where tertiary wins on carbocation stability — mechanism choice flips the order.

c12_chem_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_chem_ch07.scenario: Three unlabelled bottles hold butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol. With Lucas reagent one clouds instantly, one after ~6 minutes, one stays clear — and a student concludes 'they're all C₄H₁₀O, so the timing is just error'.
c12_chem_ch07.prompt: How should she decode the observations?

options.text: Instant = the tertiary alcohol, ~6 min = secondary, clear = primary: Lucas runs through carbocations, whose stability runs 3° > 2° > 1°, so timing is the classification showing itself.
options.outcome: Class is decided by carbons bonded to the –OH carbon, not molecular formula — the test orders the three isomers exactly.

options.text: Same formula means same class — the timing differences are noise and the bottles are interchangeable.
options.outcome: C₄H₁₀O has two primary, one secondary and one tertiary isomer; identical formula says nothing about the carbinol carbon's substitution.

options.text: Instant clouding means primary — the simplest structure reacts first.
options.outcome: Primary alcohols give no room-temperature Lucas reaction at all; the instant response belongs to the stable tertiary carbocation.

c12_chem_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_chem_ch08.scenario: A lab task: turn benzyl alcohol into benzaldehyde — and stop there. The intern reaches for acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and heat, reasoning 'an oxidant is an oxidant'.
c12_chem_ch08.prompt: Will that reagent give the aldehyde?

options.text: No — aqueous dichromate over-oxidises the aldehyde (via its hydrate) to benzoic acid; use PCC in anhydrous CH₂Cl₂, which cannot form the hydrate and halts at the aldehyde.
options.outcome: Reagent and medium decide the stopping point: primary alcohol → aldehyde only under anhydrous selective oxidation or Cu/573 K dehydrogenation.

options.text: Yes — a primary alcohol always stops at the aldehyde no matter the oxidant.
options.outcome: In water the aldehyde hydrates to a gem-diol that oxidises onward — so strong aqueous oxidants deliver the carboxylic acid, not the aldehyde.

options.text: Skip oxidation entirely — use a tertiary alcohol instead, since it oxidises straight to a ketone.
options.outcome: Tertiary alcohols have no α-hydrogen; strong acid dehydrates them to alkenes — no carbonyl at all, and the substrate was a primary alcohol anyway.

c12_chem_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_chem_ch09.scenario: Labelling a bottle of aniline, a student writes 'tertiary amine' — nitrogen, he argues, is attached to three atoms: two ring carbons and a hydrogen.

options.text: No — classify by how many of ammonia's hydrogens are replaced by carbon groups: the phenyl ring is one group and two H remain, so C₆H₅NH₂ is a primary amine.
options.outcome: You count attached groups, not total bonds at nitrogen; counting the ring's two carbons separately is the exact slip being tested.

options.text: Yes — the atom count on nitrogen is three, and that decides the class.
options.outcome: By that rule NH₃ itself would be tertiary; the class tracks substitution of H on ammonia, not the atom tally on N.

options.text: No — it's a secondary amine, and (CH₃)₂NH is mixed because it carries two methyl groups.
options.outcome: Two identical methyls make dimethylamine simple, not mixed; 'mixed' needs differing groups — and aniline with two H is primary regardless.

c12_chem_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_chem_ch10.scenario: A lab gives a student three unknown solutions: A turns brick-red with Benedict's and ignores iodine; B turns blue-black with iodine; C answers neither test. He must match them to glucose, starch and sucrose.
c12_chem_ch10.prompt: What's the correct matching, and why does sucrose fail Benedict's?

options.text: A = glucose, B = starch, C = sucrose — sucrose's glucose–fructose bond ties up both anomeric carbons, leaving no free carbonyl to reduce the reagent.
options.outcome: Reducing power lives in a free anomeric carbon: maltose has one and gives a positive test, sucrose doesn't — hydrolysis first, then it would.

options.text: A = glucose, B = starch, C = sucrose — and sucrose is non-reducing only because it isn't sweet enough to react.
options.outcome: Sweetness is irrelevant; the cause is structural — the C1–C2 link occupies both anomeric carbons.

options.text: C = glucose, A = sucrose — any disaccharide with a glycosidic bond reduces Benedict's.
options.outcome: Disaccharides split both ways: sucrose and trehalose are non-reducing; the anomeric carbons have to stay free, as in maltose.

c12_cs_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_cs_ch01.scenario: Setting up a college fest stall, two laptops are linked by one Ethernet cable, given IPs on the same subnet, and they ping and share files fine. A teammate scoffs: 'No router, no internet — that's not a real network.'

options.text: No — nodes, a link, and agreed protocols are already in place and resources are being shared; routers, switches and internet only scale a network, they don't define it.
options.outcome: A network is defined by communication and sharing, not by specific infrastructure — this is a valid two-node LAN.

options.text: Yes — no internet means no network; Wi-Fi or the web is what makes devices networked.
options.outcome: That confuses the internet with the definition: wired labs and Bluetooth photo-sharing are networks with zero internet access.

options.text: Yes — every real network needs at least a dedicated server to count.
options.outcome: Peer-to-peer and ad-hoc networks share resources with no dedicated server at all; only client-server setups require one.

c12_cs_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_cs_ch02.scenario: An office on a coaxial bus network suffers constant collisions. The admin proposes rewiring all 20 desks to a central switch; the boss objects that a star 'wastes cable'.

options.text: The admin — a switch gives each port its own collision domain so collisions essentially vanish; the extra per-desk cable pays for itself in recovered throughput almost immediately.
options.outcome: Physical shape costs cable, but the logical behaviour is what matters — star over switch removes the shared collision domain that bus forces on everyone.

options.text: The boss — a star uses more cable, so it's strictly worse.
options.outcome: Cable metres aren't the only cost: one shared collision domain keeps throttling all 20 machines, and retransmission losses dwarf the one-time wiring bill.

options.text: Neither — the cable layout is the topology, so whether the centre is a hub or switch changes nothing.
options.outcome: Physical and logical topology differ: the same star cabling with a hub still behaves like a logical bus — the forwarding device decides.

c12_cs_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_cs_ch03.scenario: A student shows off a portfolio site built in React — ten static blog posts, a dark-mode toggle saved in localStorage — and insists it's 'obviously Web 2.0 because it uses a modern framework'.
c12_cs_ch03.prompt: Does the site qualify as Web 2.0?

options.text: No — Web 2.0 is about architecture: bidirectional data flow, server-side state, and user-generated content; a framework that compiles to static files with no backend is still Web 1.0 underneath.
options.outcome: The label follows the data flow, not the toolchain — no accounts, no shared dynamic data, no participation means no Web 2.0.

options.text: Yes — anything running JavaScript with smooth interactions is Web 2.0.
options.outcome: Web 1.0 sites used JavaScript too, for rollovers and validation; what makes 2.0 is server communication and persistent user state.

options.text: Yes — Web 2.0 is simply the newer protocol that replaced HTTP.
options.outcome: Web 2.0 isn't a protocol at all; it still runs on ordinary HTTP/HTTPS — it's a design philosophy, not a wire format.

c12_cs_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_cs_ch04.scenario: A clinic keeps each patient's record in a separate Word file. Reception can't find all patients with one diagnosis, and the doctor and receptionist overwrite each other's edits. The owner resists a DBMS: 'files give us full control'.
c12_cs_ch04.prompt: What does a DBMS actually fix here?

options.text: SQL queries plus indexing make the diagnosis search instant, and concurrency control stops simultaneous edits clobbering each other — with transactions, backup and the metadata catalogue thrown in.
options.outcome: A DBMS isn't 'a better filing cabinet' — it's a managed layer for consistency, concurrent access and recovery that ad-hoc files can't reproduce cheaply.

options.text: Nothing — a DBMS is just a fancier way to store files, so files are fine.
options.outcome: Files have no query language, no locking, no transactions and no catalogue; the 'control' claimed is really unpriced maintenance and inconsistency risk.

options.text: Just split the files by doctor — that gives the same result with zero new software.
options.outcome: Fragmenting the data worsens the exact failures at hand: cross-cutting search gets harder and concurrent edits still collide.

c12_cs_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_cs_ch05.scenario: Migrating a school project from MySQL to PostgreSQL, a student copies her script over unchanged — 'SQL is a standard, so it'll just run' — and watches it fail on `AUTO_INCREMENT` and `LIMIT`.

options.text: The standard covers core SELECT/INSERT/CREATE, but every RDBMS bolts on its own syntax — AUTO_INCREMENT vs SERIAL, LIMIT vs FETCH FIRST, backticks vs double quotes — so porting means translating the dialect.
options.outcome: SQL is the language, MySQL is one product speaking it with an accent; the script needs dialect conversion, not blind copying.

options.text: SQL and MySQL are two names for the same thing, so 'MySQL queries' are inherently portable.
options.outcome: SQL is the language standard; MySQL is one implementation — conflating them hides exactly the proprietary features that broke.

options.text: PostgreSQL must be buggy — standard-compliant SQL can't fail.
options.outcome: AUTO_INCREMENT and backticks are MySQL-only extensions; the failures mark non-standard syntax, not a faulty server.

c12_cs_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_cs_ch06.scenario: A library app's 'return book' feature runs without errors, yet the book still shows as issued in MySQL. The Python code executed the UPDATE, then closed — but never called conn.commit().

options.text: Nowhere permanent — with autocommit off, the UPDATE sat in an uncommitted transaction and rolled back when the connection closed; add conn.commit() after the execute.
options.outcome: Connection manages the transaction boundary: DML only persists on commit, and cleanup means close cursor, close connection.

options.text: The connector auto-saves everything — the bug must be in the UPDATE's WHERE clause.
options.outcome: Executed SQL isn't persisted SQL; without commit the write vanishes on close, whatever the WHERE clause matched.

options.text: Importing mysql.connector already opened the database, so conn was redundant and broke things.
options.outcome: The module only supplies the API — connect() creates the session object whose cursor() runs SQL; neither is optional.

c12_cs_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_cs_ch07.scenario: A hospital alert rule reads: notify the doctor if heart rate is high OR blood pressure is low AND oxygen is low. A nurse implementing it says the parentheses don't matter — 'it's just three conditions with OR and AND'.
c12_cs_ch07.prompt: Is the nurse right about the logic?

options.text: No — H + (B·O) and (H + B)·O are different rules: with H high, B normal, O normal they give opposite answers, so the AND/OR grouping changes who gets alerted.
options.outcome: Boolean grouping is clinical here — one reading alarms on high heart rate alone, the other demands low oxygen too.

options.text: Yes — OR and AND are interchangeable connectives, so any reading of the sentence works.
options.outcome: They aren't interchangeable: 'any one true' versus 'all required' is exactly the difference between + and ·.

options.text: Yes — and anyway 1 + 1 = 2 in Boolean, so the counts always sort it out.
options.outcome: Boolean values are truth states, not tallies: 1 OR 1 = 1 — the {0,1} system is closed and arithmetic intuition misfires.

c12_cs_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
