c12_cs_ch08.scenario: A team is building 'undo' for a text editor. One developer proposes a queue 'because it stores things in order'; the code review has to pick the right structure before they build.

options.text: A stack — undo must reverse the most recent action first, which is LIFO; a queue would undo the oldest action first and corrupt the document's history order.
options.outcome: Match the structure to the access pattern: undo, reshelving trolleys and call stacks all pop from the top.

options.text: A queue is fine — 'in order' is 'in order' whether it's FIFO or LIFO.
options.outcome: FIFO serves the earliest arrival first — the opposite of what undo needs; order of access, not storage, is the deciding feature.

options.text: Either works — data structures are just named lists and the choice is cosmetic.
options.outcome: Each structure encodes a different legal sequence of access; picking wrong changes program behaviour, not just style.

c12_cs_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_cs_ch09.scenario: A canteen-billing script computes base price plus 18% GST in twenty separate places. When GST changes, the student sighs and prepares to edit all twenty spots.

options.text: Wrap the pricing rule in one function — calculate_final_price(base) — so the rate change is a single edit and every caller picks it up automatically.
options.outcome: Functions centralise a rule: reuse for each item, one fix propagates everywhere, and the main script reads as intent rather than arithmetic.

options.text: Keep the twenty copies — the code works, and functions are really just for mathematical formulas anyway.
options.outcome: Functions name any repeated task — printing menus, writing files, sending bills — not just math; twenty copies mean twenty chances to miss one.

options.text: Put everything, billing included, inside one giant run_shop() function so the code is 'modular'.
options.outcome: One monolith isn't modularity — no reuse, hard to test, and one bug sinks the whole flow; modularity means small single-job functions.

c12_cs_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_cs_ch10.scenario: An attendance logger opens 'records.txt' in 'w' mode each morning to add the day's entries. Every evening, yesterday's data is mysteriously gone.

options.text: The 'w' mode itself — opening for write truncates the file to zero before writing; switching to 'a' (append) keeps existing lines and adds new ones at the end.
options.outcome: The mode letter is a decision: 'w' erases, 'a' appends, 'r' only reads — picking 'w' for logging silently wipes history.

options.text: Nothing — 'w' appends by nature, so the missing data must be a Python bug.
options.outcome: That's the misconception itself: 'w' truncates unconditionally; the vanished days are the expected behaviour, not a bug.

options.text: The .txt extension forces text mode weirdness — renaming to .dat would fix it.
options.outcome: Extensions are labels, not behaviour: the same file reads as text or bytes depending on the mode you open with.

c12_cs_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_cs_ch11.scenario: In a quiz app, a student needs triple the total of [85, 90, 78] and writes total = scores * 3. The printed 'total' is a nine-element list, not a number.

options.text: List repetition — it built [85,90,78,85,90,78,85,90,78]; what she wanted was sum(scores) * 3, since * on a sequence repeats rather than multiplies elements.
options.outcome: Operators are overloaded by type: * on a list means 'repeat the sequence', so reading it as arithmetic multiplication silently produces a longer list.

options.text: It multiplied every element by 3 — Python must have a display bug.
options.outcome: Element-wise multiplication isn't what * does on lists — that's why nine values appeared instead of [255,270,234].

options.text: It summed and tripled correctly — the printed list is just a formatting quirk.
options.outcome: The output literally shows repetition; a genuine 759 would print as an integer, not a bracketed sequence.

c12_cs_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_cs_ch12.scenario: A friend gets an SMS: 'Your bank account closes in 2 hours — verify at http://bank-verify-login.xyz'. He clicks, types in his credentials on the plain-HTTP page, and shrugs: 'I have antivirus, so I'm covered.'

options.text: He was phished — a spoofed domain over unencrypted HTTP harvested his credentials, and antivirus doesn't catch deception: the defences were checking the domain, insisting on HTTPS, and never following unsolicited links.
options.outcome: Antivirus scans files for known malware; it can't judge a fake page's intent or encrypt traffic — layered defence is the actual model.

options.text: He's fine — antivirus blocks all hackers and phishing by definition.
options.outcome: No single tool covers every threat class: antivirus won't stop a deceptive link, an HTTP snoop, or a DDoS flood.

options.text: The only issue was the padlock icon being absent — HTTPS alone would have made the fake page safe.
options.outcome: HTTPS encrypts the channel to whichever site you reached; it doesn't certify the site is genuine — domain-checking is separate.

c12_cs_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c12_cs_ch13.scenario: A student writes a project report: 'UPI is purely good for street vendors — free, instant payments.' A vendor mentions his phone dying mid-day means lost sales, and that a fake UPI callback nearly emptied his account.
c12_cs_ch13.prompt: How should the report frame UPI's impact?

options.text: As dual-impact: intended gains (faster payment, lower cash risk) alongside unintended effects at individual level (dead battery = lost sales) and systemic level (phishing targeting vendors) — impact comes from how tech meets human conditions.
options.outcome: Separating intended/unintended and individual/systemic exposes effects a 'it's just convenient' story hides — and each cell needs a different remedy.

options.text: Keep it positive — listing benefits IS an impact analysis.
options.outcome: Feature-listing isn't impact analysis: the question is how the capability changed behaviour and what harm followed, not what the app offers.

options.text: Flip to 'purely negative' — the vendor's losses outweigh the convenience.
options.outcome: Swapping one monovalent verdict for another isn't analysis; the point is holding both effects in view at once.

c12_eco_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eco_ch01.scenario: On Sunday a student picks a free cricket match over a ₹500 tutoring shift and a study block, then tells his mother the outing 'cost nothing — entry was free'.
c12_eco_ch01.prompt: What did the afternoon actually cost?

options.text: The value of the next best alternative forgone — the ₹500 earnings if work outranks study for him; zero ticket price doesn't make the choice costless because his time was scarce.
options.outcome: Opportunity cost is what you gave up, not what you paid; a free event still consumes hours that had a best alternative use.

options.text: Nothing — with no money spent, there's no cost at all.
options.outcome: Scarcity binds through time even when price is zero; every choice forfeits a next-best use.

options.text: The combined value of everything else he could have done — tutoring pay plus study gains together.
options.outcome: Opportunity cost is the single best alternative, not the sum of all forgone options — you could only ever have picked one of them.

c12_eco_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eco_ch02.scenario: At a free golgappa stall a friend keeps eating 'until total utility starts falling'. After plate seven he's visibly uncomfortable and wonders why the free food left him worse off.
c12_eco_ch02.prompt: Where should a rational consumer actually stop?

options.text: At the unit where marginal utility hits zero — the peak of total utility; eating into negative MU actively subtracts satisfaction even though the food costs nothing.
options.outcome: TU rises while MU is positive, peaks at MU = 0, and falls once MU goes negative — 'stop when TU falls' means you've already overshot.

options.text: After just one — the first unit has the highest marginal utility, so stopping there maximises satisfaction.
options.outcome: Highest MU is not highest TU; total utility keeps climbing through every positive-MU unit.

options.text: Keep going — since it's free, more units can only add to total utility.
options.outcome: Free kills the budget constraint, not the biology: negative marginal utility drags total utility down regardless of price.

c12_eco_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eco_ch03.scenario: A cloud kitchen with two ovens and hired chefs has run for two years. The owner declares 'we're in the long run now — it's been over a year' while deciding whether to hire more chefs or lease a bigger kitchen.
c12_eco_ch03.prompt: Is 'two years' the right test for the long run?

options.text: No — run is defined by input fixity, not the calendar: hiring chefs is short-run (ovens fixed); leasing a bigger kitchen makes capital variable and is the long-run decision, whenever it happens.
options.outcome: A firm could reach its 'long run' in three months or stay in the short run for five years — what matters is whether the fixed factor can finally be changed.

options.text: Yes — short run means under a year, long run means over a year, and two years clears the bar.
options.outcome: Calendar time isn't the criterion; if ovens still can't be added, every hiring decision remains short-run no matter how many years pass.

options.text: Yes — a lean startup with rented space has no fixed factors, so it's always long-run anyway.
options.outcome: Flexible space doesn't free everything: equipment, licences and key contracts can stay fixed — the long run needs ALL inputs variable.

c12_eco_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eco_ch04.scenario: At a grain mandi where hundreds of farmers sell identical wheat at ₹20/kg, one farmer reasons: 'I'll charge ₹21 — a few buyers will pay a premium for my grain.' His sacks sit unsold all day.

options.text: He's a price taker in near-perfect competition: identical wheat plus many sellers mean buyers simply walk to the next stall — above the market price his demand is zero.
options.outcome: The firm's demand curve is horizontal at the market price; there was no 'premium niche' to capture because nothing distinguishes his wheat.

options.text: Bad luck — small price rises only trim a little demand, so a few sales should still have happened.
options.outcome: That downward-sloping response is the market's demand curve, not the firm's; for one tiny seller it's perfectly elastic.

options.text: He should have cut to ₹19 — lower prices always win extra sales and more revenue.
options.outcome: He could already sell all his stock at ₹20; cutting just loses ₹1/kg on the same volume — no extra customers exist to win.

c12_eco_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eco_ch05.scenario: A minister announces an MSP for wheat well above the market-clearing price, telling the press 'farmers will sell more, buyers will still buy — everyone wins'. Grain starts piling up unsold in godowns.
c12_eco_ch05.prompt: What does the equilibrium logic predict?

options.text: A surplus — above equilibrium, supply exceeds demand, so the quantity actually traded falls to the demand side and someone must absorb the unsold stock.
options.outcome: A price floor fixes the price, not the quantities: farmers want to sell more at the high price but buyers want less — the shorter side decides.

options.text: He's right — a higher price raises supply and demand together since both sides 'benefit'.
options.outcome: Higher price moves opposite directions on the two curves: it raises quantity supplied but lowers quantity demanded.

options.text: It's fine — at the new price everyone who wants wheat still gets it, since equilibrium just means needs are met.
options.outcome: Equilibrium means the market clears, not that all wants are met — and a floor above it isn't even an equilibrium.

c12_eco_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eco_ch06.scenario: A city's water supply needs ₹10,000 crore of pipes plus trivial per-litre cost. A consultant urges splitting the network between two companies 'because competition always lowers prices'.

options.text: No — this is a natural monopoly: huge fixed cost spread over the whole market beats two duplicated grids; splitting raises average cost for everyone, so regulated single supply is cheaper.
options.outcome: Competition helps where entry is feasible; where scale economies run past total demand, a second network is pure duplication.

options.text: Yes — any single seller is a monopoly that charges high prices, so rivals always help.
options.outcome: Monopoly is about barriers and no close substitutes, not 'high prices' — and here entry just doubles the pipes, not the pressure to cut prices.

options.text: Yes — two firms halve the fixed cost each, so total cost falls.
options.outcome: Splitting demand doesn't split the fixed cost — each firm still builds a full grid, so two sets of pipes raise total cost.

c12_eco_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eco_ch07.scenario: During a downturn, an op-ed urges every household to slash spending and save more, claiming 'if each family saves more, national saving must rise — it's just addition'.
c12_eco_ch07.prompt: Does everyone saving more lift national saving?

options.text: Not necessarily — the paradox of thrift: if all households cut consumption together, aggregate demand and income fall, and actual saving (S = I) can stay flat or even shrink despite bigger saving intentions.
options.outcome: What's true for one household is false for all at once — income is endogenous, so the aggregate doesn't behave like a scaled-up family budget.

options.text: Yes — the economy is just a big household, so saving more at the micro level always sums to more saving at the macro level.
options.outcome: That's the fallacy of composition: planned saving rises while the income drop it triggers erases the gain.

options.text: Yes — since saving equals Y minus C, cutting C mathematically must raise S.
options.outcome: Only if Y were fixed — but Y falls with the demand collapse, so the identity gives no free rise in S.

c12_eco_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eco_ch08.scenario: A headline claims India's GNP exceeds its GDP 'because of the huge remittances the diaspora sends home'. A student repeats it in a class presentation on national income.
c12_eco_ch08.prompt: Does the claim survive the definitions?

options.text: No — family remittances are transfers, not factor income; India's net factor income from abroad is actually negative, so GNP typically sits below GDP.
options.outcome: Only wages, rent, interest and profit crossing borders count as factor income — gifts and maintenance flows don't enter the GDP→GNP bridge.

options.text: Yes — money earned abroad and sent home is exactly what 'factor income from abroad' means.
options.outcome: That confuses a transfer with a factor payment; remittances for family upkeep are unilateral transfers outside the accounts.

options.text: Maybe — but if anything, subtracting NFIA from GDP gives GNP, so the headline could go either way.
options.outcome: The sign matters: GNP = GDP + NFIA; flipping the sign breaks every chained aggregate downstream.

c12_eco_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eco_ch09.scenario: Debate prep: a teammate's slide says 'a credit card is money — it buys goods without cash'. The opposing team plans to tear it apart at the functions-of-money level.

options.text: No — it merely routes a bank loan to the merchant: it isn't a unit of account, stores debt not value, and the deferred payment is owed BY the user; it's a payment instrument, not money.
options.outcome: Buying power isn't the test — the four functions are: only assets performing all of them (currency, demand deposits) qualify as money.

options.text: Yes — anything that lets you purchase goods performs the medium-of-exchange job, so it counts.
options.outcome: Medium of exchange is only one function; the card fails the other three because the 'money' is the bank's liability, not the user's asset.

options.text: Yes — and for the same reason UPI itself is the new money replacing bank deposits.
options.outcome: UPI is a rail moving deposits; the deposit is the money — the pipe isn't the water.

c12_eco_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eco_ch10.scenario: Estimating aggregate demand for a class project, a student logs a family buying ₹10 lakh of shares under 'I — investment', arguing 'investing is literally what we did'.
c12_eco_ch10.prompt: Does that purchase raise AD through I?

options.text: No — I in AD is physical capital formation (machines, buildings, inventories); buying existing shares just changes ownership of a financial asset and produces nothing.
options.outcome: Macro 'investment' means new capital goods, not financial investing — share purchases are swaps inside the economy, no new output demanded.

options.text: Yes — 'investment' is the word for buying shares, so it slots straight into I.
options.outcome: Everyday 'investment' and the national-accounts I are different things; only expenditure creating real capital counts.

options.text: Either way, the family's imports paid for the trade fees, which adds to AD as well.
options.outcome: Imports are a leakage — M is subtracted in AD = C + I + G + (X − M), never added.

c12_eco_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eco_ch11.scenario: Sorting budget items for a civics project, a student files the government's PSU stake sale under 'revenue receipts' — 'it's money coming in, so it's revenue' — and a new AIIMS under revenue expenditure too.
c12_eco_ch11.prompt: Where does the classification actually turn?

options.text: On assets and liabilities, not size or recurrence alone: selling a stake reduces a government asset → capital receipt; building a hospital creates one → capital expenditure.
options.outcome: The revenue/capital split asks 'does this change the government's balance sheet?' — interest of ₹9 lakh crore stays revenue while a small disinvestment is capital.

options.text: He's right — any inflow is revenue, and salaries-like recurring spend is what revenue expenditure covers, so both filings stand.
options.outcome: Inflows that shrink assets (disinvestment) or create liabilities (borrowings) are capital receipts regardless of being 'income'.

options.text: Swap by size — big-ticket items like AIIMS are 'capital' only because they're expensive.
options.outcome: The hospital is capital because it creates an asset, not because it's costly — a ₹1-lakh-crore interest bill is still revenue expenditure.

c12_eng_f_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch01.scenario: A district orders all schools to teach only in a new official language from tomorrow; elders crowd the notice board while a child shrugs, 'it's just a subject switch'.
c12_eng_f_ch01.prompt: Is it just a subject switch?

options.text: No — Daudet's point in 'The Last Lesson' is that language carries identity and freedom; banning the mother tongue is cultural amputation, which is why the villagers treat the last class as a shared loss.
options.outcome: A decree about 'just a language' lands as the loss of a community's voice — the story's whole weight comes from that difference.

options.text: Yes — grammar is grammar; swapping which language is taught changes nothing essential.
options.outcome: That reads the decree as administrative detail and misses how the war's terms reach into every villager's sense of self.

options.text: Sad, but attachment to one's language is nostalgia — practicality says move on.
options.outcome: The villagers' guilt and Hamel's ceremony show the attachment isn't sentimentality but belonging — dismissing it erases what was actually lost.

c12_eng_f_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch02.scenario: An NGO volunteer finds children feeding glass furnaces in a bangle-making town. The elders say, 'this is our ancestral craft — it's tradition.'

options.text: Treat it as a structural trap, not a tradition: the work is hazardous child labour sustained by middlemen, debt and dead ends — so push schooling, enforcement and viable alternatives together.
options.outcome: Like Mukesh's Firozabad in 'Lost Spring', 'tradition' is how exploitation dresses itself up; a rescued child with no alternative goes straight back to the furnace.

options.text: Respect it — it's their culture, and outsiders shouldn't interfere.
options.outcome: That confuses inherited compulsion with chosen culture; the children themselves dream of garages and schools.

options.text: Just pull the children out this week — job done.
options.outcome: Rescue without alternatives returns them to the same economic trap; the system, not just the child, has to change.

c12_eng_f_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch03.scenario: A college trek includes river wading, and a student who nearly drowned as a child wants to quit the whole trip rather than face the water.

options.text: Douglas's route — shrink the fear systematically: a trained instructor, shallow starts, staged practice, and honest testing until terror gives way to mastery.
options.outcome: Fear of fear itself is the real enemy; patient, deliberate exposure beat it for Douglas and generalises to any paralysing dread.

options.text: Throw him in the deep end — one plunge and the fear is gone.
options.outcome: A forced plunge is what created Douglas's phobia in the first place; trauma doesn't cure trauma.

options.text: Avoidance is fine — simply never go near water again.
options.outcome: Douglas shows avoidance rules your life from the shadows; the fear wins every decision you don't make.

c12_eng_f_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch04.scenario: A dhaba owner catches a hungry runaway boy pocketing bread. The staff want him handed to the police; the owner remembers how 'The Rattrap' turns.
c12_eng_f_ch04.prompt: What does the story suggest she do?

options.text: Meet him with dignity — food, shelter and honest trust first; Lagerlöf's point is that goodness awakened by kindness rehabilitates where punishment hardens.
options.outcome: The peddler became an honest man because Edla treated him like a captain, not a thief — trust is the lever that changes people.

options.text: Call the police at once — a thief is a thief, whatever his story.
options.outcome: That treats circumstance as character; the story shows the 'rattrap' of poverty made the man, and kindness unmade it.

options.text: Slip him some money and send him on his way — problem solved without drama.
options.outcome: Cash without dignity leaves the trap shut; what changed the peddler was being trusted, not being tipped.

c12_eng_f_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch05.scenario: Interning in a village, you're asked by sharecroppers to draft and file their entire grievance for them — 'you're educated, you handle it'.
c12_eng_f_ch05.prompt: What would the Champaran lesson say?

options.text: Coach them to organise and represent themselves — Gandhi's real win at Champaran was curing the peasants' fear and dependency, not merely the refund he negotiated.
options.outcome: Doing it for them leaves the helplessness intact; self-reliance was the point of the satyagraha, not the settlement.

options.text: File it yourself — they need results, and you write better petitions.
options.outcome: That wins a case but not freedom; they remain dependent on the next educated outsider.

options.text: Tell them to wait until a strong leader comes along.
options.outcome: Champaran began because ordinary people acted — waiting for saviours is the very fear the episode broke.

c12_eng_f_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch06.scenario: On a film-set internship you watch one staffer quietly solve everyone's crises — scripts, schedules, egos — while credits and praise flow to others. As the team lead you can act.

options.text: Name his contribution and formalise the role — Subbu at Gemini Studios in 'Poets and Pancakes' shows how indispensable problem-solvers get consumed while staying invisible.
options.outcome: Asokamitran's satire lands here: institutions run on unacknowledged fixers, and fairness means making that labour seen.

options.text: Keep loading him — someone that useful doesn't need titles.
options.outcome: That's exactly how studios spent Subbu; usefulness without recognition is quiet exploitation.

options.text: Resent him — he must be angling for the boss's chair.
options.outcome: The office-poet jealousy in the story shows how suspicion of a capable colleague says more about the insecure observer.

c12_eng_f_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch07.scenario: For a school magazine you must interview a survivor of a public tragedy. A classmate urges you to 'ambush him at home — raw emotion makes the best copy'.

options.text: Arrange it with consent and boundaries — 'The Interview' frames the genre as both a source of truth and a potential intrusion; ethical interviewing gets better answers and doesn't prey on pain.
options.outcome: Kipling called interviewing a crime; the craft's defence is consent — you can honour the reader and the subject at once.

options.text: Ambush — public interest justifies catching him off guard.
options.outcome: Surprise buys spectacle, not truth; the chapter's whole debate warns that intrusion deforms what it captures.

options.text: Cancel it — interviews are inherently invasive, so never do one.
options.outcome: Silvester also calls the interview 'supremely serviceable' — the flaw is in the method, not the genre.

c12_eng_f_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch08.scenario: A friend from a struggling family talks of opening a boutique and 'meeting famous people', spinning stories everyone half-believes. As her closest friend, you can choose how to respond.
c12_eng_f_ch08.prompt: How do you handle her dreaming?

options.text: Respect the dream but ground it — talk honestly about money, training and next steps; 'Going Places' shows fantasy becomes painful only when it substitutes for a plan.
options.outcome: Sophie's tragedy isn't ambition — it's that nothing connects the dream to the biscuit factory she's earmarked for.

options.text: Let the stories ride — dreaming costs nothing and planning is a buzzkill.
options.outcome: Sophie's Danny Casey fable shows untethered fantasy turns into self-deception and isolation.

options.text: Tell her bluntly she'll end up at the factory and should stop embarrassing herself.
options.outcome: Mockery kills the aspiration without offering a path — the story critiques the trap, not the dreaming.

c12_eng_f_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch09.scenario: Driving to the airport for your first hostel term, you notice how old your mother suddenly looks, and a childhood fear of losing her rises in your throat.
c12_eng_f_ch09.prompt: What does Kamala Das's poem counsel?

options.text: Acknowledge the ache but answer with love and forward motion — the poem ends 'see you soon, Amma': stay deliberately connected, keep living, don't pretend you felt nothing.
options.outcome: The poet puts the thought away only to return to it honestly; love expressed beats fear suppressed.

options.text: Suppress it — busy yourself with the new term and never look back.
options.outcome: The 'old familiar ache' returns precisely because it was suppressed; denial postpones the feeling, it doesn't resolve it.

options.text: Cancel the plan — staying home forever is the only way to never lose her.
options.outcome: The poem accepts separation as part of life; surrendering your own future is guilt, not love.

c12_eng_f_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch10.scenario: Volunteering at a slum school, you propose bright wall maps and storybooks of green valleys 'to inspire them'. Spender's poem would ask harder questions.

options.text: Not by themselves — the poem calls the map 'wicked' when it pictures a world the children can't reach; real help is systemic: nutrition, safe space, open pathways out of the slum.
options.outcome: Images of a world that excludes them only taunt; the poem demands changed conditions, not prettier walls.

options.text: Yes — showing them beautiful worlds is the first step out.
options.outcome: That's the poem's exact critique: windows that open onto unreachable worlds are cruelty, not education.

options.text: Neither — their fate is sealed by birth, so effort is wasted.
options.outcome: Spender writes against that determinism: the classroom fails them because society lets it, which is changeable.

c12_eng_f_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch11.scenario: A project team fractures in constant quarrels; deadlines force more meetings, more noise. Someone suggests the group stop and sit in silence together once a day.

options.text: Yes — Neruda's stillness is deliberate introspection, 'not total inactivity': pausing the machinery of conflict lets the team interrupt its own momentum and see itself.
options.outcome: The poem's count to twelve is an active interruption of harmful motion — stillness as insight, not idleness.

options.text: No — silence means doing nothing, and doing nothing ships no work.
options.outcome: Neruda explicitly rules that out; the pause is productive self-examination, not a strike.

options.text: No — the fix is staying even busier so there's no time to fight.
options.outcome: Busyness is the engine of the quarrel; the poem's point is that ceaseless motion is what hides us from ourselves.

c12_eng_f_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch12.scenario: A friend, worn down by exams and bad news, dismisses your suggestion to sit in the park or watch the sunset: 'pretty things don't fix real problems'.

options.text: Beauty is a resource, not a remedy — 'a joy forever' doesn't solve the problem but it loosens despair's 'pall' and keeps the spirit capable of facing it.
options.outcome: Keats, writing through grief, argued beauty is how humans endure suffering — survival equipment, not decoration.

options.text: He's right — sunsets are escapism, and only solutions matter.
options.outcome: The poem's claim is precisely that despair itself is the deeper problem; beauty restores the will that solving requires.

options.text: Sort of — but only if the sunset actually removes the problem.
options.outcome: That demands of beauty a job it never claimed; its power is renewing the sufferer, not deleting the suffering.

c12_eng_f_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_f_ch13.scenario: A new highway bypass leaves a village's fruit stalls watching traffic roar past. The council proposes fresh paint and prettier signboards to 'attract the city money'.

options.text: No — Frost's roadside stand is about structural exclusion: rural sellers are shut out of the cash flow entirely; the answer is real access — viable locations, linkages to buyers — not cosmetics.
options.outcome: The poem's vendors wanted 'city money', not city approval; paint doesn't move money off the highway.

options.text: Yes — a polished look is what draws passing customers.
options.outcome: The poem's drivers speed past indifferent to the stand itself; the failure is economic exclusion, not aesthetics.

options.text: Neither — the sensible thing is for them to abandon the village for the city.
options.outcome: Frost treats their rootedness as legitimate; telling them to migrate just accepts the neglect the poem indicts.

c12_eng_k_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch01.scenario: A colleague had a vivid dream about a train derailment and wants the whole team to cancel tomorrow's site visit. Márquez's dream-seller is suddenly the office's most quoted source.

options.text: No — dreams are stories the mind tells, not evidence about the world; check the actual safety record and travel advisories, and treat the dream as a prompt to verify, not to obey.
options.outcome: Frau Frieda's dreams sell because they feel prophetic; real decisions still need checkable facts, not portents.

options.text: Cancel — dreams have predicted things before, so why risk it.
options.outcome: One uncanny hit among thousands of forgotten dreams is an anecdote, not a forecasting system.

options.text: Ignore it entirely — feelings about a trip are irrational noise.
options.outcome: Dismissing the anxiety hides a legitimate prompt to double-check real risks; the dream is data about the dreamer.

c12_eng_k_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch02.scenario: Offered a scholarship abroad, a student freezes: a dying promise at home pulls one way, escape the other. Weeks pass and she hasn't answered the offer at all.
c12_eng_k_ch02.prompt: What does 'Eveline' warn about this limbo?

options.text: That paralysis is itself a choice — Joyce's Eveline stays not because duty won but because habit and guilt froze her; decide deliberately or the indecision decides for you.
options.outcome: The story's tragedy is that Eveline never chooses — she defaults. Naming the trade-off and choosing is the way out of paralysis.

options.text: Stay — duty to family always outranks personal freedom.
options.outcome: Joyce doesn't crown duty; he shows a mind so colonised by obligation it can't move — that's the disease, not the answer.

options.text: Let the deadline lapse — whatever happens without deciding was meant to be.
options.outcome: Defaulting is choosing by other means; Eveline 'chose' to stay precisely by failing to choose.

c12_eng_k_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch03.scenario: At a family wedding, an uncle who survived a violent displacement years ago freezes mid-dance, seeing faces that aren't there. Relatives hiss, 'it's been decades — move on.'
c12_eng_k_ch03.prompt: What does Singer's survivor-wedding story suggest instead?

options.text: Acknowledge it gently — 'A Wedding in Brownsville' shows the dead return uninvited at celebrations; trauma intrudes on joy, and recognition helps more than 'get over it'.
options.outcome: Survivor memory isn't a malfunction to suppress — the story treats the apparition as real grief doing its work.

options.text: They're right — decades should have healed it; the freeze is self-indulgence.
options.outcome: Time doesn't auto-delete trauma; the story's whole point is that annihilated worlds stay present at the feast.

options.text: Whisk him away and never mention it — silence is kindest.
options.outcome: Pretending it didn't happen isolates the survivor further; the enclave exists precisely because shared memory needs company.

c12_eng_k_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch04.scenario: A founder has rehearsed her 'big launch tomorrow' for two years. When a real customer finally shows up today, she turns them away — 'the real launch is coming.'

options.text: The fantasy of tomorrow has eaten the present — Hagberd rejects his actual returned son because the real thing can't compete with the rehearsed dream; take the imperfect today or lose it.
options.outcome: Living for an imagined tomorrow makes real arrivals look like impostors — the story's warning is to test hope against what's actually here.

options.text: Keep waiting — hope is always worth protecting from premature reality.
options.outcome: Hope without an expiry date curdles into self-deception; Hagberd's 'tomorrow' is a prison, not a promise.

options.text: Kill all hope — expectation is delusion by definition.
options.outcome: The story condemns fantasy substituted for life, not hope itself; acting on the real chance is hope working properly.

c12_eng_k_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch05.scenario: At a temple counter your daughter measures one centimetre over the free-entry height. The attendant waves you through anyway; she's watching you decide.
c12_eng_k_ch05.prompt: Pay or take the free pass?

options.text: Pay — 'One Centimetre' is about integrity measured in millimetres and watched by a child; the ticket is cheap, the lesson about rules and dignity is the real purchase.
options.outcome: Tao Ying's struggle shows the smallness of the money and the largeness of what a parent models — the centimetre is where character gets measured.

options.text: Take the pass — it's a centimetre; rules this trivial don't bind anyone.
options.outcome: That teaches her that rules apply only when inconvenient to you — the exact erosion the story dissects.

options.text: Take it — money saved is money spent on her later, which is more honest love.
options.outcome: Ends can't launder means a child is watching; she'll remember the shrug, not the arithmetic.

c12_eng_k_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch06.scenario: Two co-founders courted each other with polished masks; now the startup struggles and each privately hides bad metrics 'to keep the other confident'.

options.text: Drop the disguises — Donne's point is that love (or partnership) only stays at 'noon' when shadows, the little deceits of courtship and decline, stop growing between the two.
options.outcome: Early 'infant' disguises and late concealments are the same shadow at different hours; constancy needs daylight honesty.

options.text: Keep hiding — smooth confidence is what partnerships run on.
options.outcome: The poem argues exactly the reverse: managed appearances are shadows that lengthen until they blot out the thing itself.

options.text: Let it fade quietly — once the shadows start, decline is natural.
options.outcome: Donne's speaker fights decline with constancy; treating decay as destiny is surrender dressed as wisdom.

c12_eng_k_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch07.scenario: A school's board debates an expensive marble statue for a beloved retiring teacher versus funding the reading programme she built her life around.
c12_eng_k_ch07.prompt: Which honours her — the marble or the work?

options.text: The work — Milton's 'On Shakespeare' argues the true monument is built in transformed readers' minds; fund what she changed, not what commemorates her.
options.outcome: Shakespeare needs no tomb because his books are the sepulchre; a legacy lives in continued effect, not in stone.

options.text: The statue — a lasting monument is the only real proof of legacy.
options.outcome: Milton's point is precisely that marble is the weaker memorial; people who carry the teaching are the monument.

options.text: Neither — legacies are vanity; dissolve the programme and move on.
options.outcome: That confuses humility with erasure; sustaining her work honours her without feeding ego.

c12_eng_k_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch08.scenario: An NGO head notices their flagship 'compassion programme' quietly depends on keeping beneficiaries visibly needy for donors. Nobody wants to say it aloud.
c12_eng_k_ch08.prompt: What would Blake's paired poems flag here?

options.text: That a 'virtue' feeding on others' misery is already corrupt — 'The Human Abstract' shows pity engineered by those who need poverty to continue; redesign for dignity and self-sufficiency.
options.outcome: Blake's contrary states: the same organisation can house innocent intention and experienced cynicism — examine which your structure actually rewards.

options.text: Nothing — compassion is compassion; don't overthink a good deed.
options.outcome: The Divine Image taken alone misses that unexamined virtue can be manufactured by the very suffering it claims to relieve.

options.text: Shut it down — all organised charity is hidden cynicism.
options.outcome: Blake doesn't crown Experience as truth; he shows both states are human and the task is integration, not abandonment.

c12_eng_k_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch09.scenario: A writer is mid-flow on a dazzling draft when a 'person from Porlock' — a routine visitor — breaks the trance; the vision never fully returns.
c12_eng_k_ch09.prompt: What does the Kubla Khan story teach a team managing creative work?

options.text: Protect uninterrupted flow — Coleridge's lost dream shows a vision in motion can't simply be 'resumed later'; guard creative trance and capture what's salvageable rather than demanding instant re-entry.
options.outcome: The fragment is a wound, not a design: interruption destroyed the vision, and the surviving piece is still worth keeping.

options.text: No protection needed — you can always pick a thought back up where you left it.
options.outcome: Coleridge tried for hours and got only fragments; vision in flow is not a parked car.

options.text: Discard the fragment — unfinished work is failed work.
options.outcome: Kubla Khan became a touchstone precisely as a fragment; incompleteness can still be monumental.

c12_eng_k_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch10.scenario: Editing a young poet's manuscript, a colleague wants to strip out all her odd dashes and strange capitalisations 'to fix the grammar before we publish'.
c12_eng_k_ch10.prompt: Correct the strangeness or keep it?

options.text: Keep it until proven decorative — Dickinson's dashes and capitals aren't errors but tools that hold pauses and double meanings; 'fixing' them flattens the poem.
options.outcome: Before editing style into compliance, ask what the oddity is doing — in Dickinson the form carries the meaning.

options.text: Fix it — standard grammar exists so readers aren't confused.
options.outcome: That treats deliberate prosodic choice as a mistake; her compressed strangeness is the precision.

options.text: Publish it, but note she's a recluse so expect the work to be small and private anyway.
options.outcome: Her window-narrow life produced startlingly universal poems; biography doesn't bound imagination.

c12_eng_k_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch11.scenario: Back at a childhood lake for the first time in twenty years, a middle-aged alum watches the birds scatter unchanged and says bitterly, 'they're the same — only I've aged.'
c12_eng_k_ch11.prompt: How does Yeats frame that bitterness?

options.text: As the real subject — 'The Wild Swans at Coole' holds both truths at once: the swans' brilliant continuity and the speaker's nineteenth autumn; the pain is the gap, and naming it is the poem's consolation.
options.outcome: Continuity in the world plus change in the self is exactly the tension Yeats sits with — the swans aren't mocking him; they're measuring time.

options.text: He's right to be bitter — unchanging things exist to reproach the aging.
options.outcome: The poem reads permanence as beautiful, not mocking; turning it into an accusation is the bitterness talking.

options.text: Cheer up — nothing really changes, including him.
options.outcome: That denies the poem's whole grief; Yeats insists the change in the observer is real and counts.

c12_eng_k_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch12.scenario: A city's peace committee proposes demolishing a clock tower scarred by an old riot 'so the cycle of conflict is forgotten'.
c12_eng_k_ch12.prompt: Does erasing the landmark break the cycle?

options.text: No — Ramanujan's time-worn city shows violence repeats time and time again when memory is paved over; keep the scar visible and fix the causes, not the evidence.
options.outcome: The poem's looped time warns that forgetting is how the cycle reloads; honest memory is the interruption.

options.text: Yes — remove the symbol and the hostility loses its rallying point.
options.outcome: The poem's violence outlives its monuments; symbols don't cause the repetition, unaddressed grievances do.

options.text: It doesn't matter — history always repeats, so nothing we do helps.
options.outcome: Ramanujan observes the cycle to indict it; fatalism just agrees to the next round.

c12_eng_k_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch13.scenario: A daughter is told she must keep the crumbling ancestral house and 'the oldest blood in the world' — abandon her career in the city to guard the lineage.
c12_eng_k_ch13.prompt: What does Kamala Das's 'Blood' make of that demand?

options.text: It backs her break — the poem loves the house yet shows 'blood' pride as a script that cages women; she can honour the inheritance and still refuse the role it assigns her.
options.outcome: The speaker stays haunted but leaves anyway — loyalty to memory doesn't mean submission to the lineage's demands.

options.text: She must stay — bloodline duty outranks any individual life.
options.outcome: The poem reports the great-grandmother's claim ironically, exposing how 'oldest blood' talk serves the feudal order, not her.

options.text: She should go and feel nothing — attachment to an old house is irrational.
options.outcome: The poem refuses that easy exit too; the haunting is real, and denying it just hides the cost rather than paying it honestly.

c12_eng_k_ch14.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch14.scenario: A firm advertises 'total freedom at work' while wages force everyone into overtime obedience; meanwhile a visiting guru sells 'inner liberation' workshops to the same exhausted staff.
c12_eng_k_ch14.prompt: Shaw and Krishnamurti would diagnose this how?

options.text: Two different cages — Shaw's 'wage slavery' names the economic chain, Krishnamurti's 'conditioning' names the psychological one; fix the pay structure AND the mind, neither talk alone liberates.
options.outcome: Outer constraint and inner conditioning are separate problems; a mindfulness seminar can't shorten a workday.

options.text: The guru is right — freedom is an inner state, so circumstances don't matter.
options.outcome: That's Krishnamurti without Shaw; the wage chain binds regardless of how free the mind feels.

options.text: Only the law matters — pass rules and freedom follows automatically.
options.outcome: Shaw himself mocks that faith; conditioning survives rulebooks, which is why both diagnoses are needed.

c12_eng_k_ch15.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch15.scenario: Reviewing an experiment, the team spots an odd mark in the data and someone demands 'classify it now and move on'.
c12_eng_k_ch15.prompt: What would Woolf's mark on the wall suggest?

options.text: Sit with it first — the essay's whole method is resisting the reflex to label; let perception roam before deciding, because the premature category decides what you're allowed to see.
options.outcome: The mark turns out to be a snail — but the thinking it provoked was the real content; observation before classification is the skill.

options.text: Label it immediately — a mystery is just a task awaiting a tag.
options.outcome: That's the habit Woolf is unweaving: the instant category closes perception and you never see what the thing actually is.

options.text: Skip it — if it ends up trivial like a snail, the reflection was wasted anyway.
options.outcome: Judging the process by the triviality of the answer misses that the noticing itself was the point.

c12_eng_k_ch16.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch16.scenario: A studio buys rights to a dense literary novel and instructs the director: 'translate it page-for-page — faithfulness is everything.'

options.text: No — Bergman says film and literature are different languages; a literal translation wastes enormous effort for little fruit — reinvent the story in film's own terms or don't adapt it.
options.outcome: The conjurer works with rhythm and image on the nerves, not with sentences; fidelity to the letter can betray the spirit.

options.text: Yes — faithful means page-for-page, anything less betrays the book.
options.outcome: Bergman's warning is that the 'complicated adjustments' of literal adaptation usually bear no fruit; faithfulness is to the experience, not the page order.

options.text: Adapt anything — a film is basically an illustrated book anyway.
options.outcome: That erases the medium's distinct address to emotion; film isn't literature with pictures.

c12_eng_k_ch17.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch17.scenario: A health app tells a student 'we know you better than you know yourself — your sleep score, glucose and screen time say who you are.'

options.text: The metrics are parts — useful shadows of him, but the whole living, contradictory, changing person is greater than any dashboard; use the data without being reduced to it.
options.outcome: Lawrence's 'I am greater than my soul' logic applies: the finger, the gland, the score are fragments of 'man alive', never the sum.

options.text: True — the numbers are the person, finally measured.
options.outcome: That's exactly the reductionism Lawrence attacks: a part claiming to be the whole produces a 'man dead in life'.

options.text: Delete it — since no data can capture him, all metrics are worthless.
options.outcome: Anti-reductionism isn't anti-data; parts are still informative about the parts.

c12_eng_k_ch18.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch18.scenario: Drafting a club speech, a student writes: 'Indians have always argued, so democracy here is automatic and always included everyone.'

options.text: No — Sen qualifies everything: the argumentative tradition is real but historically excluded women, lower castes and classes; public reasoning strengthens democracy only when it's deliberately inclusive, not 'natural'.
options.outcome: The essay's power is in its qualifications — pride-affirming soundbites are precisely what it refuses to offer.

options.text: Yes — a talkative culture makes democracy inevitable.
options.outcome: Sen rejects cultural determinism; argument is a resource that must be used, not a guarantee.

options.text: Yes — and the tradition was open to everyone from the start.
options.outcome: Sen documents exactly who was shut out; romanticising the past as universal is the selectivity he warns against.

c12_eng_k_ch19.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch19.scenario: Marketing debates whether a quiet family drama aboard a generation ship 'counts' as science fiction for the catalogue — 'there isn't a single ray gun in it.'

options.text: Yes — Asimov's test is the background, not the props: a world running on different discovered rules makes it SF even if the plot is a domestic drama.
options.outcome: Spaceships and lasers are content; the genre marker is a society significantly transformed by science — which this has.

options.text: No — no gadgets, no aliens, no SF.
options.outcome: That's the marketing-trope definition Asimov dismantles; the background society is what does the classifying.

options.text: Yes — and anything set in the future or with magic like the Force is SF too.
options.outcome: Over-correcting breaks the other boundary: fantasy tropes in space costumes aren't SF because the laws of nature aren't the engine.

c12_eng_k_ch20.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch20.scenario: A long-excluded teammate is suddenly given real authority on the project — and immediately uses it to control and belittle the others.

options.text: That being recognised as human and learning to wield freedom are different steps — Prakriti's awakening curdles into possessive power because liberation arrived without maturity; coach her, don't just crown or strip her.
options.outcome: The play's tragedy is the gap between dignity granted and self-command learned — neither pure empowerment nor revoked authority is the answer.

options.text: Empowerment alone was the fix — oppression ends the moment power changes hands.
options.outcome: Act II exists precisely to disprove that; freedom without maturity can reproduce the very domination it escaped.

options.text: Take the authority back — this proves the marginalised can't handle power.
options.outcome: Tagore's point is the opposite: it's the long denial of humanity that deforms the first use of it, not unfitness.

c12_eng_k_ch21.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_k_ch21.scenario: An Indian novelist wins a big English-language prize and starts publicly disowning her earlier vernacular books as 'practice work in a smaller language'.
c12_eng_k_ch21.prompt: What would Karnad's Broken Images say?

options.text: That English success is legitimate but the denial fractures the self — the play interrogates a bilingual writer who must hold both languages without ranking one as the betrayal and the other as the coronation.
options.outcome: The 'broken images' are the selves she can't integrate; prestige in one tongue doesn't require disowning the other.

options.text: She's right — the English prize proves which language mattered.
options.outcome: That's the hierarchy the play dismantles; conflating market prestige with literary worth is the wound, not the win.

options.text: She's a traitor — writing in English at all is the betrayal.
options.outcome: Karnad lists a whole tradition of bilingual Indian writers; the guilt-trip is as false as the triumphalism.

c12_eng_v_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_v_ch01.scenario: A classmate drowning in board-exam stress swears he found a forgotten stairwell in the old school block that opens into the town as it looked decades ago — gaslights, quiet streets, no exam timetables. Everyone laughs; he insists it's real and keeps trying to go back.
c12_eng_v_ch01.prompt: How do you respond, having read 'The Third Level'?

options.text: Neither mock him nor book a ticket — hear it the way the psychiatrist frames Charley's third level: a waking-dream wish fulfillment. Ask what he's escaping, because the vividness of the refuge is a map of the anxiety he's fleeing.
options.outcome: Finney grounds the fantasy in an ordinary man under 'insecurity, fear, war, worry' — the experience is psychologically true even if the corridor isn't, so the useful move is listening to what the escape is escaping from.

options.text: Take his detailed description as proof and start searching for the stairwell yourself.
options.outcome: Vivid detail is exactly what makes wish fulfillment convincing — Charley's gaslights and derby hats felt real too; treating the description as evidence misses that the detail serves the longing, not the claim.

options.text: Tell him plainly he's making it up and should get back to revision.
options.outcome: That repeats Louisa's anger and the friends' disbelief — the story shows dismissal isolates the believer without touching the wish that produced the dream.

c12_eng_v_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_v_ch02.scenario: A senior's horoscope once 'warned' he'd fail at his hundredth venture, so he's obsessively raced through 99 small projects and is now engineering the hundredth to be bulletproof — while ignoring a trivial, silly flaw in it.
c12_eng_v_ch02.prompt: What does 'The Tiger King' suggest here?

options.text: Watch for the wooden tiger — the Maharaja survives 99 real tigers but is killed by a sliver from a toy; obsession with defeating a prophecy blinds you to the absurd, insignificant thing that actually fulfils it.
options.outcome: The story's situational irony is that the prophecy arrives disguised as a birthday gift; treating the threat as a tiger-shaped contest is exactly the blindness that gets the Maharaja.

options.text: Help him make project number hundred genuinely flawless so the prediction can't bite.
options.outcome: That's the Maharaja's own logic — hunting the 100th tiger harder; the dewan's planted, half-dead tiger already shows the real danger isn't the one you're staging.

options.text: Tell him prophecies are nonsense, so project hundred carries no special risk at all.
options.outcome: The story doesn't disprove the prophecy — it fulfils it through the least respected object in the tale; dismissing the warning entirely misses that anxiety about the wrong target is itself the hazard.

c12_eng_v_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_v_ch03.scenario: You're back from an internship field visit to a shrinking wetland and must write it up. Your draft is a day-by-day diary: arrived, walked, sampled water, came home.
c12_eng_v_ch03.prompt: How would the structure of 'Journey to the End of the Earth' improve it?

options.text: Restructure it as an argument, not a diary — open with the sensory arrival, flash back to the wetland's deep history, lay out the human damage, describe the restoration effort, and end on one epiphanic moment of physically standing in the water.
options.outcome: Doshi makes structure the argument: the Gondwana timescale reframes the present, the Students on Ice section pivots from despair to agency, and the walk on the frozen ocean condenses the whole thesis into one moment.

options.text: Keep the diary — chronological order is the most honest record of what you actually did.
options.outcome: That produces the summary-level reading the chapter warns against: the geological flashback isn't 'background', it's the device that makes the later data mean something; without it the visit is a list of events.

options.text: Cut the personal parts and report only the data so it reads as objective science.
options.outcome: The text's first-person reflective voice is what anchors geological scale in human perception; stripping the 'I' loses the epiphany that turns information into responsibility.

c12_eng_v_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_v_ch04.scenario: You're a first-aid volunteer at a zonal tournament. An opposing team's player — who earlier got your teammate fouled out and is widely hated by your side — collapses near your post, bleeding and alone. Your teammates mutter 'let their own people handle him.'
c12_eng_v_ch04.prompt: What would Sadao's choice in 'The Enemy' prescribe?

options.text: Treat him first and quietly — Sadao operates on the American POW because the surgeon's duty to a bleeding human overrides the wartime label 'enemy'; afterwards you can let the officials sort out the politics, as Sadao lets the General's system handle the rest.
options.outcome: The story's climax is the surgery itself — 'My friend' murmured to an enemy under the knife — and its resolution is deliberately quiet: doing the human thing without needing to be seen as a hero or a traitor.

options.text: Call his side's medical tent and wait — he's their responsibility.
options.outcome: That's the servants' and Yumi's position in the story — the refusal that makes Sadao act alone; the chapter treats deferring to the group as the failure, not the safe middle path.

options.text: Treat him but report him to the organisers afterwards to stay safe.
options.outcome: That reverses the story's architecture — Sadao provides the boat and signal code instead of the General's assassins; the chapter's point is that professional mercy isn't complete until the person is out of danger, not merely bandaged.

c12_eng_v_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_v_ch05.scenario: A new teammate with a facial scar always sits alone at lunch and skips group events. You've had one warm conversation with her and promised 'I'll sit with you tomorrow' — then your own friends pull you to their table.
c12_eng_v_ch05.prompt: What does 'On the Face of It' say about your promise?

options.text: Keep it — actually go back. Mr Lamb's bitter aside 'They never do come back' exists because kindness without return is the pattern; Derry's return matters precisely because everyone else failed to, and the tragedy is arriving after the chance is gone.
options.outcome: The play's three-scene arc builds everything on whether Derry returns; the garden means nothing as a one-visit kindness and everything as a chosen connection — your table tomorrow is the point, not your sympathy today.

options.text: She probably prefers being left alone anyway, like Derry claims to.
options.outcome: That's the misreading the play dismantles — Derry's 'I don't care' is armour built from others' stares, not preference; Mr Lamb reads the withdrawal as a wound to be answered with welcome, not respected as a wish.

options.text: One kind conversation already counts — you showed her someone cares.
options.outcome: The off-stage fall makes the point brutally: single visits don't save anyone, and the window is short; the play measures connection by the return, not the first approach.

c12_eng_v_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_eng_v_ch06.scenario: At your coaching institute, a girl from a marginalised community is quietly served tea last and made to sit apart 'as per tradition.' She's furious and ready to drop out; others say either fight publicly or swallow it.
c12_eng_v_ch06.prompt: Which path does 'Memories of Childhood' validate?

options.text: Annan's answer to Bama: the humiliation is real and rage is justified, but the durable reply is to study, excel, and make yourself impossible to keep out — Bama tops her class and the same village comes to her.
options.outcome: Both episodes pair violation with response: Zitkala-Sa loses her hair to forced assimilation; Bama converts the vadai-packet humiliation into academic climb, because education is the one door the hierarchy can't hold shut.

options.text: Make a scene right there — public protest is the only language such insults understand.
options.outcome: The chapter distinguishes anger from strategy: Bama's fury is validated but channelled; Annan explicitly warns that indignation without education changes nothing about who gets served last.

options.text: Advise her to endure quietly — making waves will only make the exclusion worse.
options.outcome: That's the reading the paired structure refutes: neither woman resigns — one resists bodily and is overpowered, the other resists through achievement; the chapter never treats silent endurance as dignity.

c12_geo_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_geo_ch01.scenario: On an internship with a district development cell, you're reviewing two proposals for a flood-prone river valley: one diverts 90% of the river for an industrial estate, the other tunnels a metro link under the floodplain but fits flood-gates and leaves minimum ecological flow.
c12_geo_ch01.prompt: Which proposal does human geography's determinism-possibilism-neo-determinism debate support?

options.text: The flood-gated tunnel — it humanises nature through technology while still obeying the 'red signals' neo-determinism demands; the 90% diversion is possibilism ignoring ecological limits, like hydropower projects that dry downstream springs.
options.outcome: The chapter's middle path is the point: technology lets humans modify nature, but Griffith Taylor's 'stop-and-go' determinism says you stop when nature signals — downstream springs drying is exactly that signal.

options.text: The full diversion — technology exists precisely to free humans from nature's constraints, so bigger modification means bigger development.
options.outcome: That's pure possibilism without the brake; the chapter's own test case shows diverting nearly all of a river's flow is unsustainable humanisation that triggers the very 'red signal' neo-determinism warns about.

options.text: Reject both — any modification of a river valley violates the environment; leave it to nature.
options.outcome: That swings to naturalisation — humans dictated by nature; the chapter treats technology within ecological limits as legitimate, so refusing all modification throws away the neo-determinist option.

c12_geo_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_geo_ch02.scenario: An investment pitch for an agri-startup shows a region's crude density is only 90 persons per sq km and concludes 'land is plentiful — pressure on farmland is low.' A glance at the map shows most of the region is desert and rocky upland.
c12_geo_ch02.prompt: How do you check that claim before endorsing the pitch?

options.text: Compute physiological density — population divided by net cultivable area. Like Egypt, where crude density is low but nearly everyone crowds onto the Nile strip, the real pressure on farmland could be extreme once uncultivable land is removed from the denominator.
options.outcome: Crude density dilutes pressure by counting desert and mountain; physiological density is the honest measure of population-land stress, and the pitch's conclusion can flip completely.

options.text: Accept the pitch — 90 per sq km is objectively sparse, so farmland pressure must be low.
options.outcome: That's the crude-density trap the chapter warns about: total area includes land that can never grow a crop, so a 'sparse' region can be one where every cultivable acre is overworked.

options.text: Use agricultural density instead — farmers per cultivable area tells you everything the pitch needs.
options.outcome: Agricultural density measures labour intensity, not population pressure on land; a region can have few farmers per hectare yet still carry a huge non-farming population that cultivable land must feed.

c12_geo_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_geo_ch03.scenario: Interning at a state policy cell, you're asked which of two districts deserves a 'model development' citation. District A has higher per-capita income; District B has lower income but better life expectancy, higher literacy, and stronger public services.
c12_geo_ch03.prompt: What does the human development framework say?

options.text: Cite District B — growth is quantitative and value-neutral while development is qualitative and value-positive; the capability approach counts health and education as capabilities in themselves, so lower income can still mean higher development, as Kerala shows against richer states.
options.outcome: The chapter's core claim: development happens only when capabilities enlarge real choices — B's life expectancy and literacy are development; A's income is only growth.

options.text: Cite District A — higher income means higher development; health and literacy follow money automatically.
options.outcome: That's the income approach the chapter refutes: positive growth does not always lead to development, and identical-income states can sit far apart on human development once you look at capabilities.

options.text: Declare it a tie — since the comparison mixes economic and social indicators, no ranking is possible.
options.outcome: False neutrality misses the framework: the capability approach exists precisely to rank such cases — B's superior health and education outcomes make it more developed despite lower income.

c12_geo_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_geo_ch04.scenario: At a district planning internship, a fast-growing settlement of 6,000 people with paved streets and dense housing is up for classification. Your supervisor calls it 'obviously urban now' — but the data shows 80% of its male main workers still work in agriculture and it has no municipal notification.
c12_geo_ch04.prompt: How does the Census of India classify it?

options.text: Rural — it passes the 5,000 population and 400/km² density tests but fails the strict third test: at least 75% of male main workers in non-agricultural work; all three criteria apply conjunctively, so urban looks don't make it urban.
options.outcome: The chapter's point is that the rural-urban line is multi-dimensional: morphological urbanism (concrete, crowding) with an agrarian workforce stays rural in Census terms until it clears every threshold.

options.text: Urban — 6,000 people and urban morphology settle it; workforce composition is a secondary detail.
options.outcome: That's the classic board-exam error: rounding 'mostly' to urban while ignoring the exact 75% non-agricultural cut-off; a big farming village is still a village to the Census.

options.text: It's a census town, since any settlement crossing 5,000 qualifies statistically.
options.outcome: Census town status needs all three criteria — population, density, and the 75% non-agricultural workforce; crossing only the population bar is not enough.

c12_geo_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_geo_ch05.scenario: A resource company scouting a dry savanna reports the land is 'virtually empty — under one person per sq km — and unproductive,' so acquiring it for a project should be simple. You know scattered forager camps use the area seasonally.
c12_geo_ch05.prompt: How does the geography of hunting and gathering change the assessment?

options.text: Low density is carrying capacity, not emptiness — wild resources are dispersed and unpredictable, so a small forager group legitimately needs a vast range; 'unproductive' land is the group's entire food system, as with the San in the Kalahari.
options.outcome: The chapter explains why such activity survives only in marginal environments and why densities stay under one per sq km: the land is fully used, just at an extensive intensity that maps and headcounts miss.

options.text: Agree — with under a person per sq km, the camps are a rounding error and relocation is trivial.
options.outcome: That misreads the density: the small number is the *result* of needing huge area per person; displacing the group means taking away an enormous foraging territory, not a tiny plot.

options.text: The camps are pastoralists moving herds, so buying grazing rights covers their use anyway.
options.outcome: Foragers aren't pastoralists — they depend on wild game and plants, not domesticated herds; the distinction matters because fencing 'grazing land' still removes the wild tubers and game they actually live on.

c12_geo_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_geo_ch06.scenario: A friend's agri-startup is pitching two units to investors: a sugar mill and a beverage-bottling plant. To save on 'factory costs', the deck puts both units side-by-side at a single industrial park near the city market.
c12_geo_ch06.prompt: What does the geography of manufacturing say about that site plan?

options.text: Split them — the sugar mill belongs in the cane fields because cane loses sucrose within a day or two of cutting and sheds weight as it's crushed; the bottling plant belongs near the market because adding water makes the product heavier, so value-to-weight pulls it marketward.
options.outcome: Perishability and weight-loss push raw-material-oriented location; weight-gain pushes market-oriented location — the same industrial park can't be right for both ends of that logic.

options.text: Approve it — co-locating shares power and labour, and raw materials can always be trucked in.
options.outcome: Trucking cane loses sucrose to enzymatic inversion on the way — the value literally evaporates in transit; the chapter's 24–48 hour crushing window is why mills sit inside cane belts, not beside markets.

options.text: Object that neither counts as real manufacturing anyway — both are just processing, not factory production.
options.outcome: That's the scale misconception: manufacturing is any transformation of raw material into a more valuable product — a village oil ghani and a pulping plant qualify; the objection discards the framework instead of using it.

c12_geo_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_geo_ch07.scenario: Your college incubation cell is helping a farmer collective export Alphonso mangoes to the Gulf. A junior's plan books the cheapest surface freight and lists the route as 'port to port', with no mention of cold storage, customs, or ripening at the destination.
c12_geo_ch07.prompt: What does the tertiary-activities framework flag in this plan?

options.text: That trade is door-to-door spatial transfer, not port-to-port — perishable mangoes need reefer trucks, phytosanitary certification, cold-chain continuity and ripening chambers as auxiliary services, so the 'cheapest' leg can be the most expensive failure.
options.outcome: The chapter treats transport, banking, insurance and customs as the enabling services that make exchange real; for a 3–4 week shelf-life fruit, transferability — not distance — decides whether the trade exists at all.

options.text: Approve it — trade just means buying cheap here and selling dear there; the rest is logistics detail.
options.outcome: That reduces trade to arbitrage and deletes exactly what makes it tertiary: the value is added by services bridging space, and without them the mangoes arrive as pulp, not product.

options.text: Switch the plan to domestic mandis only — exports are what 'trade' really means, but they're too complex for a small collective.
options.outcome: Both the premise and retreat are wrong: domestic wholesale and retail are trade too — employing far more people than foreign trade — and perishability can be engineered with a cold chain, not avoided by staying local.

c12_geo_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_geo_ch08.scenario: On a logistics internship, your team must move 2,500 tonnes of coal 1,500 km to a southern port. A colleague argues for booking 100 trucks because 'each truck arrives faster than a train, so road wins on speed.'
c12_geo_ch08.prompt: How do you evaluate that argument?

options.text: Send it by rail — one broad-gauge rake of 58 wagons carries the whole consignment in a single movement, and for bulk commodities over long hauls capacity and cost-per-tonne beat per-vehicle speed; road's door-to-door flexibility doesn't change that physics.
options.outcome: The chapter's comparison is about matching mode to cargo: rail is high-capacity long-distance haulage, while a hundred trucks is a hundred vehicle movements doing one rake's work.

options.text: Back the trucks — faster per vehicle means the coal arrives sooner, and that's what the client pays for.
options.outcome: Per-vehicle speed confuses unit velocity with consignment throughput; coordinating 100 truck trips over 1,500 km is slower, costlier and more failure-prone than one scheduled rake for bulk freight.

options.text: Recommend converting any metre-gauge section on the route to broad gauge first so the line runs faster.
options.outcome: Gauge conversion is about interoperability and axle-load, not speed, and Project Unigauge's own economics show conversion is only justified where traffic density repays the cost — it's a separate decision from this consignment.

c12_geo_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_geo_ch09.scenario: A classmate's infographic on Indian population density declares Uttar Pradesh 'the most crowded state because it has India's biggest population', and uses five equal-width colour classes from 17 to 11,297 persons per sq km — leaving almost every state the same colour.
c12_geo_ch09.prompt: What corrections does this chapter demand?

options.text: Two fixes — density is persons per unit area, not total population, so Bihar, West Bengal and Kerala outrank UP and Delhi (11,297) dwarfs all states; and an outlier like Delhi needs its own class or inset, or equal intervals flatten every real difference.
options.outcome: The chapter separates arithmetic density from population size and warns that classification schemes decide whether a map informs or misleads — an extreme value can't share a linear scale.

options.text: Keep it — biggest population does mean most crowded; density is just population restated.
options.outcome: That's the exact misconception the chapter names: UP's 828/km² sits below Bihar's 1,102 and far below Delhi; size and crowding measure different things.

options.text: Report physiological density instead so farmland pressure is captured accurately for every state.
options.outcome: Physiological density answers a different question — pressure on cultivated land — and needs net-cultivated-area data the map doesn't have; the fix for this graphic is better classes and outlier handling, not a different indicator.

c12_geo_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_geo_ch10.scenario: On a field survey in the lower Himalayan valleys, your team finds a revenue village made of five small hut-clusters 200–500 m apart across terraces, each with its own name. A teammate writes in the report: 'no real village here — just scattered isolated houses.'
c12_geo_ch10.prompt: How should the settlement actually be classified?

options.text: Hamleted — physically separate, separately named units that still share one village identity and administration; such units are locally called panna, para, palli, nagla, dhani or tola in different regions, so the fragmentation isn't absence of a settlement.
options.outcome: The chapter's distinction is precise: hamleted villages break into named sub-units but keep common revenue identity, while truly dispersed settlement lacks nucleation altogether — the teammate conflated the two.

options.text: Dispersed — five separated clusters on terraces fits 'scattered huts' by definition.
options.outcome: Dispersed means isolated dwellings without shared nucleation — Kerala homesteads or Meghalaya jhum clearings; named clusters under one village administration is the signature of hamleted, not dispersed.

options.text: Clustered — since people still group into huts rather than living alone, the core pattern is nucleation.
options.outcome: Clustered means one compact nucleus; five distinct named groups separated by cultivated terraces is precisely the in-between form the hamleted category exists to describe.

c12_geo_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_geo_ch11.scenario: At a journalism internship, your editor drafts a celebratory headline: 'India's forests grew from 14% to 24% — green cover nearly doubled since 1950.' The source is a land-revenue statistics table, not satellite imagery.
c12_geo_ch11.prompt: What correction does the land-use chapter require before publishing?

options.text: Reframe it — 'area under forest' in revenue records means legally notified forest land, not measured tree canopy; the rise reflects administrative reclassification while actual forest cover may have stagnated or degraded.
options.outcome: The chapter drills exactly this trap: legal category and physical cover are different variables, and the revenue table answers 'how much land is reserved for forests', not 'how much forest exists'.

options.text: Run it — a 10-point rise in the official statistics is a solid story either way.
options.outcome: The number is real but the claim isn't: notified area grew while satellite-measured cover tells a different story, so the headline converts a bookkeeping change into an ecological claim.

options.text: Flip the headline to 'net sown area rose, so farmland is not scarce' — land-use data is too ambiguous for forest claims anyway.
options.outcome: That makes the opposite error: net sown area grew by drawing down culturable wasteland and fallows — the cultivable stock shrank even as the cropped share rose, which is why the chapter pushes land-saving technology.

c12_geo_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_geo_ch12.scenario: In a school water-policy debate, a teammate argues: 'Just dam the Brahmaputra and the Ganga — they carry most of India's surface water, so our scarcity problem is engineering laziness, not geography.'
c12_geo_ch12.prompt: What's the strongest counter from the water-resources chapter?

options.text: Availability isn't harnessability — the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Barak basins hold ~60% of surface water on a third of the land, but Himalayan rivers carry huge sediment loads, run through seismic zones, braid in the plains and cross international boundaries; the fully-dammed basins are the seasonal Peninsular ones where storage was technically easy.
options.outcome: The chapter's paradox is that the biggest rivers are the least harnessed precisely because geology and geopolitics constrain them — scarcity policy must work around that, not pretend it's laziness.

options.text: Concede — whichever basin holds the most water is the obvious first place to build.
options.outcome: That reads the flow table and skips the constraints: sediment chokes reservoirs, seismicity threatens dams, braided channels defy storage, and the Brahmaputra involves China and Bangladesh — big water, hard walls.

options.text: Counter that all Himalayan rivers are snow-fed and all Peninsular rivers are seasonal, so the comparison is meaningless.
options.outcome: The binary breaks at sub-basin scale — the chapter notes the Narmada's perennial upper reaches and the Kaveri's near-perennial Western Ghats catchment; regimes are hybrid, which actually strengthens the site-by-site analysis the debate needs.
