options.text: Challenge the rigidity — the Deccan ryots faced an 'average-rent' demand that stayed fixed while rainfall didn't, so they borrowed from moneylenders and slid into debt; the 1875 riots were the system's design meeting the land's reality, not farmer failure.
options.outcome: The chapter's lesson: an elegant theory (Ricardo's surplus) produced a debt trap because the demand was inflexible against a volatile climate — fairness on paper isn't fairness in the field.

options.text: Endorse it — cutting out intermediaries and assessing each field directly protects the farmer.
options.outcome: That was Munro's stated aim and the system's promise — but direct settlement meant the ryot faced the state alone with no buffer; removing the middleman didn't protect him, it exposed him.

options.text: Accept it with longer terms — the only flaw was the 30-year revision cycle.
options.outcome: Revisions made it worse, not better — rates climbed at each resurvey while depressions got no relief; the asymmetry captured upswings and ignored downturns, so time alone doesn't fix the design.

c12_hist_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hist_ch10.scenario: After identical flash protests erupt at a dozen colleges in one week — same signal, same slogans, same sequence — a dean insists 'it was clearly all spontaneous imitation, so there's no organiser to talk to.'
c12_hist_ch10.prompt: What does the 1857 spread tell you about 'spontaneous' identical patterns?

options.text: The pattern is the coordination — cantonments repeated signal → arms → treasury → proclamations because regiments wrote to each other, emissaries moved, and nightly panchayats decided; identical steps across distance are a network's fingerprint, not proof of no one talking.
options.outcome: The chapter's evidence: sepoy letters and panchayats are documented — 'spontaneous' is how coordination looks from outside when the channels are informal.

options.text: Agree — if there's no single mastermind, it was spontaneous.
options.outcome: 1857 had no mastermind either — Bahadur Shah and Nana Sahib were pushed into leadership by the sepoys; distributed coordination through networks still leaves a structure to read.

options.text: Conclude the opposite — an identical pattern must mean a single central command.
options.outcome: That over-corrects: the revolt's channels were lateral — regiment to regiment, panchayat to panchayat — coordination without a commander; 'one pattern' doesn't require 'one hand.'

c12_hist_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hist_ch11.scenario: Researching a 1919 hartal for a paper, you find a police fortnightly report saying 'the peasantry is harvesting, students are in exams — meetings excite little or no interest.' Your partner wants to cite it as proof the hartal failed.
c12_hist_ch11.prompt: What should a historian ask of that report first?

options.text: Whose interest does it serve, and when was it written — colonial police reports minimised unrest as a matter of job description and were filed before full information arrived; the same source class dismissed Punjab's tension right up to Jallianwala Bagh.
options.outcome: The chapter's source-criticism lesson: an interested narrative isn't a neutral fact — the report documents what the administration wished were true, which is itself evidence of what it feared.

options.text: Cite it — a government report is a primary source, so it's hard evidence the hartal failed.
options.outcome: Primary doesn't mean neutral: the report is primary evidence of the Home Department's posture, not of crowd size — using it to prove absence of unrest reads the author's wish as the event.

options.text: Discard it — a biased source can teach nothing.
options.outcome: The opposite error: the report's very need to downplay the hartal is evidence the administration felt the pressure — bias tells you what the state feared, which is historical data too.

c12_hist_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hist_ch12.scenario: A school exhibition poster declares 'Ambedkar wrote our Constitution single-handedly' — and a classmate counters 'he was just the chairman, he wrote nothing.'
c12_hist_ch12.prompt: What does the Drafting Committee's record actually support?

options.text: Split the difference precisely — Ambedkar piloted the draft through clause-by-clause debates and shaped its core, but the Committee had six other members, B.N. Rau built the blueprint before it met, and the Assembly adopted thousands of amendments; it's a collective text he steered.
options.outcome: The chapter's verdict: 'Ambedkar's Constitution' is half-true — he's first among equals, not sole author, and 'just chairman' erases the hand that stitched committee reports into legal articles.

options.text: Keep the poster — chairman of the drafting body effectively means sole author.
options.outcome: That erases Munshi, Aiyar, the Ayyangars and Rau's prior blueprint — and the Assembly's 2,000-plus amendments; sole authorship is a myth the records don't bear.

options.text: Side with the classmate — a committee product means no individual mattered.
options.outcome: Collective doesn't mean anonymous: Ambedkar's fingerprints are on Article 17's absolutism and the strong-Centre stance alike; the process was collective but the steering was his.

c12_hs_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch01.scenario: At a career seminar, a speaker says a neighbour who cooks, cleans and cares for an elderly parent all day 'doesn't work', while her husband's office job 'counts.' A classmate also argues that the street vendor outside, who has a municipal licence, 'does informal work, so it's basically illegal.'
c12_hs_ch01.prompt: How does the paid/unpaid and formal/informal matrix correct both claims?

options.text: Separate the two axes — the neighbour does unpaid informal work with real economic value and no protection; the vendor is paid but informal — legal yet without contract, PF or sick leave; 'informal' describes missing legal safeguards, not illegality or low worth.
options.outcome: The chapter's matrix exists to expose the double blindness: unpaid care work substitutes for market services and enables others' paid work, while informal workers lack protection — neither means 'not work' or 'illegal.'

options.text: Agree on both — unpaid work isn't employment, and no-contract work is outside the law.
options.outcome: Both conflate categories the chapter separates: unpaid ≠ valueless, and informal ≠ illegal — a licensed vendor trades lawfully; she just lacks the employer-employee relationship that carries statutory protection.

options.text: Fix it by re-labelling — call the vendor 'formal' since she has a licence, and the caregiver 'paid' since her work has value.
options.outcome: A vending licence grants spatial legitimacy, not employment status, and economic value isn't wages; renaming the cells doesn't move the worker into them — the matrix is about protection and pay, not dignity labels.

c12_hs_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch02.scenario: A fitness-app founder pitches at your school: 'Food is fuel — macros, calories, nothing more. We strip the sentiment out of eating.'
c12_hs_ch02.prompt: Which of the three functions of food does the pitch erase?

options.text: Two of them — the pitch covers only the physiological function; food also works psychologically (comfort, pleasure, security) and socio-culturally (festival dishes, langar, hospitality) — a festival sweet is the same flour and sugar as any dessert, but the occasion is what it feeds.
options.outcome: The chapter's point: context decides the dominant function — identical nutrients serve energy in one meal and identity in another; 'just fuel' reads composition and misses the reason for eating.

options.text: Endorse it — nutrition science is objective; attaching emotion to food causes bad eating.
options.outcome: The chapter treats the psychological and social functions as real functions, not noise — comfort eating and festival food meet needs the calorie count can't see; stripping them doesn't make eating 'pure', it makes it incomplete.

options.text: Concede partially — keep a 'cheat meal' slot for the emotional side.
options.outcome: That quarantines what the chapter integrates: one meal can serve all three functions at once — comfort, bonding and nourishment aren't separate courses to be scheduled.

c12_hs_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch03.scenario: A neighbour is in a panic because a milestone-checklist app flagged her three-year-old for 'not yet speaking in full sentences', while her own mother shrugs that 'children bloom differently.'
c12_hs_ch03.prompt: How do the eight development stages advise her?

options.text: Stages are signposts, not stopwatches — early childhood spans two to six years and its milestones mark the typical range; development is plastic and rates vary, so a range flag invites observation and if needed guidance — not a verdict that the child is 'behind.'
options.outcome: The chapter frames milestones as anchors within wide stages, not rigid deadlines — multidimensional, modifiable development means an app flag is a reason to watch, not to panic.

options.text: Trust the app — milestones exist precisely because there's a correct schedule.
options.outcome: That reads stages as rigid rules, which the chapter rejects: the eight stages describe sequence with varying rate; a single flag is a screening prompt, not a diagnosis.

options.text: Dismiss the flag entirely — all children catch up, so there's nothing to look at.
options.outcome: Plasticity cuts both ways — development varies AND responds to support; ignoring the flag throws away the early-help window the stages exist to open.

c12_hs_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch04.scenario: A junior merchandiser is choosing between two cotton bales for a fine shirting yarn: both show 28 mm mean length, but bale B is cheaper. The lab sheet shows B's length-uniformity index is 72% against A's 84%.
c12_hs_ch04.prompt: What does the fibre data say about the cheaper bale?

options.text: Reject B for this yarn — identical mean length hides B's heavy share of short fibres that slip drafting control, causing thick-thin places, fibre fly and ends-down; spinning performance runs on length distribution, not the average.
options.outcome: The chapter's trap is exactly this: quoting the 28 mm average while missing uniformity — the short-fibre fraction is what degrades evenness and productivity.

options.text: Buy B — same staple length at lower cost is pure margin.
options.outcome: Same mean, different distribution: the savings get spent on breakages, uneven yarn and rework — the lab numbers already priced the difference, the merchandiser just didn't read it.

options.text: Blend both bales to average out the risk.
options.outcome: Blending dilutes but doesn't remove short fibres — they still float in the drafting zone; mixing keeps the failure mode alive at half strength instead of removing it.

c12_hs_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch05.scenario: Planning a family function on a tight budget, one cousin wants to outsource everything — caterer, decorator, tailor — 'money is the resource, let's spend it.' Your aunt counters that the family's own skills should carry the load.
c12_hs_ch05.prompt: How does the human/non-human resource classification settle it?

options.text: Classify before spending — the aunt's tailoring, the cousin's negotiation skill and everyone's time are human resources that grow with use; the savings and hired services are non-human and only deplete — so deploy skills first and let money cover what skills can't.
options.outcome: The chapter's rule: the label dictates the management — human resources you develop and use, non-human you acquire and conserve; spending money where a skill exists buys depletion instead of growth.

options.text: Side with outsourcing — paying professionals is simpler and frees everyone's time.
options.outcome: That conserves one resource by draining the other — and on a tight budget, money is the scarcer cell; skills left unused don't replenish the account that outsourcing empties.

options.text: Side with the aunt entirely — use only family skills and spend nothing.
options.outcome: Time and energy are human resources too and they deplete in the day — a plan that burns the family ragged to save every rupee misreads 'human' as 'free.'

c12_hs_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch06.scenario: Your college NSS team plans a 'Scientific Goat Rearing' camp in a tribal block: three days of PowerPoint lectures on breeds and feed charts. On day one the hall is half-empty and a village woman mutters that nobody asked what the goat-keepers actually need.
c12_hs_ch06.prompt: What do the principles of extension education say went wrong?

options.text: Everything structural — the topic was officer-driven not need-driven, the classroom format ignored the oral, hands-on culture, and one-way slides violated participation; fix it with a needs assessment first, demonstrations in the local dialect, and experienced local keepers as co-trainers.
options.outcome: Extension is voluntary — learners can walk out, so the worker must earn relevance; the failure here is pedagogy contradicting the philosophy, not bad logistics.

options.text: The problem was scheduling — shift the lectures to evenings when villagers are free.
options.outcome: Timing treats a design failure as logistics: even a full hall of slide-watchers is one-way communication; participation and felt need are what make extension stick, not attendance hours.

options.text: Make attendance mandatory through the panchayat so the information reaches everyone.
options.outcome: Extension is voluntary by definition — compelled attendance turns the facilitator into an authority figure and kills the trust that makes communities adopt change.

c12_hs_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch07.scenario: A playschool coordinator designs a toddler motor-skills hour that opens with bead-threading 'because it's quiet,' ends with running, and publishes a weekly 'fastest developer' chart ranking the children.
c12_hs_ch07.prompt: Which development principles does the design violate?

options.text: Both — the sequence runs backwards: proximodistal and cephalocaudal order says whole-body and arm control come before finger work, so gross motor should precede beads; and the ranking chart violates individuality — children share the sequence but not the timetable.
options.outcome: The chapter separates what directionality fixes (order of skills) from what individuality permits (pace of arriving); the session inverts the first and denies the second.

options.text: Only the chart is wrong — starting with beads is fine because fine motor needs the freshest attention.
options.outcome: Attention isn't the constraint the principles describe — distal control matures after proximal; demanding precise finger work before the large-muscle foundation asks for a skill that isn't built yet.

options.text: Only the ordering is wrong — the chart is motivating because kids compete.
options.outcome: Competition presumes a shared timetable, which individuality denies — a 'fastest developer' chart ranks children against a schedule that was never theirs, misreading normal variation as speed.

c12_hs_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch08.scenario: A student designing costumes for a school play wants the short lead actor to 'look bigger on stage' and reaches for a bold horizontally-striped fabric; the director wants the character to read as dignified and tall.
c12_hs_ch08.prompt: What do the elements of design say to cut instead?

options.text: Vertical lines — they stress up-and-down movement, emphasise height and read severe, dignified, reserved; horizontal stripes create the illusion of width and a placid effect — the opposite of what the role and the actor need.
options.outcome: The chapter's line-effect map is the tool: line direction is chosen for the visual job — elongation, width or movement — not for what looks 'bold' on the bolt.

options.text: Keep the horizontal stripes — bold pattern reads as presence from the back rows.
options.outcome: The chapter maps horizontal lines to width and stability — 'bigger' sideways, not taller or more dignified; boldness of motif doesn't change the direction the eye travels.

options.text: Use diagonal zigzags — movement reads as energy, which is bigger than height.
options.outcome: Diagonals signal motion and restlessness, not the stillness of dignity; the role's requirement is elongation plus reserve, which is vertical line's job — energy answers a different brief.

c12_hs_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch09.scenario: A newly pregnant colleague's grandmother insists she 'eat for two' — double rotis, double milk — while her doctor has prescribed folic acid and a modest calorie increase. The family calls the doctor 'stingy.'
c12_hs_ch09.prompt: What does the pregnancy RDA actually say?

options.text: The doctor is calibrated — ICMR adds roughly 350–450 kcal and about 10–23 g of protein, not double portions; the big demands are micronutrients like iron and folic acid, with folate's largest increment in the first trimester for the neural tube, not a second stomach's worth of food.
options.outcome: The chapter's point: 'eating for two' describes quality and specific nutrients, not quantity doubled — blood volume, fetal skeleton and neural tube each bill specific nutrients, not bulk calories.

options.text: Side with the grandmother — a growing baby needs double the intake, simple arithmetic.
options.outcome: The arithmetic is wrong: the fetus is a fraction of the mother's mass, and the RDA's increments are modest and timed — doubling calories buys surplus weight, not the iron and folate the physiology actually demands.

options.text: Split it — keep normal calories but double the folic acid through all nine months.
options.outcome: Folate isn't flat either: its biggest increment covers the first-trimester neural tube window and tapers later; doubling it throughout misses that the demand is critical-period, not constant.

c12_hs_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch10.scenario: Your hostel mess serves an identical thali to everyone. The state-level footballer finishes still hungry while the sedentary day-scholar leaves half — and the warden calls it 'fair: same food for all.'
c12_hs_ch10.prompt: What do the factors affecting meal planning say about 'same for all'?

options.text: Fair isn't identical — age, activity and economics set each person's RDA; the athlete's energy and protein needs run roughly a thousand calories above the sedentary student's, so identical plates underfeed one and overfeed the other; equity means portioning to need within the same budget.
options.outcome: The chapter's logic chain — age and activity → RDA → servings → cost — exists so menus match bodies, not uniforms; 'same food for all' is equal input, not fair nutrition.

options.text: Keep the identical thali — standardisation is how messes stay within budget.
options.outcome: Budget is one of the three factors, not the only one — the RDA gap is real regardless of the constraint; the chapter's own method is low-cost nutrient-dense substitutions, not flattening every need to the mean.

options.text: Just give the athletes a second thali — extra food solves the gap.
options.outcome: Doubling doubles the budget line without matching the actual RDA difference; the method is to scale servings by computed requirement — arithmetic, not a duplicate plate.

c12_hs_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch11.scenario: At your internship in a 40-room guesthouse, a corporate client checks in at noon and finds the room still uncleaned — the previous guest left at 8 AM. The supervisor shrugs: 'housekeeping cleans when they notice a room is empty.'

options.text: The control-desk relay — front office should push departure info to housekeeping's desk control, which assigns an attendant, then the floor supervisor inspects and hands the room back for resale; 'cleaning when noticed' skips the information system entirely.
options.outcome: The chapter's point: housekeeping isn't reactive labour — it's a coordinated loop keyed to the guest cycle; the uncleaned room is a communication failure, not a cleaning failure.

options.text: The room attendant slacked — a stricter supervisor on rounds would fix it.
options.outcome: The chain broke upstream: the attendant was never told the room was vacant; supervision polices work that's been assigned, it can't replace the front-office-to-desk-control handoff that assigns it.

options.text: Just hire more cleaners — idle staff would have caught it.
options.outcome: Adding labour to a broken relay adds cost, not signal; the chapter's staffing math assumes work flows through the desk — headcount can't substitute for the missing information.

c12_hs_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch12.scenario: An agriculture officer pushes a high-yield paddy variety into a low-rainfall district because it topped the state trial charts. The first crop fails; next season, nobody turns up to her demonstrations. She concludes 'farmers here are resistant to science.'

options.text: Adaptability first, then satisfaction — a variety proven for 1500 mm rainfall isn't adaptable to a 700 mm zone, and the failed crop destroyed the visible benefit that keeps farmers coming; she read the dropout as stubbornness when it was the feedback loop doing its job.
options.outcome: The chapter links the two: unadapted advice produces no tangible gain, and no gain means no trust — 'resistant to science' misnames a community that was failed by unadapted science.

options.text: The farmers were resistant — proven yields should have been adopted on faith.
options.outcome: Extension doesn't run on faith — adoption follows demonstrated local benefit; a state-level trial chart isn't local proof, and the first season's failure confirmed for them exactly what their conditions predicted.

options.text: She should have used louder promotion — better posters and a bigger launch event.
options.outcome: Promotion solves awareness, not fit — the seed was wrong for the zone, so amplifying the message amplifies the failure; principles are operational guides, not marketing volume.

c12_hs_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch13.scenario: Your friend buys a ₹45,000 smartwatch right after a tech influencer's glowing review, though his current watch works fine — then asks you, genuinely puzzled, 'why did I even buy this?'
c12_hs_ch13.prompt: How do the five consumer-behaviour factors decode the purchase?

options.text: It was a layered pull — personal (his age and tech-job identity), psychological (the review taught him to perceive new 'needs' and superior utility), social (the influencer as an aspirational reference group) — the factors converged to override a working watch.
options.outcome: The chapter's insight: purchases are rarely single-need — the watch was bought by the interplay of identity, perception and reference-group pressure, which is exactly the design marketers build for.

options.text: It was purely economic — he could afford it, so affordability explains the buy.
options.outcome: Income permits, it doesn't motivate — the same salary bought a functioning watch last year; what changed was perception and social pull, which are the psychological and social factors.

options.text: It was just advertising — he got manipulated, full stop.
options.outcome: The influencer is a mechanism, not the whole explanation — the buy needed his self-image to answer the pull; naming 'manipulation' skips the personal and psychological levers that made him reachable.

c12_hs_ch14.title: Use it in the wild
c12_hs_ch14.scenario: In the hostel laundry room, a junior dunks a fresh blood-stained kurta in hot water and reaches for the chlorine bleach, saying 'heat and bleach kill stains.' You stop him mid-pour.

options.text: He'd set it permanently — hot water coagulates the protein into insolubility and chlorine locks it in as a yellowish chloro-protein; a protein stain wants cold water first, then an enzymatic detergent, oxygen bleach only if needed.
options.outcome: The chapter's golden rule: identify the stain's chemistry before the agent — heat and chlorine are tools for other stain classes and fixers of this one.

options.text: Let him proceed — aggressive treatment beats timid treatment on any stain.
options.outcome: Aggression isn't a principle — matching is; the strongest move is the wrong move when the chemistry turns the stain permanent, which is exactly what heat and chlorine do to protein.

options.text: Switch him to cold water but keep the chlorine — cold fixes the protein risk.
options.outcome: Half the fix: chlorine still forms the stable coloured complex on protein even cold; the sequence needs an enzyme to digest the protein, not an oxidiser to dye it.

c12_ip_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ip_ch01.scenario: Building a library-issue database for the school fest, your teammate says: 'Skip the SQL constraints — I'll just validate everything in the Python form before it inserts.'
c12_ip_ch01.prompt: What does the CREATE TABLE constraints design argue?

options.text: Enforce integrity at the table — PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY with the right delete action, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT stop bad rows at the database door, so no app bug, script or hand-edited import can ever write an orphan issue record.
options.outcome: The chapter's core insight: constraints in the schema guard the data no matter which code path touches it — form validation only guards the paths you remembered to write.

options.text: Agree — app-level checks are more flexible and you can change rules without touching the schema.
options.outcome: Flexibility is the risk: every new script, import or quick fix bypasses the form's rules, while a CHECK or foreign key can't be forgotten — the schema is the last line every write must cross.

options.text: Use constraints but cascade every delete — ON DELETE CASCADE everywhere keeps things clean.
options.outcome: Cascade is for records meaningless without the parent; issue history is an audit trail where SET NULL preserves the record — one referential action for everything deletes the data you needed to keep.

c12_ip_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ip_ch02.scenario: A teammate loads exam marks as a dictionary {'Maths': [...], 'Physics': [...]} into a DataFrame, then panics: 'pandas put the subjects as columns — my student names were supposed to be columns and it made numbered rows instead.'
c12_ip_ch02.prompt: What did the constructor actually do?

options.text: Exactly what dict-of-lists means — keys become column labels and rows get a default 0..n index; his student names were never in the input, so the table is correctly shaped — subjects as columns, anonymous numbered rows — and the fix is supplying an index, not blaming pandas.
options.outcome: The chapter's orientation rule: input structure maps to output labels — dict keys are always columns; rows need an explicit index to carry names.

options.text: He's right that pandas guessed wrong — it should know names are rows.
options.outcome: Nothing was guessed: the input contained only subject lists, so the RangeIndex is the default, not an error — expecting names that were never passed in is the actual bug.

options.text: Transpose the DataFrame — .T will fix the orientation permanently.
options.outcome: Transpose flips subjects to rows, but the student names still don't exist anywhere in the data — you can't pivot in labels that were never loaded.

c12_ip_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ip_ch03.scenario: A campus IT proposal describes the college's three buildings — linked by the college's own fibre over 2 km — as a 'MAN deployment' to justify leasing telecom circuits.

options.text: No — it's a LAN: 2 km with the organisation owning the medium end-to-end is local by scope and private by ownership; MAN means a city-scale 5–50 km reach, usually on leased lines — calling it one inflates the design and the bill.
options.outcome: The chapter's test is geography plus who owns the wire: private fibre across a campus is a LAN whatever the building count; the proposal spent MAN money on LAN facts.

options.text: Yes — three buildings means 'metropolitan' by definition.
options.outcome: Building count isn't the classifier — scope and medium are; a multi-building campus on owned fibre is textbook LAN, and 'metropolitan' starts at city scale.

options.text: Call it a WAN — any inter-building link rides the wide area.
options.outcome: WAN crosses regions and countries on public telecom infrastructure; 2 km of private fibre never leaves the campus, let alone the public network.

c12_ip_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ip_ch04.scenario: At a hackathon, a rival team lifts your app's source code, ports your matching algorithm and launches with a look-alike name and logo — shrugging, 'you never registered anything.'

options.text: Code is copyright — automatic on creation, no registration needed, so the shrug is wrong there; the algorithm would need a granted patent, which you can't claim retroactively; and the name/logo needs a registered trademark to force statutory enforcement.
options.outcome: The chapter's three-way map: expression (copyright, automatic), invention (patent, must register), identity (trademark, must register) — 'never registered' only disarms the two that needed filing.

options.text: They're fully right — unregistered means unprotected, so all three are fair game.
options.outcome: Only patent and trademark depend on registration; copyright attaches the moment the code was written, so 'you never registered' is no defence for copying it.

options.text: Copyright covers all three — code, algorithm and logo are all your 'creative work.'
options.outcome: Copyright guards expression, not function or identity: the algorithm's working method isn't protected by the code's text, and a brand name is trademark territory — one right can't stretch across all three violations.

c12_ip_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ip_ch05.scenario: A friend cancels a 2 GB upload after a network dip, convinced 'the whole file travels as one block — if it drops, everything was wasted.'
c12_ip_ch05.prompt: What does packet switching say actually happened?

options.text: The file never travelled whole — it was chopped into addressed packets that hopped independently through routers; only unacknowledged packets were lost, so resuming resends those, not the 2 GB — and routers even re-fragment when a link's MTU is smaller.
options.outcome: The chapter's model: independent packets let links be shared, lost pieces be retried alone, and congestion be routed around — 'one giant block' is the mental model the design replaced.

options.text: He's right — a file is a single unit on the wire, so the dip killed it all.
options.outcome: That's circuit-thinking: the Internet is packet-switched precisely so a dip costs a few packets, not the file — the reassembly at the destination exists because pieces take different hops.

options.text: Partially right — packets exist, but each takes the same fixed route, so one dip in the route loses everything.
options.outcome: Packets aren't rail cars on one track — each is forwarded hop-by-hop from routing tables, so paths can differ per packet; a dip disrupts what's in flight, not a fixed 'route' carrying the file.

c12_ip_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ip_ch06.scenario: Your teammate's event webpage jumps from <h1> straight to <h4> 'because h4 text looks the right size', and uses <b> everywhere for 'important' warnings.
c12_ip_ch06.prompt: What does semantic HTML say about those choices?

options.text: Both break the structure layer — headings are the document outline screen readers and search engines navigate by, so skipping levels strands users; and <strong>, not <b>, is what marks importance — size belongs to CSS, not to whichever heading tag looks right.
options.outcome: The chapter's split: headings encode hierarchy, semantic tags encode meaning, styling encodes look — borrowing h4 for its font size corrupts the outline to borrow its pixels.

options.text: It's fine — h4 just means smaller heading, so use whatever fits the design.
options.outcome: That reads tags as sizes: the levels aren't a font menu, and a screen reader walking h1→h4 reports a structure that doesn't exist; the look he wanted is a CSS line, not a heading choice.

options.text: Fix only the headings — <b> and <strong> render the same so it doesn't matter.
options.outcome: They render alike but announce differently — <strong> carries importance to assistive tech and search weighting while <b> is decoration; 'looks identical' is exactly the difference between presentational and semantic.

c12_ip_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ip_ch07.scenario: A cousin brags his banking password 'Tr0ub4dor&3' is uncrackable because 'it has every character type — upper, lower, digit, symbol.'

options.text: It's ~28 bits of pattern, not strength — leetspeak on one dictionary word is in every attacker's ruleset; character variety adds far less than length, so a long random passphrase like four random words beats his decorated word while being easier to remember.
options.outcome: The chapter's formula is about the randomness of the process, not the look of the output — predictable substitutions earn almost nothing once the method is in the cracker's dictionary.

options.text: He's right — all four character classes means the full 95-character search space.
options.outcome: The search space belongs to the generation process, not the string: his word-plus-substitutions is a pattern attacker's tools try early, so the real space is the handful of leetspeak variants, not 95^11.

options.text: It's weak only because it's short — the same pattern at 16 characters is strong.
options.outcome: Length on a deterministic pattern adds little entropy — two decorated dictionary words still sit inside the pattern space; entropy counts unpredictable choices, and a longer costume on the same word changes almost none.

c12_math_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch01.scenario: For a hostel tournament, the warden proposes grouping students by 'shares a hobby with' — anyone linked to anyone in a team joins that team. A teammate warns the grouping might leak: A bonds with B over chess, B with C over cricket, but A and C share nothing.
c12_math_ch01.prompt: Is 'shares a hobby with' an equivalence relation that partitions the hostel cleanly?

options.text: No — it's reflexive and symmetric but fails transitivity: A shares with B and B with C doesn't force A to share with C, so 'teams' can overlap and the same student lands in two groups; a clean partition needs all three properties.
options.outcome: The chapter's test: only when reflexive + symmetric + transitive all hold does a relation split a set into disjoint classes — 'linked by' without transitivity gives webs, not teams.

options.text: Yes — sharing is mutual, and that's what equivalence needs.
options.outcome: Symmetry is only one of the three conditions; without transitivity the 'groups' chain out through middle links until nobody inside a team actually shares anything.

options.text: Yes — because everyone shares a hobby with themselves, the relation is grounded.
options.outcome: Reflexivity alone never partitions anything; every 'sharing' relation on people is reflexive and symmetric by default, so the deciding test is the transitive one this grouping fails.

c12_math_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch02.scenario: A robotics intern feeds a motor the command 'rotate to arcsin(0.5)' — the sensor measured sin θ = 0.5 at 150°, and the code returns the angle straight from the arcsin library. The panel stops at 30°, not 150°.

options.text: No — arcsin only ever answers inside its principal branch [−π/2, π/2]; infinitely many angles share sine 0.5 and the function returns the one in-branch, 30°; if the mount needs 150°, the code must add the quadrant logic itself.
options.outcome: The chapter's rule: the inverse isn't 'cancel sine' — it's 'give the standard angle'; outside the branch, sin⁻¹(sin x) returns a different angle than x.

options.text: Yes — arcsin(sin 150°) must return 150°, so the library has a rounding bug.
options.outcome: That's the classic cancellation error: sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only holds when x already sits in the principal range; 150° doesn't, so 30° is the specified-correct output.

options.text: Switch to arccos — it covers 0°–180° and will return 150° for this measurement.
options.outcome: Changing the function changes the question: arccos answers for cosine input, and feeding it a sine value hands back an angle for a different measurement; the fix is quadrant logic on arcsin's branch, not a different inverse.

c12_math_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch03.scenario: A lab teammate calls a 4×4 sensor table 'a diagonal matrix because the diagonal is all filled in', while another insists a zero-filled grid 'can't be diagonal — the diagonal's empty.'
c12_math_ch03.prompt: What does the diagonal-matrix definition actually check?

options.text: The off-diagonals — a square matrix is diagonal exactly when every i≠j entry is zero; the main diagonal can hold anything including zeros, so the full-diagonal table isn't diagonal if off-diagonals carry data, and the all-zero grid is.
options.outcome: The chapter's test runs on the positions you aren't looking at: 'diagonal' is a statement about empty off-diagonals, not about a populated principal diagonal.

options.text: The first teammate is right — a matrix with a complete diagonal is by definition diagonal.
options.outcome: That inverts the condition: diagonal entries may be anything, but off-diagonal entries must be zero — a table full of sensor cross-talk fails precisely because its off-diagonals are live.

options.text: The second teammate is right — zero diagonal means no diagonal to speak of.
options.outcome: The definition never asks the diagonal to be non-zero; an all-zero square matrix satisfies aᵢⱼ=0 for i≠j vacuously and is diagonal — and also scalar and identity-like degenerate cases at once.

c12_math_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch04.scenario: Surveying a triangular plot, two juniors compute the same 3×3 coordinate determinant — one expands along row 1, the other along column 3 — and get different values. Both insist their method is 'more reliable.'
c12_math_ch04.prompt: Can a determinant depend on which line you expand along?

options.text: No — the value is invariant under choice of row or column, so at least one expansion carries a sign or arithmetic slip; rerun with the sign pattern (+ − + / − + − / + − +) marked and pick the line with the most zeros to minimise where errors breed.
options.outcome: The chapter's invariance is the tie-breaker: same matrix, same determinant — disagreement between expansion lines is a computation audit flag, not a methodological debate.

options.text: Yes — different lines weight different elements, so mild variation is expected.
options.outcome: Expansion is a theorem, not an estimator: every row and column expansion returns the identical scalar, so 'mild variation' means a mistake, not a methodological difference.

options.text: Average the two results to cancel out the line bias.
options.outcome: There's no bias to cancel — the determinant is a single number; averaging a right answer with a wrong one manufactures a third wrong answer.

c12_math_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch05.scenario: A startup's pay banding pays ₹40,000/month for tenure under 3 years and '₹48,000 starting the day you hit 3 years.' An engineer plots the salary function and asks whether it 'jumps' at the 3-year mark.
c12_math_ch05.prompt: What does the continuity test say?

options.text: Check all three quantities — the left-hand limit (₹40,000 as tenure approaches 3 years), the right-hand limit (₹48,000 just past it) and the defined value at exactly 3 years; a ₹8,000 overnight gap means LHL ≠ RHL, so the pay function is discontinuous at the boundary.
options.outcome: The chapter's criterion needs the two limits and the point-value to agree — a cliff in the rule is a discontinuity the moment the band ticks over, whatever HR calls it.

options.text: It's continuous — salary is defined at every tenure, so there's no break.
options.outcome: Defined everywhere isn't continuous anywhere: a jump discontinuity still assigns a value at the boundary; the test is whether approaching from either side lands on the same number.

options.text: It's continuous if the rule says 'at 3 years you get 48k' — the point value matches the right side.
options.outcome: Matching one side isn't the test — continuity needs LHL, RHL and f(c) all equal; matching f(3) to the right limit still leaves a ₹8,000 gap on the left.

c12_math_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch06.scenario: A junior analyst plots weekly app downloads and declares 'growth phase continues — downloads are still above last month's level.' You ask for the week-on-week change instead of the level.
c12_math_ch06.prompt: What does the first-derivative test reframe?

options.text: Direction lives in the derivative's sign, not the level — f stays strictly increasing only where f′(x) > 0; a high but falling curve is already in the decreasing stretch, so find where the change crosses zero and read the sign chart, not the height.
options.outcome: The chapter's rule: 'rising' is a statement about rate of change — a function can sit at its all-time high and already be strictly decreasing.

options.text: Agree with the analyst — a higher value than last month is increase by definition.
options.outcome: That compares two isolated points, not an interval trend — monotonicity is about every pair inside the interval, and the derivative's sign is the test, not a snapshot comparison.

options.text: Wait for downloads to actually drop before calling it a decline — you can't call direction early.
options.outcome: The turning happens at the derivative's zero, before the level visibly falls — waiting for the drop concedes the entire decreasing interval that the sign chart already flagged.

c12_math_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch07.scenario: Estimating a car's distance from a velocity readout v(t) = 2t·sin(t² + 1), your teammate tries 'u = sin(t²+1)' and gets a mess, then declares the integral 'unsolvable by substitution.'
c12_math_ch07.prompt: What was the substitution supposed to look for?

options.text: The function-plus-derivative pair — let u = t²+1 so du = 2t dt is exactly the factor sitting outside sine; the integral collapses to ∫ sin u du, and for a definite integral convert the limits too.
options.outcome: The chapter's pattern: substitution works when the integrand already contains the inner function's derivative — choosing the outer function leaves x's stranded inside du.

options.text: He's right — if the first substitution fails, the integral isn't meant for substitution.
options.outcome: A bad first choice isn't a verdict on the method — the test is whether du appears as a factor; u = t²+1 passes it instantly, so the technique was never disproved.

options.text: Try u = 2t instead — simplify the coefficient first, then the rest follows.
options.outcome: That trades the wrong variable for an irrelevant one — du = 2dt still leaves sin(t²+1) in t and the t-factor unresolved; the derivative must match what's multiplying the differential.

c12_math_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch08.scenario: Estimating paint for a wavy decorative wall whose profile dips below the base line, a junior integrates the curve over the full span and gets a suspiciously small number — 'the dips cancel the bulges, so we need less paint.'
c12_math_ch08.prompt: What did the integral actually measure?

options.text: Signed area — below-axis stretches subtracted from above-axis ones; physical area is ∫|f(x)|dx, so find where the curve crosses the baseline, split there, and sum the absolute values of each piece.
options.outcome: The chapter's split: the definite integral is net signed area — paint covers the dips too, so cancellation understates the surface, not the other way round.

options.text: He's right — net area is what the wall presents, so less paint it is.
options.outcome: The wall's face is positive area everywhere — a dip below the reference line is still surface to be coated; signed area is an accounting identity, not a coverage estimate.

options.text: Ignore the dips entirely and integrate only the parts above the baseline.
options.outcome: That under-coats the lower stretches — the fix isn't discarding negative regions but flipping their sign: integrate each sign-zone separately and take absolute values.

c12_math_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch09.scenario: A teammate modelling a pendulum writes √(d²θ/dt²) + (dθ/dt)² = 0 and files it as 'order 2, degree 1 — the second derivative is to the first power.'

options.text: No — order 2 is right, but the degree isn't defined: the equation isn't a polynomial in its derivatives while √(θ″) is a fractional power; degree only exists when every derivative appears to whole-number powers.
options.outcome: The chapter's rule: degree is judged on the equation's given form — a radical on the highest derivative disqualifies it, even if squaring would later tidy it.

options.text: He's right — under the radical the second derivative has power one.
options.outcome: The radical wraps the derivative, so its actual exponent is ½, not 1; 'inside the root it's power one' is exactly the misread the definition blocks.

options.text: Square the equation first, then read the degree — it becomes degree 1.
options.outcome: Degree is defined for the equation as given, not the polynomial you'd get after manipulation; rewriting changes the object being classified.

c12_math_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch10.scenario: Programming a delivery drone to fly from the warehouse to a building at (3, −4, 12), a junior computes the direction cosines as (3/13, 4/13, 12/13) — 'angles and cosines are positive, so drop the minus.' The drone heads for the wrong block.

options.text: At the sign — direction cosines are the components of the unit vector, so they keep the direction ratios' signs; y = −4 forces m = −4/13, and stripping the minus turned the southbound leg into a northbound one.
options.outcome: The chapter's identity: l, m, n are coordinates divided by magnitude — they encode which octant the vector points into, so a flipped sign is a flipped direction.

options.text: Nowhere mathematically — cosines should be positive; the drone hardware must be faulty.
options.outcome: Direction cosines aren't unsigned angles' absolute values — cosβ is negative for an obtuse angle with the axis; 'always positive' discards the information the sign was carrying.

options.text: In the magnitude — he should have used the raw components (3, −4, 12) as the direction cosines.
options.outcome: Raw components are direction ratios, not cosines — cosines must satisfy l²+m²+n²=1; skipping the division by 13 keeps the sign problem and adds a unit problem.

c12_math_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch11.scenario: Scripting a drone's straight-line flight in a 3D sim, a teammate writes the path as 'direction vector + λ × starting point' — the drone orbits the warehouse instead of leaving it.
c12_math_ch11.prompt: What went wrong in the line equation?

options.text: He swapped the roles — the equation is r = a + λb where a is the position vector of a fixed point on the line and b is the direction it travels; his version anchors on the direction and 'scales' the point, so λ moves the line's anchor instead of the drone.
options.outcome: The chapter's anatomy: the point fixes where the line lives, the vector fixes which way it runs — reversing them doesn't produce a line at all.

options.text: Nothing structural — any two vectors make a line; check the motor code instead.
options.outcome: The vectors have different jobs: one is a location (unchanging, λ-free), the other a direction (multiplied by the parameter); treating them as interchangeable is precisely the failure.

options.text: Use the Cartesian form instead — symmetric equations avoid the mix-up.
options.outcome: Same error survives translation — Cartesian still needs the point in the numerators and the direction ratios in the denominators; swapping roles just fails in different notation.

c12_math_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch12.scenario: The canteen committee must split the day's oven time between cakes (₹500 profit) and tarts (₹300), capped by oven hours and shelf space. A member proposes 'a balanced mix in the middle of what's allowed — safest is best.'
c12_math_ch12.prompt: Where will the maximum profit actually sit?

options.text: At a corner of the feasible region — the corner point theorem says a linear objective on a convex polygon attains its optimum at a vertex; list the corner points from the constraints, evaluate Z at each, and the 'safe middle' interior point is guaranteed worse than the best corner.
options.outcome: The chapter's geometry: linear profit pushes level lines until they touch the last feasible point — which is always a vertex, never an interior compromise.

options.text: The middle mix is right — balance hedges against either product underperforming.
options.outcome: Hedging answers a risk question the LPP doesn't contain — with linear profit and hard constraints, the optimum is at a corner by theorem; 'balanced' is a feeling, not a vertex.

options.text: Test a dense grid of interior points to be thorough.
options.outcome: Interior testing can't beat the corners — the theorem already proved the max lives on the boundary; a grid wastes effort re-checking points mathematically ruled out.

c12_math_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch13.scenario: A QC dashboard at a snack factory flags 'packet is defective.' A trainee asks: 'If the chance it's a sealing defect is 40%, is the chance it's NOT a sealing defect still 60% — or does being a defective packet change the maths?'

options.text: The complement rule survives conditioning — inside the defective-packet universe, P(E′|F) = 1 − P(E|F), so yes, 60% — but only because conditioning restricted the sample space to defective packets first; the unconditional numbers would be different.
options.outcome: The chapter's point: conditioning doesn't break probability's algebra, it relocates it — all the rules work, but they work inside F's shrunken universe, not the original one.

options.text: It's not 60% — conditioning breaks the complement rule, so you'd need the raw numbers again.
options.outcome: Conditional probability inherits every ordinary rule within the conditioned space — P(E′|F) = 1 − P(E|F) follows straight from the definition; the rule isn't broken, the denominator changed.

options.text: It's 60% because the overall defect rate never changed.
options.outcome: Right answer, wrong reason — the complement holds inside F, but the 'overall rate' is irrelevant; what changed is the sample space, and forgetting that is how conditional answers get quietly replaced by unconditional ones.

c12_phy_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch01.scenario: In the lab, a partner computes the force between +3 μC and −2 μC charges 10 cm apart as 5.4×10⁹ N — 'bigger than a rocket engine, something's off.' He plugged 3, 2 and 10 straight into the formula.

options.text: At the units — μC must become coulombs (×10⁻⁶) and cm must become metres, then the separation gets squared; done in SI, the answer is a few newtons, attractive — not a nine-digit force.
options.outcome: The chapter's discipline: k ≈ 9×10⁹ only balances when the inputs are SI — μC and cm inflate the result by twelve orders before physics even gets a say.

options.text: At the formula — he forgot that opposite charges need a minus force, so use negative F.
options.outcome: The sign already lives in the product q₁q₂ — the formula reports attraction via the direction; the numeric blow-up came from unconverted units, not a missing minus.

options.text: At the distance — he should have used r, not r², since force weakens with separation.
options.outcome: The weakening is the r²: using plain r would overstate the force further — the inverse square is the law, not an error to relax.

c12_phy_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch02.scenario: A lab report asks for the total potential at a point near two charges, +5 μC and −3 μC. Your teammate adds the magnitudes: 'field arrows point, so potential must point too — and negatives just mean weaker.'
c12_phy_ch02.prompt: How do you correct the method?

options.text: Potential is a scalar — it's work per unit charge, so you add signed values algebraically: +5 μC contributes +V₁, −3 μC contributes −V₂, and the total is the difference, not the sum of magnitudes.
options.outcome: The chapter's key contrast: field is a vector and potential is the scalar it descends from — a negative source charge lowers potential exactly the way a debt lowers a balance.

options.text: He's right — anything derived from a force law is a vector by inheritance.
options.outcome: That reverses the relationship — the field is the gradient OF the scalar potential; work is force dotted with displacement, a scalar, so V can only add with signs, never arrows.

options.text: Drop the negative charge's contribution — potential counts only positive sources.
options.outcome: Negative charges contribute negative potential — erasing V₂ changes the answer as surely as erasing the charge would change the experiment; superposition is algebraic, not optimistic.

c12_phy_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch03.scenario: An intern tests a resistor at 6 V and 12 V, gets double the current, and reports: 'R = V/I, so doubling voltage doubled the resistance — this batch is faulty.'
c12_phy_ch03.prompt: What's wrong with that reading of R = V/I?

options.text: He turned a definition into a proportionality — R = V/I just measures resistance; for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature the current rises with voltage so the ratio stays fixed — his own data (I doubled with V) is a textbook pass, not a fault.
options.outcome: The chapter's distinction: the law asserts R is constant, the ratio merely defines it — proportional V and I is the signature of a healthy ohmic resistor.

options.text: He's right — if R is computed from V/I, a bigger V must mean a bigger R.
options.outcome: That reading would make R undefined whenever V or I shifts — the whole point of an ohmic device is the ratio holding steady; both quantities moved together, leaving R untouched.

options.text: Report it as non-ohmic — only a straight line through the origin counts, and two points can't prove that.
options.outcome: Two points do lie on a straight line through the origin when I scales with V — his data is literally the ohmic signature; calling it non-ohmic punishes the batch for obeying the law.

c12_phy_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch04.scenario: A demo wire hangs between magnet poles and won't budge. A junior keeps cranking the supply — 'more current, more force, it'll move eventually.'
c12_phy_ch04.prompt: What should he check before touching the current?

options.text: The angle — F = IlB sinθ is zero when the wire runs parallel to the field; if current and B are aligned, no current on Earth produces force — rotate the wire or the magnet, don't amplify a zero.
options.outcome: The chapter's geometry: the cross product kills force at θ = 0° or 180° — scaling I multiplies a sinθ that's already zero.

options.text: He's right — force is proportional to current, so persistence pays.
options.outcome: Proportional means I multiplies the sinθ term, not replaces it — ten times the current on a parallel wire is still ten times zero.

options.text: Reverse the battery — opposite current must push instead of pull.
options.outcome: Reversal flips the force's direction, not its existence — at parallel alignment both directions give zero; the fix is geometric, not electrical.

c12_phy_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch05.scenario: Calibrating a magnetometer, a junior notes the needle settles aligned with the field, then tries to 'park it backwards — anti-aligned is also an equilibrium, so it should hold.'

options.text: Anti-aligned is the unstable equilibrium — U is maximum at θ = 180°, so the tiniest nudge produces a torque that swings it further off; only the aligned position (minimum U) restores after disturbance.
options.outcome: The chapter's map: same alignment axis, opposite stability — balanced and balanced-against are both equilibria, but only one survives contact with reality.

options.text: He's right — torque is zero at both 0° and 180°, so both hold.
options.outcome: Zero torque names equilibrium, not stability — the energy curve separates them: minimum at 0° restores, maximum at 180° amplifies any nudge into a swing.

options.text: Neither holds — a needle in a field always keeps oscillating.
options.outcome: Compasses do settle — at the potential minimum; oscillation is what happens on the way there, not the endpoint the physics predicts.

c12_phy_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch06.scenario: In an induction demo, a teammate proposes wiring the coil 'helpfully': 'let the induced current's field pull the approaching magnet in — free acceleration, bigger emf.'
c12_phy_ch06.prompt: What does Lenz's law say that design would violate?

options.text: Energy conservation — an induced current can only oppose the flux change that created it; if it aided the magnet's approach, motion would generate current that generates motion — free energy — so the induced field must push back, not pull in.
options.outcome: The chapter's minus sign is physics, not convention: 'oppose the change' is what makes you do mechanical work to induce a current — that's where the electrical energy comes from.

options.text: Nothing — induced current direction is a convention, so wire it whichever way helps.
options.outcome: The negative sign in Faraday's law encodes the direction, and it isn't negotiable: aiding the change would mean current without work — the law forbids it precisely so the energy audit closes.

options.text: It already opposes the field, so opposing the magnet's approach is the same thing.
options.outcome: Oppose the CHANGE, not the field — when the magnet recedes, the induced current builds a field in the same direction to resist the loss; opposing the field itself would flip direction mid-demo.

c12_phy_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch07.scenario: An electrical trainee argues a heater can't be drawing real power on AC mains: 'the current averages to zero over a cycle — positive half, negative half, net nothing.'

options.text: At the squaring — power is i²R, and i² is positive on both halves of the cycle, so it averages to I²rms R, never zero; that's exactly why mains ratings are quoted in RMS — 'zero average current' doesn't mean zero average work.
options.outcome: The chapter's distinction: the average of a quantity isn't the average of its square — dissipation counts both directions as heat.

options.text: He's right — net current is zero, so net energy is zero; heaters actually work on peak current.
options.outcome: Current's sign reversal doesn't undo the i² — the resistor heats on both halves; 'net nothing' averages the wrong quantity, and peak current describes stress, not energy.

options.text: Heater works because the filament's phase lags — resistive loads delay the current.
options.outcome: In a pure resistor v and i are in phase — phase lag is the inductor's story; the heater works because i²R stays positive, not because of any shift.

c12_phy_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch08.scenario: A lab partner insists there's no magnetic field between a charging capacitor's plates 'because no conduction current flows through the gap — Ampere's law gives zero.'
c12_phy_ch08.prompt: What term of the Ampere-Maxwell law answers him?

options.text: The displacement current, ε₀dΦ_E/dt — the growing electric flux between the plates plays the current's role and produces the same B the wire does; without that term Ampere's law contradicts itself depending on which surface you choose.
options.outcome: The chapter's fix: the same loop bounded by a surface through the wire and one through the gap must give one answer — the displacement term is what makes that possible, and it's the symmetry that lets EM waves exist.

options.text: He's right — no charge crosses the gap, so no B can exist there.
options.outcome: That picks one surface and ignores the paradox it creates — the wire's surface gives nonzero B for the identical loop; Maxwell's term exists because the answer can't depend on the surface you drew.

options.text: There's a small leakage current through the dielectric — that's the real source.
options.outcome: An ideal capacitor's gap carries no conduction current at all, and the field still exists — the term is a changing electric flux, not a leak; inventing one misses the mechanism.

c12_phy_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch09.scenario: A driving-school instructor teaches that the convex side mirror 'warns: objects are closer than they appear' is just legal boilerplate — 'the mirror is smaller, that's all.'
c12_phy_ch09.prompt: What does the mirror formula say the convex mirror is actually doing?

options.text: It's optically shrinking distances — a convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image behind it (v positive, |m| < 1), so the car genuinely looks smaller and farther than it is; the warning is the physics, not the packaging.
options.outcome: The chapter's map of the formula: f positive, u negative forces v small and positive, so magnification stays under one — wider field, but everything in it is compressed.

options.text: He's right — the mirror just shows a wider area; distances are true.
options.outcome: The wider field is bought with diminution — every object lands closer to the focus than the pole-side distance it actually occupies, which is exactly why the warning exists.

options.text: The mirror makes cars look farther only at long range — nearby cars appear true-size.
options.outcome: Diminution holds at every object distance for a convex mirror — |m| rises as the car approaches but stays under 1; there's no true-size zone in the formula.

c12_phy_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch10.scenario: A teammate coding an underwater camera's ray tracer assumes light 'speeds up in denser water — more stuff to push it along,' bending rays away from the normal.
c12_phy_ch10.prompt: What does Huygens' wave model say instead?

options.text: Light slows in the denser medium — wavelets advance a shorter distance in the same time, so the wavefront swings toward the normal, giving sin i / sin r = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁; the speed-up-and-bend-away model is the losing corpuscular theory.
options.outcome: The chapter's verdict: Huygens' construction forces v₂ < v₁ when r < i — the measured slowing in water (Foucault) is what killed the particle model.

options.text: He's right — denser medium means stronger propagation, hence faster light.
options.outcome: That's Newton's corpuscular prediction and experiment killed it — the wave construction necessarily bends the front toward the normal by shortening the wavelets' reach in the denser medium.

options.text: Speed stays constant — only the wavelength changes, so the bend is an illusion.
options.outcome: Frequency stays constant; speed and wavelength both drop by the refractive index — v = c/n isn't an illusion, it's what produces the measured bend.

c12_phy_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch11.scenario: A photo-sensor project fails under a blazing red lamp, so a teammate suggests 'double the brightness — more light means more energy per electron.'
c12_phy_ch11.prompt: What does Einstein's equation say is actually missing?

options.text: Frequency, not brightness — Kmax = hν − φ₀ has no intensity term; if red light sits below the threshold frequency, no electron gets out at any brightness, while doubling intensity would only multiply the count of electrons, never their energy.
options.outcome: The chapter's core: one photon pays one electron — energy per photon is set by frequency, so the fix is bluer light, not brighter light.

options.text: He's right — intensity is the total energy delivered, so raising it must raise the electrons' energy.
options.outcome: That's the wave picture Einstein displaced — energy arrives in photon packets of hν; a billion weak photons still can't do what one above-threshold photon does.

options.text: Keep the red lamp but let it run longer — the electrons just need time to accumulate enough energy.
options.outcome: There is no accumulation — the photon-electron exchange is instantaneous, which is exactly the classical impasse the photon model solved; waiting doesn't raise hν.

c12_phy_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch12.scenario: At a science-fair stall, a visitor asks why the neon sign glows a single sharp red-orange while a filament bulb pours out a continuous white — 'if electrons radiate whenever they move, why only one colour?'

options.text: The electron can't radiate in orbit — stationary states are radiation-free, and light appears only on transitions between them, with hν equal to the exact energy gap; fixed gaps give fixed frequencies, which is why the gas shows lines and the thermal filament shows a continuum.
options.outcome: The chapter's postulates exist to solve exactly this: quantised angular momentum picks the allowed orbits, and the transition rule hν = Ei − Ef turns energy differences into a discrete spectrum.

options.text: Neon simply filters the white light it emits — the tube's glass does the selecting.
options.outcome: The spectrum is generated, not filtered — each photon is born with the energy of one transition; the bulb's continuous output comes from heat, not from discrete level jumps.

options.text: Electrons spiral inward continuously — the single colour is just where they happen to be.
options.outcome: Spiralling is the classical disaster Bohr's first postulate was written to forbid — it would radiate a continuous rainbow and collapse the atom, neither of which is observed.

c12_phy_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch13.scenario: In a debate on nuclear power, a speaker claims 'splitting any nucleus releases energy — fission is fission.' A teammate wonders if splitting iron would power a reactor too.
c12_phy_ch13.prompt: What does the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve say?

options.text: Direction matters — the curve peaks near iron (~8.8 MeV/nucleon), so energy is released only when products sit higher on the curve: splitting uranium (~7.6) works because the fragments are more tightly bound, but splitting iron moves downhill and would cost energy.
options.outcome: The chapter's reading of the curve: fission pays the very heavy, fusion pays the very light — iron at the summit is the point where neither direction yields.

options.text: The speaker is right — breaking any nucleus frees binding energy.
options.outcome: Binding energy is what's released only when the products bind more tightly — iron's daughters would be less bound than iron itself, so the 'fission' would consume energy, not emit it.

options.text: Iron fission works but just gives less energy than uranium fission.
options.outcome: It's not smaller, it's negative — past the Fe peak the daughters sit lower on the curve, so the reaction runs the wrong way energetically; 'less energy' would still be a positive release.

c12_phy_ch14.title: Use it in the wild
c12_phy_ch14.scenario: A junior fabricating an n-type wafer expects the arsenic doping to 'raise both carrier counts — more electrons donated means more holes somewhere too.'
c12_phy_ch14.prompt: What does the mass-action law say actually happens to the holes?

options.text: They collapse — n_e·n_h = n_i² is fixed at a temperature, so pushing electrons up to ~N_D drives holes down by the same factor; doping doesn't create pairs, it tilts the balance — electrons become the majority by suppressing, not spawning, holes.
options.outcome: The chapter's accounting: donor electrons recombine into holes faster than thermal generation replaces them — the product is pinned at n_i², so the hole count falls off a cliff.

options.text: He's right — charge neutrality means electrons and holes must rise together.
options.outcome: Charge neutrality is a sum over donors too, not an electron-hole equality — the donor ions carry the positive charge, and the mass-action product forces holes down as electrons rise.

options.text: Holes stay at n_i — doping only adds electrons on top without touching holes.
options.outcome: Fixed n_i² forbids that: if n_e rises by six orders of magnitude, n_h must fall by six orders — 'untouched' isn't an option the equilibrium permits.

c12_psy_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_psy_ch01.scenario: A school counsellor must advise a student torn between 'I love sketching, so design' and her strong mechanical-aptitude score — her parents push 'just follow the marks card.'
c12_psy_ch01.prompt: What does psychological assessment say the decision actually needs?

options.text: Both domains, separately — interest says what she'd choose, aptitude says what she could train into skill; loving a field without the aptitude breeds frustration, aptitude without interest breeds disengagement, and a marks card answers neither.
options.outcome: The chapter's split: domains are different constructs needing different methods — assessment is purpose-driven, and stream choice needs the interest-aptitude pairing, not a single score.

options.text: Follow the marks — performance is the best single predictor of success.
options.outcome: Marks conflate ability, coaching and effort into one number and say nothing about preference or potential; the chapter treats attributes as multi-dimensional precisely because one index can't carry a career decision.

options.text: Follow her interest — passion overrides aptitude every time.
options.outcome: Interest without aptitude is the textbook mismatch — she may love the activity and still stall on the skill; the pairing exists to catch exactly this lopsided case.

c12_psy_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_psy_ch02.scenario: A classmate spiralling before boards says three things: 'I'm basically a failure,' 'I can't crack organic chemistry no matter what,' and 'I keep scrolling instead of revising.'
c12_psy_ch02.prompt: Map the three complaints to the three constructs correctly.

options.text: Self-esteem ('I'm a failure' — global worth), self-efficacy ('can't crack organic chem' — domain-specific capability belief), and self-regulation (scrolling — the monitoring/directing process breaking down); three different levers, three different fixes.
options.outcome: The chapter's triage: evaluation of worth, belief about a specific task, and control of behaviour are distinct — 'he lacks confidence' flattens all three into one vague problem.

options.text: All three are low self-esteem — the chemistry and scrolling are just symptoms.
options.outcome: Domain-specific doubt and failed self-monitoring aren't global worth judgments — a student can have intact self-esteem and still lack efficacy in chemistry; collapsing them loses the diagnosis the constructs exist to give.

options.text: All three are poor self-regulation — fixing the scrolling fixes the rest.
options.outcome: Regulation directs behaviour but doesn't rewrite self-belief — better habits won't touch 'I'm a failure' or the specific efficacy doubt; the constructs travel together without being the same thing.

c12_psy_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_psy_ch03.scenario: Two interns get the same Friday deadline. One reads it as 'a challenge — I've got the tools and the mentor on call'; the other reads it as 'a threat — I'm drowning and nobody will help.' Same brief, opposite stress.
c12_psy_ch03.prompt: What does Lazarus's appraisal theory say differs?

options.text: Both appraisals — the first appraised challenge (primary) plus sufficient coping resources (secondary), producing manageable eustress; the second appraised threat plus insufficient resources, producing distress; the event was identical — the interpretation is what differed.
options.outcome: The chapter's thesis: stress lives in the appraisal, not the event — which is why changing perceived resources changes the stress even when the deadline doesn't move.

options.text: Only their personalities differ — the deadline objectively is stressful.
options.outcome: That relocates stress into the person or the event, exactly what appraisal theory rules out — the model is transactional: the same event produces different stress through different evaluations of it.

options.text: The second intern is simply realistic — recognizing a threat is accuracy, not appraisal.
options.outcome: Both are appraising — 'realistic' is itself a judgment of harm and of resources; calling one reading objective hides the secondary appraisal that made it feel unmanageable.

c12_psy_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_psy_ch04.scenario: Watching a documentary on medieval 'possession' cases — convulsions, voices — a viewer scoffs 'they were just ignorant; today we know it's schizophrenia and we treat it right.'
c12_psy_ch04.prompt: What do the historical models add to that reaction?

options.text: Each era's model has internal logic — supernatural explains the same symptoms as spirit-work needing exorcism, biological explains it as bodily dysregulation needing antipsychotics; the treatment follows the assumed cause, so 'ignorance' misses that a different causal model was operating, not absent thinking.
options.outcome: The chapter's point: explanation and treatment travel as a pair — symptoms stay constant while the model decides whether you reach for prayer or a prescription.

options.text: He's right — only the biological model counts as real explanation.
options.outcome: Presentism aside, that misses what classification and models do — each perspective was a coherent causal system directing practice; understanding them is how you see why the same behaviour got exorcised then and medicated now.

options.text: DSM-5 is the real difference — earlier eras lacked categories, not explanations.
options.outcome: That confuses classification with causation — DSM and ICD organize how we label disorders; the supernatural/biological/psychological models are the competing answers to why they occur.

c12_psy_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_psy_ch05.scenario: In a peer-counselling workshop, a trainee responds to 'I cheated on the exam' with 'I understand, but honestly that was wrong of you.' The facilitator flags a violated core condition.
c12_psy_ch05.prompt: Which one, and why does it matter?

options.text: Unconditional positive regard — acceptance can't be contingent on what the client discloses; adding 'that was wrong' prices the warmth, and a client who senses conditions stops disclosing — which starves the alliance the therapy runs on.
options.outcome: The chapter distinguishes empathy (feeling with) from UPR (accepting regardless) — the trainee empathized fine and violated the acceptance pillar in the same sentence.

options.text: Empathy — 'I understand' was insincere, so the real breach was failed perspective-taking.
options.outcome: The understanding itself wasn't the problem — the judgment that followed was; empathy is about entering the client's frame, UPR is about not making acceptance conditional on what's found there.

options.text: The contract — correcting the client breaks the voluntary partnership terms.
options.outcome: The contract governs the relationship's frame — voluntary, time-limited, confidential — not whether the therapist may judge; the breach is acceptance made conditional, not a clause of the agreement.

c12_psy_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_psy_ch06.scenario: A health NGO wants villagers to stop a harmful practice central to their identity. The strategist asks: 'Do we attack the belief head-on, or first strengthen a related health attitude they already hold?'
c12_psy_ch06.prompt: What do the attitude features predict?

options.text: Head-on fails — a central, extreme, negative-leaning attitude resists incongruent change; the smarter lever is congruent change — deepen an existing aligned attitude (like protecting children's health) so the shift rides the system's own valence rather than fighting it.
options.outcome: The chapter's resistance map: centrality and extremeness multiply resistance in the opposite direction — you change a system by working with its gravity, not against it.

options.text: Go head-on — central beliefs change fastest because they matter most to people.
options.outcome: Centrality raises the stakes of the change, not its ease — the more a belief anchors the rest of the system, the harder incongruent pressure is to move.

options.text: Strategy doesn't matter — attitudes change at the same rate regardless of direction.
options.outcome: Valence and direction are exactly the variables — congruent change (more of what's felt) is easier than incongruent reversal, and extreme central attitudes make the gap even wider.

c12_psy_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_psy_ch07.scenario: Same coding club, two new members: Asha joins because 'nobody messes with the club's members,' while Dev joins because 'the seniors here can teach me real projects.'
c12_psy_ch07.prompt: Which distinct group-joining motives are operating?

options.text: Security for Asha — the group buffers threat — and knowledge/information for Dev — the group grants access he'd lack alone; same membership, different needs, which is why one group can recruit on several motives at once.
options.outcome: The chapter's six-need framework: identical joining behaviour can be powered by different needs, so reading motives from the group instead of the member mislabels both.

options.text: Both joined for goal achievement — the club helps both get what they want.
options.outcome: That flattens two distinct needs into one — protection from threat and access to knowledge are separate motives in the framework; 'wanting something' is too loose to do the analysis.

options.text: Both joined for status — club membership elevates them socially.
options.outcome: Neither described prestige — Asha described safety, Dev described learning; status is external recognition, and assuming every join is about looking good misses the six-way map.

c12_ps_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch01.scenario: In a Model UN on the early Cold War, a US delegate proposes 'rolling back' communist governments inside Eastern Europe with direct intervention, citing Kennan's containment doctrine as the authority.

options.text: No — Kennan's doctrine was 'firm and vigilant containment' at the frontiers of Soviet pressure, applied where resistance could still matter — aid to Greece and Turkey, reconstruction via the Marshall Plan; intervening inside an established bloc is the later 'rollback' idea, not containment.
options.outcome: The chapter's line between strategy and aggression: containment stopped expansion at its edges — it never promised to reverse what was already consolidated.

options.text: Yes — containment means opposing communism wherever it exists, by any means.
options.outcome: That's Dulles-era rollback dressed as Kennan — the original logic was that the USSR retreats before firm resistance at contested points, not that the US invades consolidated territory.
