options.text: Yes — the Marshall Plan already intervened economically, so military rollback is the same policy.
options.outcome: The instruments differ in kind — the Plan was economic reconstruction to remove communism's appeal, not force inside the bloc; treating them as interchangeable erases the strategy's own division of labour.

c12_ps_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch02.scenario: A debate speaker calls glasnost 'Gorbachev's sentimental free-speech reform' and perestroika 'an unrelated economic cleanup,' missing why they were sequenced.
c12_ps_ch02.prompt: How did the two reforms actually interact?

options.text: Glasnost was the battering ram — openness was meant to expose bureaucratic failure and build public pressure so perestroika's restructuring could break party resistance; instead, freed information also armed nationalist movements, and the loop dissolved the system it was meant to save.
options.outcome: The chapter's causal chain: political opening was the instrument of economic reform — the same free flow that weakened the centre empowered the peripheries, which is why reform became collapse.

options.text: The speaker is right — they were independent tracks, one political, one economic.
options.outcome: Sequencing is the point — glasnost came first precisely to clear the path for perestroika; reading them as parallel projects misses the strategic dependency and the feedback loop that followed.

options.text: Glasnost caused the collapse, so perestroika was the innocent half.
options.outcome: Neither was separable — restructuring without price reform produced shortages, and openness exposed both failures; the two reforms failed together, each amplifying the other's damage.

c12_ps_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch03.scenario: A quiz-bowl team is asked why the US answered 9/11 with a 'war' instead of treating al-Qaeda as criminals to be arrested and tried.
c12_ps_ch03.prompt: What did the war framing unlock?

options.text: Laws of armed conflict — the AUMF let the President use 'all necessary force,' suspects could be held as enemy combatants without trial, force could cross borders without the host's consent, and NATO's Article 5 was invoked for the first time; a criminal frame would have boxed all of that in.
options.outcome: The chapter's analysis: 'war' was a legal-strategic choice, not a metaphor — it expanded executive power and re-targeted hegemony from states to networks.

options.text: Nothing functional — 'war on terror' was just rhetoric for the public.
options.outcome: The label carried powers — detention without trial, cross-border operations, collective-defence invocation; rhetoric doesn't authorise force, the war frame did.

options.text: A UN mandate forced the war framing — the US had no choice in the matter.
options.outcome: The legal engine was domestic — the AUMF, not a UN resolution; UN endorsement of self-defence trailed the military action, marking the shift to coalitions the US assembled itself.

c12_ps_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch04.scenario: An export intern asks who decides the tariff her firm's textiles face in the EU and who could negotiate it down — 'probably the European Parliament, since it's elected.'
c12_ps_ch04.prompt: How does EU competence actually map?

options.text: The Council sets the common external tariff on a Commission proposal, and the Commission negotiates the trade deal — Parliament only approves or rejects the final text; pooled sovereignty put economics under qualified-majority supranational rule while foreign policy still needs all members' yes.
options.outcome: The chapter's institutional map: the EU acts like a state in trade and a club in war — knowing which competence governs your issue is the whole skill.

options.text: She's right — the directly elected Parliament legislates tariffs like a national parliament does.
options.outcome: Election doesn't equal competence — the Parliament's trade role is a veto on finished deals; proposing and negotiating sit with the Commission, and the tariff itself is the Council's call.

options.text: Each member state sets its own tariff — Germany and France can differ.
options.outcome: The single market exists precisely because members pooled commercial policy — a common external tariff is what makes the bloc negotiate with one weight; national tariffs would dissolve it.

c12_ps_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch05.scenario: A student presenting 'three Kashmir wars' folds 1971 into the same Kashmir storyline as 1947-48 and 1965 — 'same neighbours, same cause, bigger scale.'

options.text: 1971's cause was the East Pakistan crisis — the liberation movement, ten million refugees crossing into India and Pakistan's pre-emptive strikes; its outcome was Bangladesh and 93,000 POWs — a humanitarian-geopolitical rupture the Kashmir file doesn't explain.
options.outcome: The chapter separates causation: the first two wars were Kashmir-centred; 1971 redrew the map for a different reason — grouping them hides the event's actual logic.

options.text: The framing holds — every India-Pakistan war is ultimately about Kashmir.
options.outcome: The evidence says otherwise — East Pakistan's crisis, the refugee influx and Bangladesh's creation belong to a different causal chain; Kashmir was where the two earlier wars lived, not this one.

options.text: Half right — 1971 started over Kashmir and escalated into East Pakistan.
options.outcome: Sequence is the error — the war grew out of the eastern crisis and refugee emergency, not a western-front escalation; reversing cause and consequence scrambles the whole analysis.

c12_ps_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch06.scenario: A newsroom junior writes 'UN demands ceasefire, 140-10' — then the Security Council session ends in a single P5 veto and nothing binds. 'But the vote passed overwhelmingly?'
c12_ps_ch06.prompt: What did the two outcomes actually differ on?

options.text: Legal force — the General Assembly's vote is universal but recommendatory, moral pressure without obligation; the Security Council alone can bind members under the Charter, and the veto is the design feature that lets one great power stop it — world opinion outvoted, enforcement outvoted it back.
options.outcome: The chapter's architecture: universality lives in the GA, power lives in the SC — the Charter deliberately traded sovereign equality for great-power consensus on security.

options.text: Nothing — both are UN resolutions, so the GA majority should override the veto.
options.outcome: No override exists — the GA's authority is deliberative, the SC's is binding under Chapter VII; 140 votes of opinion can't compel what one veto of enforcement blocks.

options.text: The veto was illegitimate — fairness should govern the Council like the Assembly.
options.outcome: The veto wasn't a bug but the price of the great powers joining — the Charter chose enforceable peace over fair voting, which is exactly why the SC's one-country block stands.

c12_ps_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch07.scenario: A columnist calls the 1998 nuclear tests a failure 'because Kargil happened the very next year — so much for deterrence.'
c12_ps_ch07.prompt: What does deterrence theory actually say about Kargil?

options.text: Deterrence caps the ceiling, not the floor — the stability-instability paradox says nuclear cover permits limited conflict below the threshold, and India's refusal to cross the LoC is the threshold visibly working: limited aims stayed limited because escalation's price was mutual destruction.
options.outcome: The chapter's subtlety: nuclear weapons don't prevent war — they prevent the war from becoming unlimited; Kargil staying conventional is deterrence operating, not failing.

options.text: The columnist is right — if deterrence held, no conflict would have occurred at all.
options.outcome: That expects deterrence to freeze all hostility, when its promise is narrower — making the full-scale option irrational; the paradox predicts exactly the kind of limited incursion Kargil was.

options.text: India should have crossed the LoC — restraint proved the weapons worthless.
options.outcome: Crossing would have signalled existential aims and risked the red lines deterrence is built around — restraint was the strategy's rational output, not evidence against it.

c12_ps_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch08.scenario: In a mock constituent assembly, a student declares the 565 princely states 'automatically became India's on 15 August 1947 — the British left, so the map was settled.'
c12_ps_ch08.prompt: What did the lapse of paramountcy actually do?

options.text: It freed every state legally — rulers could accede to India, Pakistan, or stay independent, which is why Patel ran a staged integration: Instrument of Accession for three subjects, popular will as the legitimising test, merger agreements after; 'automatic' skips both the legal vacuum and the diplomacy that filled it.
options.outcome: The chapter's core: independence Day created a sovereignty question, not an answer — the union was negotiated into existence, with force only where consent failed.

options.text: He's right — Partition decided everything; the states just followed their provinces.
options.outcome: Partition's religious-majority logic applied to British provinces, not princely states — paramountcy's lapse made each ruler a separate legal question, which is exactly why Hyderabad and Junagadh needed more than a signature.

options.text: The Instrument of Accession merged them fully — one signature made them Indian states.
options.outcome: The IoA surrendered only defence, external affairs and communications — it was stage one of a sequence (accession → standstill → merger → constitutional integration), not the whole event.

c12_ps_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch09.scenario: A debate rival claims '1950s India was a one-party state, same as any authoritarian system — Congress always won.'
c12_ps_ch09.prompt: What distinguishes the Congress System from one-party rule?

options.text: The dominance was competitive, not coercive — opposition parties contested free elections, Congress worked as a broad coalition whose internal factions did the opposing, and FPTP amplified a ~45% vote into ~75% seats; nobody was banned — that last part is the whole difference.
options.outcome: The chapter's key distinction: dominance through inclusion and arithmetic versus dominance through exclusion — India had a dominant party inside a democracy, not a democracy replaced by a party.

options.text: He's right — one party winning every election is one-party rule by definition.
options.outcome: The test isn't who wins but who may contest — China's dominance rests on legal exclusion of rivals; Congress's rested on winning open contests and absorbing dissent internally.

options.text: The difference was just Nehru's personality — remove him and it was authoritarian.
options.outcome: Personality isn't the mechanism — the system ran on coalition breadth, faction management and FPTP mechanics; individual virtue can't explain seat shares or the opposition's legal freedom.

c12_ps_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch10.scenario: A policy-club debate: 'Independent India should have led with heavy industry in 1951 — the First Plan wasted a decade on dams and land ceilings.'
c12_ps_ch10.prompt: What was the First Plan's actual reasoning?

options.text: Start where the constraint was — a Partition-hit, food-short agrarian economy needed irrigation (Bhakra Nangal replacing canal headworks lost to Pakistan) and land reform against unequal holdings, and K.N. Raj's 'hasten slowly' kept the pace inside what democracy could survive.
options.outcome: The chapter's logic chain: identify the binding constraint (land, water, food), design the institutional fix, and pace it politically — industry-first skips the subsistence reality the plan was answering.

options.text: The debater is right — industry compounds faster, so agriculture-first was timidity.
options.outcome: Faster compounding needs fed people and functioning markets — with consumption already at subsistence and Partition's irrigation rupture, industrial lead would have meant coercion, which is precisely what 'hasten slowly' refused.

options.text: The real reason was just lack of capital — nothing ideological about it.
options.outcome: Capital was a symptom, not the diagnosis — the plan named unequal land distribution the principal obstacle and chose democracy-compatible pacing; 'no money' can't explain why land reform, not inputs, came first.

c12_ps_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch11.scenario: A foreign-affairs columnist dismisses Nehru's non-alignment as 'Swiss-style fence-sitting — refusing to judge anyone to stay out of trouble.'
c12_ps_ch11.prompt: What does non-alignment actually look like in practice?

options.text: Independent judgment per issue — condemning the Suez invasion as neo-colonial while staying measured on Hungary wasn't fence-sitting but case-by-case evaluation; neutrality withdraws equally from all disputes, non-alignment engages on India's own terms.
options.outcome: The chapter's distinction: not joining blocs isn't refusing to judge — it's keeping the right to judge each issue on its merits rather than inheriting a camp's verdict.

options.text: The columnist is right — staying out of both blocs is neutrality by another name.
options.outcome: Neutrality is withdrawal; non-alignment was loud engagement — Bandung, Belgrade, Suez protests — the difference is between refusing the question and reserving the right to answer it independently.

options.text: Non-alignment meant balancing — condemn both sides equally to stay credible.
options.outcome: That reads it as a fairness quota, not a strategy — India condemned Suez and was restrained on Hungary because the cases differed on their merits and stakes; equal-opposite condemnation is a posture, not a policy.

c12_ps_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch12.scenario: In a history-debate simulation of the 1969 Presidential election, one side argues every MP who voted for V.V. Giri 'defied the party whip and betrayed Congress discipline.'
c12_ps_ch12.prompt: Does the whip bind a Presidential vote?

options.text: No — the whip governs the government's survival in the legislature, not the electoral college's choice of President; a conscience-vote tradition in Presidential elections gave cover to vote independently, which is exactly the institutional seam Indira Gandhi used to defy the Syndicate.
options.outcome: The chapter's mechanism: the split weaponised two different kinds of party authority — organisational whip versus prime-ministerial appeal — and the Presidential vote was where they collided.

options.text: Yes — a whip is a whip; party members must vote as directed in every election.
options.outcome: That treats all party voting as identical — Presidential elections carry an accepted conscience tradition and don't topple governments, which is why the 'conscience vote' call could split the party legally.

options.text: The vote was a loyalty test — supporting Giri proved the MPs wanted a split.
options.outcome: Indira framed it as conscience, not defection — the split followed the vote, it wasn't declared by it; reading the votes backward as intent confuses the trigger with the outcome.

c12_ps_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch13.scenario: A school exhibit labels Chipko 'anti-development villagers who wanted zero tree-cutting anywhere' — a caption a visiting forest officer disputes.
c12_ps_ch13.prompt: What did the movement actually oppose?

options.text: The displacement of subsistence by market — villagers opposed commercial felling that replaced mixed forests giving fuel, fodder and food with pine monocultures for resin; local cutting for genuine need stayed accepted — it was livelihood justice, not a ban on axes.
options.outcome: The chapter's political economy: 'anti-logging' flattens a fight over whose needs the forest serves — community subsistence versus state-licensed commerce.

options.text: The exhibit is right — hugging trees is absolute protection, no cutting at all.
options.outcome: Chipko itself approved cutting for village needs — its target was commercial extraction that stripped the 'four Fs' locals lived on; absolutism misreads a livelihood claim as a preservation cult.

options.text: It was mainly a women's cultural ritual — symbolic, not economic.
options.outcome: Women led because they collected the biomass the logging destroyed — the gendered participation expressed a material stake, not ceremony; calling it ritual erases the subsistence economics underneath.

c12_ps_ch14.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch14.scenario: An essay argues 'regional movements like the Dravidian one are centrifugal — they weaken national unity and should be constitutionally discouraged.'
c12_ps_ch14.prompt: What does the Dravidian movement's trajectory show instead?

options.text: The opposite — a protest movement channelled into elections, won Tamil Nadu in 1967 through the ballot, and later sat in national coalitions; federal democracy absorbed regional aspiration rather than being threatened by it — the system worked by accommodation, not suppression.
options.outcome: The chapter's civic principle: regional identity became a governing party inside the union — democratic expression of regional demands strengthened integration rather than dissolving it.

options.text: The essay is right — anti-Hindi agitation was secessionist energy that luckily faded.
options.outcome: The movement didn't fade — it converted into electoral power and coalition partnership; what changed was the register, from street to assembly, not the aspiration itself.

options.text: Only half-right — DMK won, but regional parties never mattered at the centre.
options.outcome: Dravidian parties joined national ruling coalitions from the 1990s onward — regional players became load-bearing in Delhi, which is accommodation operating at full national scale.

c12_ps_ch15.title: Use it in the wild
c12_ps_ch15.scenario: In a politics seminar, a student says 'Hindutva is just another word for the Hindu religion — BJP's ideology is basically faith.'
c12_ps_ch15.prompt: What does the distinction between Hindutva and Hinduism say?

options.text: They're different kinds of thing — Hinduism is a diverse religious tradition; Savarkar's Hindutva is a political doctrine defining nationhood by whether India is both fatherland and holy land to you — collapsing them hides the exclusivist nationalist claim inside a familiar word.
options.outcome: The chapter's precision: one is a faith with many practices, the other a test of national belonging — the slide between them is the politics, not a synonym.

options.text: He's right — Hindutva is simply Hindu religious identity expressed politically.
options.outcome: Savarkar's definition is a criterion of nationhood, not worship — 'holy land' filters who counts as fully Indian; a religion describes practices, an ideology adjudicates belonging.

options.text: The difference is only about violence — Hindutva is just Hinduism made militant.
options.outcome: The distinction is definitional, not behavioural — Hindutva is cultural nationalism with a belonging test even in its mildest form; reducing it to militancy misses the exclusion the concept itself encodes.

c12_soc_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch01.scenario: A field-research intern studying a denotified tribe writes that the community's stigma 'comes from their own nomadic culture — an old prejudice with no history.'
c12_soc_ch01.prompt: What does the colonial analysis show instead?

options.text: The state manufactured the category — the 1871 Act branded whole nomadic communities 'criminal by birth,' confined and surveilled them until the label produced its own evidence; denotification repealed the law, but the stigma, police bias and missing documents outlived it.
options.outcome: The chapter's argument: colonialism didn't just label society — it built categories (census jatis, criminal tribes, zamindars) that still structure present life.

options.text: The intern is right — stigma attaches to the lifestyle, so time alone erases it.
options.outcome: That reads a state-made category as cultural fact — the stigma was legislated into being and survived denotification; 'no history' is exactly the amnesia the analysis exists to correct.

options.text: Partially — the law mattered then, but today's stigma is purely economic backwardness.
options.outcome: The poverty and the stigma share the same root — exclusion from land, documents and credit was created by the label; treating present disadvantage as independent severs the colonial thread the chapter traces.

c12_soc_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch02.scenario: A data-lab team sees a country's stats — birth rate 35, death rate 10 — and declares 'permanent population explosion; Malthus was right, food will never catch up.'
c12_soc_ch02.prompt: What does Demographic Transition Theory say they're looking at?

options.text: Stage 2, the transitional explosion — mortality has fallen (medicine, sanitation) while fertility hasn't adjusted yet, so the gap bulges; it's a lag, not a destiny — births follow deaths downward as development continues, which is why the explosion is temporary by definition.
options.outcome: The chapter's mechanism: the bulge is structural lag, not proof of Malthusian doom — the same transition that produced it carries the society toward low-low stability.

options.text: They're right — the gap proves Malthus's arithmetic is finally playing out.
options.outcome: The data is transition, not doom — a low death rate with a high birth rate is the signature of a stage that ends; calling it permanent freezes a moving process at its widest point.

options.text: It's Stage 1 — high births plus any deaths means the old stagnant pattern.
options.outcome: Stage 1 needs a HIGH death rate near the birth rate — 35 against 10 is the mortality-collapse signature of Stage 2; misreading the death rate flips the diagnosis.

c12_soc_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch03.scenario: A sociology student watching her own family insists on 'same-caste matches only' asks why the elders treat inter-caste marriage as a threat to 'everything', not just a preference.
c12_soc_ch03.prompt: Which pillar of the caste system explains the panic?

options.text: Endogamy is the keystone — caste-bound marriage keeps the purity-pollution hierarchy and the birth-to-occupation link intact; mixed marriage produces children whose ritual status and inherited role can't be fixed, which is why a 'preference' polices itself like a load-bearing wall.
options.outcome: The chapter's architecture: the three pillars interlock — endogamy doesn't preserve 'culture,' it preserves the closed boundaries the whole stratification system needs to reproduce.

options.text: It's just hierarchy — elders want to protect status, and marriage is where status shows.
options.outcome: Hierarchy names the ranking, not the mechanism that keeps it — the ranking survives only because endogamy seals it; status anxiety is the symptom, boundary-closure is the load.

options.text: It's occupational — they fear losing hereditary trades more than matches.
options.outcome: Occupation is a pillar, but the elders aren't guarding a trade — they're guarding the boundary; endogamy is the 'key' precisely because it's what keeps both rank and occupation assignable by birth.

c12_soc_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch04.scenario: A startup proposes 'digitising' a tribal weekly haat — replace it with a delivery app 'because a market is just buyers, sellers and price discovery; the rest is noise.'
c12_soc_ch04.prompt: What would embeddedness analysis warn them they're deleting?

options.text: The social structure that makes the market work — the haat is constituted by caste, kinship, ritual and state wage flows: who trades with whom, who extends credit, what gets trusted; strip those relations and you don't streamline the market, you dissolve the institution that was running it.
options.outcome: The chapter's Polanyi point: markets aren't price-machines with social decoration — the relations ARE the mechanism; 'the rest is noise' deletes the load-bearing parts.

options.text: Nothing — the app replicates transactions, which is all a market is.
options.outcome: That assumes the economic view the chapter disputes — trust, credit and access in the haat run on caste and kin networks; an app can't transact what only those relations make possible.

options.text: Only the gossip and festivals — the trade part transfers cleanly.
options.outcome: The 'extras' are the infrastructure — kinship decides creditworthiness, ritual timing brings the crowd, caste position sets the terms; separating 'trade' from 'social' is the analytical error, not a clean cut.

c12_soc_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch05.scenario: A landlord refuses a student tenant saying 'people from that community are trouble — I had a bad experience once, so this isn't prejudice, it's pattern recognition.'
c12_soc_ch05.prompt: How do the three concepts map onto this refusal?

options.text: All three at once — 'they're trouble' is the stereotype, the hostile pre-judgment of this applicant is prejudice, and the refusal is discrimination; one past incident doesn't make it evidence — prejudice is defined by resisting counter-evidence and generalising a group onto an individual.
options.outcome: The chapter's triad: cognition (fixed group trait), attitude (pre-judgment), behaviour (denial) — 'experience' is the rationalisation prejudice wears, not an exemption from it.

options.text: He's right — real experience converts prejudice into reasonable caution.
options.outcome: Prejudice is judged by what it does, not what it cites — applying one incident to every member of a group is the generalisation mechanism itself; experience is the story the stereotype tells.

options.text: Only discrimination occurred — the thought and the feeling don't count until the law is broken.
options.outcome: The concepts mark the chain, not just the endpoint — the stereotype and the prejudice are what produced the refusal; treating only the act ignores how exclusion is manufactured upstream.

c12_soc_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch06.scenario: A roommate shrugs at a 'locals only' job drive: 'Just say you're from here — community is like a club membership; you join whichever fits.'
c12_soc_ch06.prompt: What does the ascriptive/achieved distinction say about that advice?

options.text: It fails — community identity is ascriptive: mother tongue and region are assigned at birth, unconditional and unearned, and others will keep identifying you by them no matter what you claim or learn; achieved identities are the ones you can adopt.
options.outcome: The chapter's split: 'what we are' versus 'what we become' — fluency and food can be achieved, but the markers the nativist test checks can't be switched on demand.

options.text: The roommate is right — twenty years of living somewhere makes you a local, so identity is flexible.
options.outcome: Assimilation is achieved, belonging is ascribed — the nativist criterion reads mother tongue, not years of residence; adapting your habits doesn't rewrite the marker they're testing.

options.text: It's about confidence — identity is whatever you identify as, so self-declaration settles it.
options.outcome: Self-declaration doesn't control others' ascription — the chapter's point is that community markers stick even when disowned; the drive's test is imposed, not chosen.

c12_soc_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch07.scenario: A student's project proposal wants to study the unwritten seating rules of the school canteen — who sits where and why — using a 200-person questionnaire: 'big sample, scientifically solid.'
c12_soc_ch07.prompt: Is the survey the right method for this question?

options.text: No — the phenomenon is implicit norms people may not even notice they follow; observation records actual behaviour without relying on respondents' self-report; a questionnaire asks them to articulate rules that are unwritten precisely because they're never spoken.
options.outcome: The chapter's matching logic: method follows the nature of the phenomenon, not the size of the sample — implicit practice calls for watching, not asking.

options.text: Yes — more respondents always means better data, whatever the topic.
options.outcome: Breadth doesn't fix blindness — 200 answers about rules respondents can't perceive are 200 guesses; the strength of a survey is standardised opinions, and this question has none to standardise.

options.text: Use interviews instead — deep conversation will surface the unwritten rules.
options.outcome: Interviews still depend on respondents verbalising what they may never have consciously registered — the method-fit issue is awareness, not depth; watching behaviour bypasses the reporting problem entirely.

c12_soc_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch08.scenario: A debate speech argues 'colonialism modernised India — railways, ports and cities like Bombay prove the British developed the country.'
c12_soc_ch08.prompt: What does colonial capitalism analysis say those ports and rails were for?

options.text: Extraction infrastructure — ports linked the Indian periphery to the British core for raw-material export and manufactured-goods import, which is why Bombay grew while Surat and Dhaka declined; the same industrialisation that built Britain's mills dismantled India's through one-way tariff policy.
options.outcome: The chapter's reframing: 'modern' features were engineered to serve British accumulation — judging them as development mistakes the function for the intent.

options.text: The speech stands — railways move people and goods, so they developed India regardless of motive.
options.outcome: Function followed extraction — the routes ran to ports, not inland markets; the paradox the chapter names is that the same process modernised Britain and deindustrialised India.

options.text: Both happened — colonialism just modernised and exploited equally, a wash.
options.outcome: The two weren't parallel effects — the extraction IS what produced the distorted shape: artisan collapse, cash-crop forcing, port enclaves; 'equal and opposite' reads a one-directional restructuring as a balanced ledger.

c12_soc_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch09.scenario: A village community that prospered from a cooperative dairy adopts vegetarianism, Sanskritised rituals and new surnames, announcing 'we've ended caste for ourselves — status achieved.'
c12_soc_ch09.prompt: What does Sanskritisation say about this claim?

options.text: It's positional mobility, not structural change — emulating the locally dominant caste's customs may raise this group's rank, but it operates inside the hierarchy it borrows from: the ladder stays, the group climbs a rung; 'ending caste' would be abolishing the ranking itself.
options.outcome: The chapter's critique: Sanskritisation changes who occupies a position, never the system of positions — success within caste is not the end of caste.

options.text: The claim stands — adopting higher-caste ways makes you higher-caste, dissolving the boundary.
options.outcome: The emulation presumes the hierarchy it's climbing — the new practices are valued because they mark rank; the Kumud Pawade lesson is that the community's caste identity persists despite cultural adoption.

options.text: It only counts if the model is Brahmins — copying a dominant non-Brahmin caste isn't Sanskritisation.
options.outcome: The reference is the locally dominant caste, not Brahmins always — Srinivas's de-Sanskritisation covers lower groups adopting non-Sanskritic dominant-caste ways; the mechanism is dominance-following, not Brahmin-following.

c12_soc_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch10.scenario: In a mock parliament, a member moves an amendment abolishing judicial review, arguing 'Article 368 lets Parliament amend anything — majority rules the Constitution.'
c12_soc_ch10.prompt: Does the Basic Structure Doctrine allow that?

options.text: No — Kesavananda Bharati capped Article 368: core features — judicial review, democracy, secularism, separation of powers, federalism — sit beyond amendment; a temporary majority can rewrite clauses but not the Constitution's soul, and abolishing review attacks the core directly.
options.outcome: The chapter's safeguard: amending power is wide but not sovereign — the doctrine exists precisely to stop a numerical majority from rewriting the architecture it governs within.

options.text: Yes — Article 368's text gives Parliament unlimited amending power.
options.outcome: That was the pre-1973 reading — Kesavananda established that the power to amend is not the power to destroy; 'anything' was judicially fenced at the basic features.

options.text: It's valid if two-thirds plus state ratification agree — procedure cures substance.
options.outcome: The doctrine limits substance regardless of procedure — even a perfect special majority can't remove a basic feature; the threshold governs amendments, not the unamendable core.

c12_soc_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch11.scenario: A paralegal intern in a 1960s-set case file finds a landlord legally kept 170 surplus acres — benami transfers to relatives, 'personal cultivation' claims, paper partitions — and concludes 'land reform simply never happened.'
c12_soc_ch11.prompt: What does the implementation-gap analysis say?

options.text: The law happened, the loopholes absorbed it — ceilings counted paper families not effective control, so benami deeds, khudkasht evictions and fictitious splits let dominant-caste landowners keep command; zamindari abolition worked better precisely because it cut one recorded legal layer instead of restructuring village power.
options.outcome: The chapter's lesson: reform-on-paper versus power-on-ground — evasion was systematic and socially sanctioned where the dominant caste ran the local administration meant to implement it.

options.text: She's right — if the land stayed put, there was no reform at all.
options.outcome: That erases zamindari abolition, which did remove an entire intermediary class — the verdict isn't 'nothing happened' but that each pillar met a different wall of legal fiction and local power.

options.text: The fault was just poor drafting — tighter wording alone would have delivered the land.
options.outcome: Drafting was only half the constraint — identifying oral tenancies and concealed surplus needed bureaucratic penetration and political will that dominant-caste-controlled administration wouldn't supply; better text doesn't move power.

c12_soc_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch12.scenario: A debate-team member argues 'industrialisation levelled society — nobody asks your caste on a metro or a factory floor, so equality followed the machine.'
c12_soc_ch12.prompt: What do the classical sociologists add to that claim?

options.text: Half the picture — public anonymity did weaken ritual markers in shared spaces, but the factory also built a detailed division of labour and new class lines; Marx's alienation names the worker cut off from product, process and peers — equality in the queue, inequality on the payslip.
options.outcome: The chapter's balance: industrial society trades caste visibility for economic stratification — 'nobody asks your caste' is real, and so is the income gap that grew alongside it.

options.text: He's right — machines replaced birth with merit, so hierarchy ended.
options.outcome: Merit arrived inside a new hierarchy — bourgeoisie and proletariat replaced estates; anonymous work relations didn't dissolve rank, they rebuilt it on capital.

options.text: The opposite — industrialisation only deepened every old hierarchy unchanged.
options.outcome: The shift was real too — Durkheim's move from mechanical to organic solidarity and anonymous public spaces did change how people relate; 'nothing changed' misses the urbanisation and solidarity shift as much as the equality claim misses the class structure.

c12_soc_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch13.scenario: An essay claims 'globalisation is just the latest word for something eternal — Silk Road, empire, internet, all the same process.'
c12_soc_ch13.prompt: What does the phased history of globalisation say to that?

options.text: The phases differ in kind, not just degree — pre-colonial trade was voluntary exchange, colonial integration was coerced subordination built for extraction, post-war was state-gated import-substitution, and post-1991 is ICT-speed financial interconnection; calling them one process flattens who connected, on whose terms.
options.outcome: The chapter's timeline: each phase built different structures — the same word covers connection by caravan, conquest, container and fibre, and those are not the same phenomenon.

options.text: The essay is right — connection is connection, whatever the century.
options.outcome: Connection erases the coercion — colonial integration moved indentured labour and raw material under force for another economy's profit; equating that with Silk Road exchange confuses linkage with subordination.

options.text: The real break is only the internet — everything before 1991 was one phase.
options.outcome: That merges the colonial and post-war phases, which ran opposite designs — one forced open India's markets for extraction, the other gated them for self-development; ICT speed isn't the only axis that changed.

c12_soc_ch14.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch14.scenario: A media-studies student credits the 1990s explosion of Hindi and Telugu dailies purely to 'rising literacy — more readers, more papers, simple.'
c12_soc_ch14.prompt: What did the language-paper revolution actually run on?

options.text: Organisational innovation, not just literacy — district-specific editions and local ad networks served village-level demand the city-centric English press ignored; the same printing technology that once carried nationalist mobilisation now ran on market segmentation — the press is shaped by who owns it and whom it sells to.
options.outcome: The chapter's throughline: each phase of the press answers a different master — colonial censorship, developmental state, market discipline — and 'more readers' alone explains none of the editions' local engineering.

options.text: He's right — demand side explains it fully; supply just follows readers.
options.outcome: Literacy created possible readers, not the product — the district-daily format, hyper-local content and rural advertiser networks had to be invented; demand without that supply-side redesign produced nothing.

options.text: The papers grew because censorship ended — free press naturally expands.
options.outcome: The post-1991 constraint isn't censorship but market discipline — the expansion and the infotainment tilt share one driver; 'freedom' explains neither the format nor the commercialisation that came with it.

c12_soc_ch15.title: Use it in the wild
c12_soc_ch15.scenario: A headline calls a tribal movement blocking a mining lease 'a revolutionary uprising'; a classmate counters 'it's reformist — they cite the Forest Rights Act.'
c12_soc_ch15.prompt: Where does the typology place it?

options.text: Primarily resistance — the core aim is defensive: stop dispossession, protect customary land and identity; the legal demands are reformist instruments in service of survival, but neither headline's 'revolutionary' (no new order sought) nor a pure 'reform' label captures the dominant defence-of-rights orientation.
options.outcome: The chapter's test is goal and scope, not tactics or outcomes — defending what exists isn't overthrowing what exists, even when the tools are legal ones.

options.text: The headline is right — confrontation with the state makes it revolutionary.
options.outcome: Confrontation isn't revolution — revolutionary movements seek to transform the structure of power itself; resisting a lease to keep existing rights is the textbook resistance case, however forceful the stand.

options.text: The classmate is right — using a statute makes it purely reformist.
options.outcome: Method doesn't settle type — a movement can invoke a law while its driving aim is survival-level defence of land; intent outweighs instruments, and here the intent is holding ground, not tweaking policy.
